class NodeType(type):
    """A metaclass for nodes that handles the field and attribute
    inheritance.  fields and attributes from the parent class are
    automatically forwarded to the child."""

    def __new__(mcs, name, bases, d):  # type: ignore
        for attr in "fields", "attributes":
            storage: t.List[t.Tuple[str, ...]] = []
            storage.extend(getattr(bases[0] if bases else object, attr, ()))
            storage.extend(d.get(attr, ()))
            assert len(bases) <= 1, "multiple inheritance not allowed"
            assert len(storage) == len(set(storage)), "layout conflict"
            d[attr] = tuple(storage)
        d.setdefault("abstract", False)
        return type.__new__(mcs, name, bases, d)

patterns.rationale: Storing compiled field metadata as a class-level constant means field introspection (fields(), has(), asdict()) is O(1) — it reads a pre-computed tuple, not __annotations__ or __init__ signature. The named-property tuple subclass allows both index access (fields(Cls)[0]) and name access (fields(Cls).x), matching how users naturally think about fields. The metadata is computed once at decoration time, not on every introspection call.

patterns.rationale: Request bodies can come from files, streams, strings, or custom iterables — all need .read(). Rather than defining an ABC and requiring inheritance (which excludes third-party file-like objects), a Protocol accepts any object with the right method. This is the modern Python equivalent of the AuthBase __call__ pattern — structural typing via Protocol instead of nominal typing via ABC. The runtime_checkable flag allows defensive isinstance() checks where needed. [Merged from P364: Allows Pillow to accept numpy arrays, Arrow tables, or any future array format without hard dependencies. The Protocol describes the duck-typed interface — any object with __array_interface__ qualifies. This is the type-safe way to accept 'anything numpy-like' without importing numpy.]

patterns.name: Code generation via string templating + eval
patterns.description: Instead of dynamically building methods via closures or descriptors, generate Python source code as strings, compile and eval them at class-definition time. The generated code is registered with linecache for debugger support. This produces real function objects with correct __qualname__, __doc__, and stack traces, not lambdas or wrappers.
patterns.rationale: Generated methods (like __init__, __repr__, __eq__) need to be fast — they're on every hot path. String-generated code compiles to real bytecode with direct attribute access (self.x = value), avoiding the overhead of getattr/setattr loops or generic dispatch. The linecache registration makes the generated code visible to debuggers like PDB, closing the gap between generated and hand-written code. [Merged from P204: Runtime type-checking requires per-callable custom validation logic. Code generation produces O(1) wrappers with zero interpretation overhead — the type-check is baked into the generated code as a single boolean expression, not dispatched at runtime. compile()+exec() is preferred over eval() because compile() allows setting a custom co_filename for debuggability.]

def _linecache_and_compile(script, filename, globs, locals=None):
    locs = {} if locals is None else locals
    count = 1
    base_filename = filename
    while True:
        linecache_tuple = (len(script), None, script.splitlines(True), filename)
        old_val = linecache.cache.setdefault(filename, linecache_tuple)
        if old_val == linecache_tuple:
            break

patterns.name: Builder pattern for class construction with deferred method assembly
patterns.description: A _ClassBuilder object accumulates method-generation snippets (script + globals + attach hook) as tuples in a list. Methods are not applied immediately — they're queued via add_repr(), add_init(), add_eq(), etc. On build_class(), all snippets are concatenated into one script, compiled and evaluated in a single pass, then hooks attach the resulting methods to the class dict.
patterns.rationale: Deferring evaluation to build_class() means all generated methods share a single compile pass and a single set of globals — no per-method compilation overhead. The builder also serves as a configuration object: it decides whether to create a slots class (new type()) or patch the original class, whether to add __setattr__ hooks, whether to cache hash, etc. This separates the 'what methods to generate' decision from the 'how to install them' decision.

patterns.name: Sentinel object for distinguishing 'no value' from None
patterns.description: A dedicated sentinel enum member (NOTHING) used as the default for optional fields where None is a valid user-supplied value. The sentinel is falsy (bool(NOTHING) == False) and has a custom __repr__ returning 'NOTHING'. Type annotation uses Literal[NOTHING] via NothingType.
patterns.rationale: When None is a legitimate value (e.g., a field that can be null), you can't use None as the 'no default provided' marker. A sentinel object distinguishes 'user didn't provide a value' from 'user explicitly passed None'. Making it an enum variant (not a bare object()) gives it a stable identity for pickling and a repr that's meaningful in error messages. [Merged from P267: When None is a semantically valid value (e.g. autoescape=None means disable escaping), a plain default=None is ambiguous — you can't tell if the user explicitly chose None or just didn't pass the argument. A sentinel object is identity-comparable (is _UNSET), has no false-positive collisions, and self-documents intent via its type annotation.]

patterns.name: Converter as field post-processor with arity adaptation
patterns.description: A Converter class wraps a callable and adapts its arity: the underlying function can take 1 arg (value), 2 args (value, instance), or 3 args (value, instance, field). The Converter's __call__ is assigned at construction time as a lambda matching the requested arity, avoiding runtime dispatch. The converter runs after __init__ receives the value but before it's stored on the instance.
patterns.rationale: Different conversion functions need different context: simple ones just transform the value, but some need the instance being constructed (e.g., to compute derived defaults) or the field metadata (e.g., to access type info). Arity adaptation lets users write natural function signatures while the Converter normalizes the call. Assigning __call__ as a lambda at construction time avoids branching on every call — the dispatch is paid once at class definition.

patterns.name: Validator as callable class with custom __repr__
patterns.description: Validators are not plain functions but callable classes (with __call__) that carry their configuration as attributes and provide a custom __repr__ for debugging. Factory functions (instance_of, ge, matches_re) return instances of these validator classes. Validators can be composed via and_() which flattens nested _AndValidator instances.
patterns.rationale: A plain function loses its configuration in error messages and repr — you see '<function instance_of at 0x...>' instead of '<instance_of validator for type int>'. Callable classes carry their config (the type, the threshold, the pattern) and display it in repr. The and_() composer flattens nested compositions to avoid deep wrapper chains: and_(and_(v1, v2), v3) becomes _AndValidator((v1, v2, v3)), not nested wrappers.

patterns.name: Global validation toggle with context manager override
patterns.description: A module-level boolean (_run_validators) controls whether validators execute globally. A context manager (disabled()) saves the current state, disables validation, yields, then restores — enabling selective validation bypass for hot paths or testing without changing field definitions.
patterns.rationale: Validation has a runtime cost. In production hot paths or when loading trusted data, you may want to skip validation entirely. A global toggle + context manager lets you disable validation for a code block without modifying any class or field definition. The context manager ensures the toggle is always restored, even on exceptions.

patterns.name: on_setattr hook pipe for post-construction attribute mutation
patterns.description: After construction, attribute assignment can trigger a pipeline of hooks (convert → validate) via setters.pipe(). Each hook receives (instance, attribute, new_value) and returns the (possibly transformed) value. NO_OP sentinel disables hooks per-attribute. The pipe is composable: a list of setters is auto-wrapped into pipe(*setters).
patterns.rationale: Construction-time validation is common, but post-construction mutation (obj.x = new_value) usually bypasses validators. The on_setattr hook extends the validation/conversion pipeline to every attribute assignment, not just __init__. The pipe composition allows ordering (convert before validate), and NO_OP gives per-field escape hatches without disabling the class-wide policy.

patterns.name: Dual API: legacy aliases bridging to modern defaults
patterns.description: Two parallel APIs coexist: legacy (attr.s, attr.ib) with conservative defaults (slots=False, kw_only=False) and modern (attrs.define, attrs.field) with opinionated defaults (slots=True, weakref_slot=True, kw_only=True). The modern API is implemented as thin wrappers calling the legacy implementation with different defaults. Legacy aliases (s=attributes=attrs, ib=attr=attrib) provide backwards compatibility.
patterns.rationale: Libraries with large user bases cannot break existing APIs. The dual API lets new code adopt better defaults (slots by default, keyword-only args) without forcing migration on existing users. The legacy API stays frozen; the modern API is a pure wrapper — no code duplication, just different default values. The aliases (s, ib) are for historical brevity and are never removed.

patterns.name: evolve() for non-destructive immutable updates
patterns.description: evolve(inst, **changes) creates a new instance of the same class with specified fields overridden. It reads the existing field values via getattr, fills in unchanged fields from the original instance, and constructs a new instance via cls(**changes). Works with both frozen and mutable classes.
patterns.rationale: Frozen (immutable) classes can't be updated in place — but you still need to 'change' a field. evolve() provides a copy-with-changes operation that reads the compiled field metadata (__attrs_attrs__) to know which fields to copy and which to override. This is the functional update pattern: instead of obj.x = new_x, you write evolve(obj, x=new_x), getting a new instance.

patterns.name: Factory wrapper for deferred default computation
patterns.description: A Factory class wraps a callable used as a field default. Instead of evaluating the default at class-definition time (mutable default bug), the factory is called at instantiation time. Supports takes_self=True to pass the partially-initialized instance, enabling computed defaults that depend on other fields.
patterns.rationale: Python's mutable default argument bug (def f(x=[]) means all calls share the same list) also affects class fields. A Factory wrapper defers evaluation to instantiation: each instance gets a fresh value from the factory call. The takes_self option enables inter-field dependencies — a field's default can read other already-set fields on the same instance during __init__.

patterns.name: cmp_using: dynamic type generation for custom comparison operators
patterns.description: cmp_using(eq=fn, lt=fn, ...) dynamically creates a class with __eq__, __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__ methods wrapping user-supplied comparison functions. Uses types.new_class() for class creation and functools.total_ordering to fill missing ordering operators from a minimal set. The resulting class wraps a single 'value' attribute.
patterns.rationale: Sometimes you need custom comparison semantics for a field (e.g., compare paths by resolved string, compare versions by tuple). cmp_using generates a wrapper type with full operator support from minimal user input — you provide eq and one of lt/le/gt/ge, and total_ordering fills the rest. The generated class is a proper type with __slots__, not a closure, so instances are picklable and repr-able.

patterns.name: Recursive serialization with type-dispatched handling
patterns.description: asdict() serializes attrs instances to dicts by dispatching on the value's type: atomic types (int, str, bool, None, etc.) are passed through; attrs instances recurse via asdict(); tuples/lists/sets map over elements; dicts serialize both keys and values. A value_serializer hook runs on every value after filtering. retain_collection_types controls whether to preserve exact container types or normalize to list.
patterns.rationale: Serialization needs to handle arbitrarily nested data structures — an attrs instance may contain other attrs instances, lists of attrs instances, dicts with attrs values, etc. Type-dispatched recursion handles this: each value type has a specific serialization strategy, and the function recurses into containers. The value_serializer hook provides a single interception point for custom serialization (e.g., datetime → ISO string) without subclassing or monkey-patching.

patterns.name: Auto-detect existing dunder methods to skip generation
patterns.description: When auto_detect=True, the decorator checks whether the class already defines __eq__, __repr__, __init__, etc. (via _has_own_attribute) and skips generating those methods. This lets users selectively override specific dunders while letting attrs generate the rest, without explicitly setting eq=False, repr=False for each one.
patterns.rationale: Without auto_detect, users must remember to pass eq=False when they write a custom __eq__, or attrs silently overwrites it. auto_detect makes the decorator intelligent: it inspects the class for existing implementations and only generates what's missing. This reduces configuration boilerplate and prevents accidental overwrites of user-provided methods.

patterns.name: Thread-local proxy for global access to current instance
patterns.description: A Proxy object wraps a thread-local getter function. Accessing any attribute on the proxy calls the getter to retrieve the current instance for this thread, then forwards the attribute access. This provides global access to the 'current' app/task without passing it explicitly, while remaining thread-safe.
patterns.rationale: Distributed systems need a 'current context' concept (current app, current task) accessible from any code path without explicit parameter passing. Thread-local storage ensures each thread sees its own instance. The proxy pattern makes this transparent — `current_app.conf` looks like a normal attribute access but resolves dynamically at call time.

patterns.name: PromiseProxy: lazy one-time evaluation proxy
patterns.description: A Proxy subclass that evaluates its target exactly once on first access, then caches the result. Subsequent accesses return the cached object. Supports a `__then__` method to queue callbacks that fire after evaluation. The proxy implements all dunder methods (__getattr__, __setattr__, __call__, __getitem__, arithmetic operators, etc.) by forwarding to `_get_current_object()`, which either returns the cached `__thing` or triggers `__evaluate__()`.
patterns.rationale: Task registration via `@app.task` decorator must be deferred until the app is fully configured (broker URL, backend, etc. may be set later). The PromiseProxy lets the decorator return an object that looks and acts like a task immediately, but only creates the actual task class when first accessed. This avoids import-time side effects while providing a transparent API — `my_task.delay()` works whether the task is already created or lazily deferred.

patterns.name: Blueprint with bootstep DAG for component lifecycle
patterns.description: A Blueprint holds a set of Step classes. Each Step declares `requires` (dependencies on other steps). The Blueprint builds a DependencyGraph from these declarations, topologically sorts them, and applies them in order. Steps have a lifecycle: `create → include → start → stop → close → terminate`. The Blueprint manages state transitions (RUN, CLOSE, TERMINATE) and propagates lifecycle calls to all steps in order (forward for start, reverse for stop).
patterns.rationale: A distributed worker has many components (connection, consumer, heart, gossip, events, control, etc.) that must start and stop in dependency order. Hardcoding the order is fragile. By declaring dependencies on each Step and topologically sorting at apply time, the system self-orders and is extensible — new steps declare their dependencies and the graph re-sorts automatically.

patterns.name: StepType metaclass for automatic naming and identification
patterns.description: A metaclass that automatically sets `__qualname__` and `name` attributes on class creation. The name is derived from `__module__.__name__` unless explicitly overridden. This provides a stable, unique identifier for each class without manual declaration, usable as a registry key.
patterns.rationale: Blueprint steps need to be referenced by name (for dependency resolution, logging, graph visualization). Forcing developers to manually set `name` on every step class is error-prone. The metaclass generates a unique name from the class's module and name, which is stable across pickle/unpickle cycles and human-readable in logs.

patterns.name: Signal: observer pattern with weak references and robust dispatch
patterns.description: A Signal object maintains a list of receiver callables. `connect()` registers receivers with optional `dispatch_uid` for dedup, `weak` references for automatic cleanup, and `sender` filtering. `send()` calls all live receivers, catching exceptions per-receiver and returning `(receiver, response_or_exception)` pairs. Dead weak references are cleaned lazily. Supports `retry` mode that wraps receivers with `retry_over_time` for transient failures.
patterns.rationale: A distributed task system emits events at many lifecycle points (task received, started, succeeded, failed, retried, revoked). Extensions need to hook into these events without modifying core code. The observer pattern decouples event emission from handling. Weak references prevent memory leaks when handlers are garbage collected. Per-receiver exception isolation prevents one broken handler from crashing the entire dispatch chain. [Merged from P307: GUI callbacks are a major source of memory leaks when bound methods hold references. Weakrefs allow the receiver to be GC'd. Exception isolation prevents one bad callback from crashing the entire event dispatch. The signal filter prevents typos from silently creating dead callbacks.]

patterns.name: Signature as serializable dict subclass with operator composition
patterns.description: A workflow primitive that inherits from `dict` for serialization compatibility. Stores task name, args, kwargs, and options as dict keys. Implements `__or__` for chaining (task | task → chain), `__call__` for execution, `clone()` for deep copy, `freeze()` for pre-assigning IDs without execution. A `TYPES` registry on the base class allows subclass registration via a class decorator, enabling polymorphic deserialization from dict.
patterns.rationale: Task workflows must be composable (chain, group, chord), serializable (sent over the wire to brokers), and cloneable (for retries and ETA scheduling). Inheriting from dict makes the signature natively serializable by any JSON/pickle serializer, without a custom encoder. Operator overloading (`|` for chaining) provides an ergonomic DSL: `add.s(2, 2) | add.s(4) | add.s(8)`. The TYPES registry enables polymorphic deserialization: a dict with `subtask_type: 'group'` reconstructs as a `group` instance.

patterns.name: Backend capability flags as class-level attributes
patterns.description: A base Backend class declares boolean capability flags as class attributes: `supports_native_join`, `supports_autoexpire`, `persistent`. Subclasses (Redis, Database, RPC, etc.) override these to declare what they support. Callers check `backend.supports_native_join` instead of `isinstance(backend, RedisBackend)`, enabling capability-based dispatch without coupling to concrete types.
patterns.rationale: Different result backends (Redis, database, S3, RPC, filesystem) have wildly different capabilities. Some support native join (Redis pipelining), some auto-expire results (TTL), some are persistent. Using isinstance checks creates tight coupling and makes adding new backends require modifying all check sites. Class-level capability flags shift the contract to 'what can you do' rather than 'what are you', following the Liskov substitution principle. [Merged from P273: Streaming vs buffering is a per-handler capability, not a per-request choice. Using a decorator to set a class flag is cleaner than checking for the presence of a data_received method (which might exist for other reasons) or requiring inheritance from a base class. The flag is checked once at _execute() entry, routing the request through the streaming path. This is a Python-specific alternative to interfaces/traits for declaring capabilities.]

patterns.name: Autoretry as transparent run-method wrapping
patterns.description: A function `add_autoretry_behaviour(task)` wraps the task's `run` method with a try/except that catches specified exception types (`autoretry_for`), excludes others (`dont_autoretry_for`), and calls `task.retry()` with exponential backoff and jitter. The original `run` is preserved as `_orig_run`. The wrapper is invisible to callers — `task.run(*args)` still works, but now retries automatically on configured exceptions.
patterns.rationale: Retry logic is a cross-cutting concern that should not pollute task business logic. Manually writing try/except/retry in every task body is repetitive and error-prone. By wrapping `run` at registration time, retry behavior is declared via decorator options (`@app.task(autoretry_for=(ConnectionError,), retry_backoff=True)`) and applied transparently. The `_orig_run` preservation allows unwrapping if needed.

patterns.name: Deferred registration via app-finalize callbacks
patterns.description: A module-level function decorated with `@connect_on_app_finalize` is added to a global set of callbacks. When any Celery app is finalized, all callbacks are invoked with the app instance. This allows built-in tasks and extensions to register themselves lazily — only when an app actually exists and is configured — rather than at import time.
patterns.rationale: Built-in tasks (backend_cleanup, chord_unlock, accumulate) need to be registered on every app instance, but the app may not exist at import time. Registering at import time would require a global app singleton. Instead, the callback set is populated at import time (cheap — just adds to a set), and the actual task creation happens when an app is finalized (has broker, backend, config). This enables multi-app scenarios where different apps have different built-in task configurations.

    for callback in callbacks:

patterns.name: PendingConfiguration: lazy config evaluation triggered by first access
patterns.description: A UserDict subclass that holds raw config data and a callback. It stores key-value pairs but defers full configuration loading until any key is accessed via the `data` cached_property, which triggers the callback to produce the final configuration. This allows `app.conf` to be set freely before `config_from_object()` is called, with all settings merged and finalized on first read.
patterns.rationale: Celery apps often have configuration set in multiple stages: constructor kwargs → config_from_object → config_from_cmdline → add_defaults. Reading config too early (before all sources are configured) produces incomplete settings. PendingConfiguration defers the merge until first actual read, ensuring all sources have been registered. The callback approach keeps the lazy logic in one place rather than scattering `if self._conf is None` checks throughout.

patterns.name: Registry as dict subclass with __missing__ guard
patterns.description: A registry that inherits from `dict` and overrides `__missing__` to raise a custom NotRegistered error when an unregistered key is accessed. Registration accepts either a class (auto-instantiated) or an instance. The registry enforces that registered items have a `name` attribute used as the key.
patterns.rationale: Using dict as the base class provides free serialization, iteration, and standard dict operations. The `__missing__` override turns silent KeyError into a meaningful domain error (NotRegistered) that users can catch. Auto-instantiation of classes simplifies registration: `registry.register(MyTaskClass)` instead of `registry.register(MyTaskClass())`.

patterns.name: Option type with type coercion for config defaults
patterns.description: An Option class declares each config setting's default value, type (string/int/float/bool/dict/tuple/list), and backward-compatibility aliases. A `to_python()` method coerces string values from environment variables and command-line arguments to the correct Python type. Without type coercion, `broker_heartbeat=120` from a config file and `broker_heartbeat='120'` from an env var behave differently (int vs str comparison). The Option class centralizes type information and coercion logic. The old/new namespace mapping enables backward compatibility without polluting the config interface.

patterns.name: Sans-IO architecture: protocol-agnostic core + IO adapter subclass
patterns.description: Split the application into a sans-IO base class (sansio/app.py) that contains all protocol-agnostic logic (routing, config, error handlers, template setup), and a concrete subclass (app.py) that adds WSGI/async IO. The base class can be reused by alternative server interfaces (ASGI, test harnesses) without duplicating routing or config logic.
patterns.rationale: Decouples request processing logic from transport protocol. The same app configuration, URL routing, and error handling work regardless of whether the server is WSGI, ASGI, or a test client. This avoids forking the entire framework for each server interface, and allows testing core behavior without HTTP overhead.

    provides a WSGI implementation at :cls:`werkzeug.wrappers.Request`.
    """

patterns.name: Blueprint as deferred registration with setup state
patterns.description: A Blueprint records registration functions (route handlers, error handlers, before/after request hooks) as deferred callbacks at decoration time. When registered on an app, a BlueprintSetupState object is created carrying the app reference, URL prefix, subdomain, and options. Each deferred function is replayed against the state, transferring registrations to the app. Blueprints can nest (register_blueprint on a Blueprint) and be registered multiple times with different names.
patterns.rationale: Allows defining application functionality (routes, handlers) without an app instance — modules can declare their routes independently and be composed later. The deferred callback + setup state pattern decouples definition time from registration time, enabling URL prefixing, name spacing, and conditional registration without modifying the original module.

patterns.name: ContextVar + LocalProxy for implicit context access
patterns.description: Per-request/per-app state is stored in ContextVar objects (not thread-locals). Module-level LocalProxy instances read from these ContextVars, providing implicit access to current_app, request, session, g without passing them as parameters. The proxy raises a descriptive error when accessed outside a context.
patterns.rationale: View functions and helpers access request/app state without explicit parameter passing, keeping signatures clean. ContextVar (over thread-local) is async-safe — works correctly with asyncio, greenlets, and concurrent requests. The LocalProxy transparently delegates attribute access, so `request.json` works exactly as if request were a local variable.

patterns.name: Context manager as request/app lifecycle boundary
patterns.description: AppContext and RequestContext implement __enter__/__exit__ to manage setup and teardown. push() binds the context to the current ContextVar, pop() runs teardown handlers and resets the token. The request lifecycle is: ctx.push() → dispatch → ctx.pop(error), wrapped in try/finally. Teardown functions always run, even on error.
patterns.rationale: Context managers ensure cleanup (teardown handlers, DB disconnection) runs regardless of success or failure. The try/finally in wsgi_app guarantees ctx.pop() even on unhandled exceptions. This is the pipeline boundary between HTTP transport and application logic — everything inside is per-request scoped.

occurrences.snippet:
def __enter__(self) -> Self:
    self._depth += 1
    push_context(self)
    return self

def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, tb) -> bool | None:
    self._depth -= 1
    exit_result: bool | None = None
    if self._depth == 0:
        exit_result = self._close_with_exception_info(exc_type, exc_value, tb)
    pop_context()
    return exit_result

async def __aenter__(self) -> "BaseConnector":
    return self

async def __aexit__(self, exc_type=None, exc_value=None, exc_traceback=None) -> None:
    await self.close()

patterns.name: Config as dict subclass with typed attribute descriptors
patterns.description: Config subclasses dict directly, adding from_object(), from_pyfile(), from_file(), from_mapping(), from_prefixed_env(), get_namespace(). ConfigAttribute is a Generic[T] descriptor that forwards attribute access to config[key], with optional get_converter for type coercion. Uppercase-only convention filters config keys.
patterns.rationale: Config is both a dict (for arbitrary key access) and a typed object (for documented attributes with type conversion). The uppercase-only convention prevents accidental mixing of config values with module internals. from_object/from_file methods support multiple config sources (Python files, objects, env vars, JSON/TOML) through a uniform load interface. ConfigAttribute descriptors let `app.debug` transparently read `app.config['DEBUG']` with type safety.

patterns.name: Error handler lookup by MRO + scope cascade
patterns.description: Error handlers are registered in a nested dict: {scope: {code: {exception_class: handler}}}. Lookup walks the exception's MRO to find the most specific handler, cascading through blueprint scope → app scope, and HTTP code → generic. This allows registering handlers at different granularities: per-blueprint 404, app-wide DatabaseError, etc.
patterns.rationale: Flexible error handling without a class hierarchy. A single registration system handles both HTTP status codes (404, 500) and arbitrary exception types (DatabaseError, ValidationError). MRO walk means registering a handler for HTTPException catches all subclasses. Blueprint scoping allows modules to handle their own errors without affecting the rest of the app. [Merged from P380: Enables registering a single handler for a base exception class (e.g. ValueError) that catches all subclasses automatically. No need to register every possible subclass. The MRO walk ensures the most specific handler is found first.] [Merged from P381: HTTP errors can be categorized by either status code (404, 500) or exception type (ValueError, KeyError). Two registries let users register handlers in whichever dimension is natural for their error. HTTPException bridges both: it carries a status code AND is an exception class.]

patterns.name: JSONProvider as swappable serialization strategy
patterns.description: JSON operations are abstracted behind a JSONProvider base class with dumps/loads/response methods. The app holds a provider instance (app.json), and the default (DefaultJSONProvider) uses stdlib json. Subclassing the provider and setting json_provider_class swaps the entire JSON stack (e.g., to use orjson) without touching app code. The provider holds a weakref to the app, not a strong reference.
patterns.rationale: Decouples JSON serialization from the application framework. Different deployments can use different JSON libraries (stdlib json, orjson, ujson) without forking Flask. The weakref prevents reference cycles between provider and app. Class-level attribute (json_provider_class) makes the strategy pluggable at class definition time, while instance attribute (app.json) allows runtime swapping.

patterns.name: Pluggable class attributes for framework extension points
patterns.description: The App class declares overridable class attributes (request_class, response_class, session_interface, json_provider_class, jinja_environment, url_map_class, url_rule_class, test_client_class) that serve as extension points. Subclassing Flask and overriding these attributes customizes behavior without rewriting methods. This is a declarative plugin system: set the class, get the behavior.
patterns.rationale: Class attributes are the simplest possible extension point — no registry, no decorator, no hook. Just subclass and set an attribute. This is sufficient for most customization needs (custom Request class, custom JSON provider, custom session backend) and avoids the complexity of a full plugin system for the common case. The default class attributes also serve as documentation of what's pluggable.

patterns.name: setupmethod guard: fail-fast on post-registration modification
patterns.description: A decorator (@setupmethod) wraps every method that registers routes, handlers, or hooks. It calls _check_setup_finished() which raises AssertionError if the app/blueprint has already been registered. This prevents silent data loss: routes added after registration wouldn't be in the URL map, but without the guard the app would start without error.
patterns.rationale: Registration order bugs are silent and hard to debug. A route added after register_blueprint() is called would be stored on the blueprint but never transferred to the app's URL map. The guard makes this a loud failure at the point of the mistake, not a 404 in production. The decorator pattern keeps the guard logic in one place and applies it uniformly to all registration methods.

patterns.name: Middleware via wsgi_app attribute swap
patterns.description: Instead of wrapping the app object (app = MyMiddleware(app)), Flask recommends wrapping app.wsgi_app: app.wsgi_app = MyMiddleware(app.wsgi_app). The __call__ method delegates to self.wsgi_app, so middleware is applied without losing the reference to the app object for route registration, config access, etc.
patterns.rationale: Wrapping the app object itself (app = Middleware(app)) makes the original app unreachable — you can't add routes or access config through the wrapper. The wsgi_app attribute swap keeps the app object as the primary interface while allowing the WSGI callable to be layered. This is a clean separation: the app object is for configuration, wsgi_app is for serving.

patterns.name: MethodView: __init_subclass__ for automatic method dispatch
patterns.description: MethodView uses __init_subclass__ to scan the class for HTTP method names (get, post, put, etc.) and automatically populate the methods attribute. A class-based view dispatches by HTTP method to instance methods. init_every_request controls whether a new instance is created per request or shared.
patterns.rationale: REST endpoints naturally map to HTTP methods. __init_subclass__ eliminates the boilerplate of manually listing methods — defining `def get(self)` automatically registers GET. The init_every_request flag (default True, set False for stateless views) is a performance optimization: a single instance handles all requests when no per-request state is needed on self. [Merged from P251: Eliminates boilerplate registration — defining a Message subclass automatically creates the handler name convention. The @on decorator provides selector-based routing (match by CSS selector) without a separate registration call. Metaclass collection at class-definition time means dispatch is O(1) lookup at runtime, not reflection per-message.]

patterns.name: ensure_sync: sync/async transparent bridge
patterns.description: The app.ensure_sync(func) method returns func as-is if it's a plain def, or wraps it with async_to_sync if it's async def. Every call site that invokes user-provided callbacks (view functions, before_request, after_request, teardown) routes through ensure_sync. Override this single method to change how async code is run.
patterns.rationale: Flask supports both sync and async view functions transparently. Instead of duplicating the entire request pipeline for sync/async (like httpx does for Client/AsyncClient), Flask wraps async functions at the call site. The overhead is one iscoroutinefunction() check per call. Overriding ensure_sync allows alternative async runtimes (e.g., using gevent instead of asyncio).

patterns.name: TypedDict-style protocol aliases for callback contracts
patterns.description: Framework callback signatures are defined as type aliases in a dedicated typing.py module using Union of Callable variants (sync and async). These aliases (RouteCallable, BeforeRequestCallable, AfterRequestCallable, ErrorHandlerCallable, etc.) are used throughout the codebase as parameter types, providing documentation and type-checking without runtime overhead.
patterns.rationale: Callback contracts are the framework's API surface — they define what users must provide. Type aliases make these contracts explicit and machine-checkable. The Union of sync/async variants documents that both are accepted. Centralizing in typing.py gives users one file to read for the full callback API, and allows the aliases to evolve (e.g., adding async support) without touching call sites.

patterns.name: ImmutableDict for framework defaults
patterns.description: Framework-wide default configurations and options use ImmutableDict (from werkzeug), a dict subclass that raises TypeError on mutation. Class-level defaults like default_config are ImmutableDict, signaling that these are read-only templates to be copied, not mutated in place.
patterns.rationale: Class attributes are shared across all instances. If default_config were a regular dict, mutating it in one instance would affect all others. ImmutableDict prevents this at the language level — the only way to customize config is to copy and modify, which is the correct pattern. It also signals intent to readers: this value is a specification, not a working copy.

patterns.name: Scaffold base class: shared registration interface for app and blueprint
patterns.description: Both Flask (app) and Blueprint inherit from Scaffold, which provides the registration interface (route, errorhandler, before_request, after_request, teardown_request, context_processor, url_value_preprocessor, url_defaults). Each registration method uses the same decorator pattern and stores into the same data structures (dict[scope, list]). The only difference is _check_setup_finished implementation.
patterns.rationale: App and Blueprint share 90% of their API surface — routes, error handlers, request hooks — but differ in lifecycle (app is permanent, blueprint is registered once). Scaffold captures the shared registration logic, ensuring that any registration method added to one is available to both. The _check_setup_finished abstract method is the single point of behavioral difference.

patterns.name: Dependency injection via parameter name introspection
patterns.description: Function parameters are inspected via inspect.signature() to discover required dependencies by name. The framework matches parameter names to registered providers (fixtures), resolving the dependency graph at runtime without type annotations or explicit wiring. The fixture's own dependencies are recursively discovered the same way, forming a closure computed by BFS over the dependency graph.
patterns.rationale: Type-based DI (Java Spring, FastAPI Depends) requires types to be unique and importable. Name-based DI allows multiple fixtures of the same type to coexist, and allows fixtures to be defined in conftest.py without importing them. Parameter names are the contract — the function signature declares what it needs, and the framework resolves it. This is more Pythonic: names are first-class, types are advisory.

patterns.name: Type-safe heterogeneous container (StashKey + Stash)
patterns.description: A Stash is a dict-like container where keys are StashKey[T] objects (Generic, opaque, no value). Each key is associated with type T at definition time. The container is created without knowing what will be stored in it; plugins/modules create their own StashKey instances at module level and use them to store/retrieve typed values from a shared Stash instance. __getitem__ returns T because the key carries the type.
patterns.rationale: Standard dict with string keys has no type safety and risks key collisions between plugins. StashKey objects are unique by identity (no __eq__, no __hash__ override), so different modules cannot accidentally collide. The Generic[T] parameter means type checkers know the return type from the key. This allows plugins to attach private data to shared objects (Config, Node) without modifying their class definitions.

patterns.name: Metaclass-enforced factory method
patterns.description: NodeMeta intercepts __call__ to raise an error, blocking direct construction like Node(name, parent). The only public path is the from_parent() classmethod, which calls _create() internally. _create() is the escape hatch that actually calls super().__call__(). This forces all Node subclasses to be created through the factory, allowing the parent to inject config/session/identity at construction time.
patterns.rationale: Direct construction bypasses parent-child linking and identity assignment. By blocking __call__ and requiring from_parent(), the framework guarantees every node has a valid parent chain, config, session, and unique nodeid. The metaclass is the enforcement mechanism because __init_subclass__ cannot block __call__ — only a metaclass can intercept the class call itself.

patterns.name: Deferred-fill error capture object
patterns.description: ExceptionInfo.for_later() creates an unfilled ExceptionInfo with _excinfo=None. The object is returned from __enter__() before the exception has occurred. When __exit__() catches the exception, fill_unfilled(exc_info) populates the object in place. Properties (type, value, tb, traceback) assert _excinfo is not None before accessing, failing loudly if used prematurely.
patterns.rationale: The context manager protocol requires __enter__ to return the object the user will interact with, but the exception hasn't been raised yet. Creating the ExceptionInfo in __enter__ and filling it in __exit__ lets the user write 'with pytest.raises(X) as excinfo:' and then inspect excinfo.value after the block. The assert in properties is a temporal safety check — using the object before the context exits is a programming error, not a runtime failure.

patterns.name: Stack-based resource lifecycle with finalizers
patterns.description: SetupState maintains a stack of (node, finalizers) pairs. setup(item) walks the collector chain from root to item, pushing each node and running its setup(). Teardown pops nodes from the stack and runs their finalizers in reverse order. Finalizers are registered dynamically via addfinalizer() during setup. The stack ensures that shared scoped resources (session fixtures, module fixtures) are set up once and torn down only when the last item using them finishes.
patterns.rationale: Fixture scopes (function/class/module/session) create a nested resource lifecycle: a session-scoped fixture must outlive all module-scoped fixtures, which must outlive all function-scoped fixtures. A stack naturally models this nesting: setup pushes outward-to-inward, teardown pops inward-to-outward. The next-item parameter in teardown_exact() allows the stack to persist shared resources across items — only popping nodes that the next item doesn't also need.

patterns.name: Dual-mode decorator via __call__ dispatch
patterns.description: MarkDecorator.__call__ inspects its arguments: if called with a single callable or class (no extra kwargs), it stamps the mark onto that object and returns it. If called with any other arguments, it returns a NEW MarkDecorator with updated mark args/kwargs. This enables both @pytest.mark.skip (applied directly) and @pytest.mark.skip(reason='x') (returns new decorator) from the same object.
patterns.rationale: A decorator that sometimes applies and sometimes returns a new decorator is the only way to support both @decorator and @decorator(args) syntax from a single object. The alternative (separate objects) requires the user to know which syntax is valid for each mark. This pattern makes all marks uniformly support both forms, which is critical for user experience: the distinction between parameterized and non-parameterized marks is invisible at the call site.

patterns.name: __getattr__ as dynamic attribute factory
patterns.description: MarkGenerator.__getattr__ creates a new MarkDecorator for any attribute name accessed on the pytest.mark singleton. Unknown names trigger a warning (configurable to hard error via strict_markers). Known names from config are cached in a set. The factory is the only way to access marks — there is no pre-registration step.
patterns.rationale: Marks are open-ended: users define their own mark names without registration. Pre-defining all marks would require a registration step and still couldn't cover user-defined marks. __getattr__ makes any attribute access produce a valid MarkDecorator, then validation happens lazily (warning or error) based on config. This separates mark creation (always succeeds) from mark validation (configurable strictness). The warning-not-error default allows progressive adoption of mark registration.

patterns.name: Private constructor guard via sentinel parameter
patterns.description: Constructors accept a trailing _ispytest: bool = False parameter. check_ispytest(_ispytest) warns if False. Internal code passes _ispytest=True. The parameter name starts with _, signaling it's not for public use. This allows the class to be technically instantiable (for testing and internal use) while discouraging external construction, without the brittleness of name-mangling or __init__ overrides.
patterns.rationale: Making __init__ truly private (double-underscore name mangling) breaks subclassing and testing. Making __init__ public invites misuse. The sentinel parameter is a middle ground: external users get a deprecation warning, internal callers pass _ispytest=True. It's also forward-compatible — the warning can be upgraded to an error in future versions without changing the API.

patterns.name: Ordered enum with navigation methods
patterns.description: Scope(Enum) uses @total_ordering with __lt__ based on declaration order index. Provides next_lower() and next_higher() for navigating the scope hierarchy. from_user() classmethod converts a string to enum with a friendly error message including context (where the conversion happened). The ordering (Function < Class < Module < Package < Session) is semantically meaningful: higher scopes outlive lower scopes.
patterns.rationale: Fixture scopes form a hierarchy where containment matters: a session-scoped fixture must be set up before any module-scoped fixture, and torn down after all of them. An ordered enum with navigation methods lets the framework compare scopes (scope_a < scope_b), find adjacent scopes (for caching decisions), and convert user strings to enums with context-rich errors. @total_ordering provides all comparison operators from __lt__ + __eq__ for free.

patterns.name: Frozen dataclass with object.__setattr__ bypass for custom init
patterns.description: Mark is declared as a @dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True) but __init__ uses object.__setattr__(self, 'name', name) to set each field, bypassing the frozen restriction. This pattern allows frozen dataclasses to have custom initialization logic (validation, transformation) while maintaining immutability after construction.
patterns.rationale: frozen=True prevents attribute mutation after construction, which is desirable for value objects like Mark. But frozen also prevents __init__ from using self.attr = value, forcing object.__setattr__ for custom init. The alternative — not using frozen and relying on convention — is fragile. The bypass is intentional: it gives the safety of immutability with the flexibility of custom initialization. Mark needs custom init for the _ispytest guard and for internal field manipulation in combined_with().

patterns.name: Dependency closure BFS from initial names
patterns.description: FuncFixtureInfo computes the transitive closure of fixture dependencies using a working-set BFS: start with initialnames (the function's own parameters + autouse fixtures), for each name look up its FixtureDef, add the fixture's own argnames to the working set, repeat until empty. The result is names_closure — an ordered list of all fixtures that need to be set up. prune_dependency_tree() recomputes the closure when direct parametrization shadows some fixtures.
patterns.rationale: Fixture dependencies are recursive: fixture A may depend on fixture B which depends on fixture C. The framework needs the complete set of fixtures to set up, in dependency order. BFS from the function's parameters naturally produces topological order (a fixture is added to the closure only after its dependencies). Pruning is needed because direct parametrization (@pytest.mark.parametrize) can override a fixture, removing it and its subtree from the dependency graph.

patterns.name: Immutable invocation spec with copy-on-modify
patterns.description: CallSpec2 is a @dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True) representing a planned parametrized test invocation. setmulti() creates a NEW CallSpec2 with updated fields instead of mutating self. Multiple parametrize() calls produce a cartesian product: each call's setmulti() is applied to every existing CallSpec2, creating new instances for each combination. The result is a list of immutable specs, each representing one test invocation.
patterns.rationale: Parametrization is multiplicative: @parametrize('x', [1,2]) then @parametrize('y', [3,4]) produces 4 invocations. Copy-on-modify makes this clean: for each existing spec, create a new spec for each new parameter value. If specs were mutable, the cartesian product would require careful cloning to avoid aliasing bugs. Frozen dataclass prevents accidental mutation of specs after collection, which would break test isolation.

patterns.name: Adapter mounting as transport strategy by URL prefix
patterns.description: Session maintains an OrderedDict of {url_prefix: adapter}. get_adapter(url) matches the longest prefix to select the transport adapter. mount(prefix, adapter) registers new adapters, keeping them sorted by prefix length (longest first). This decouples transport selection from transport implementation — any adapter implementing BaseAdapter.send() can be mounted for any URL scheme.
patterns.rationale: Different URL schemes (http, https, custom) need different transport logic (connection pooling, TLS, SOCKS proxy). Rather than hardcoding scheme→transport mapping, the prefix-based registry lets users register custom adapters for any scheme (e.g. 'ftp://') without modifying Session internals. Longest-prefix matching allows host-specific overrides ('https://api.example.com') over scheme-wide defaults ('https://').

patterns.name: CaseInsensitiveDict — dual-store key normalization
patterns.description: A MutableMapping subclass that stores (original_key, value) tuples in an OrderedDict keyed by lowercased key. Lookups normalize via .lower(), but iteration returns original-case keys. This preserves the last-set casing for display while enabling case-insensitive access.
patterns.rationale: HTTP headers are case-insensitive by specification, but users expect to see the original casing (e.g. 'Content-Type' not 'content-type'). Storing both the normalized key (for lookup) and the original key (for display) in a single data structure eliminates the need for a separate normalization layer. Using OrderedDict preserves insertion order, which matters for HTTP header rendering.

patterns.name: Callable auth interface — __call__ as the contract
patterns.description: AuthBase defines a single-method interface via __call__(self, r: PreparedRequest) -> PreparedRequest. Auth implementations (HTTPBasicAuth, HTTPDigestAuth) are callable objects that mutate the request in-place and return it. No register/login/verify methods — the entire auth contract is one callable transformation.
patterns.rationale: Auth is fundamentally a request transformation: take a prepared request, add credentials. Making it __call__ means auth handlers compose naturally — they can be passed where callables are expected, chained, or used as hooks. It also means the auth handler has mutable state (e.g. HTTPDigestAuth tracks nonce_count per-thread) without needing a method-based API. This predates typing.Protocol but achieves the same structural typing: anything callable with the right signature is an auth handler.

patterns.name: Exception hierarchy with context-carrying base
patterns.description: A single RequestException base class accepts request and response objects via kwargs in __init__, automatically deriving request from response if not provided. All specialized exceptions (ConnectionError, Timeout, SSLError, etc.) inherit from it, forming a tree where catching the base catches all request errors, but catching a leaf catches only that specific failure. Multiple inheritance creates category overlaps (ConnectTimeout inherits both ConnectionError and Timeout).
patterns.rationale: HTTP errors have rich context (which request failed, what response was received) that plain exception messages lose. Carrying request/response on the exception lets catchers inspect context without parsing strings. The multiple-inheritance tree (ConnectTimeout ⊂ ConnectionError ∩ Timeout) mirrors the domain: a connect timeout is both a connection error and a timeout, and catchers should be able to catch it as either. This is more expressive than a flat exception enum. [Merged from P134: CLI errors need progressively more context: a bad parameter needs to say which parameter, a usage error needs to show usage, a missing command needs suggestions. The hierarchy lets each level add its layer of context in format_message() without the caller needing to assemble it. The 'did you mean' pattern turns a cryptic error into a helpful suggestion using stdlib difflib.]

patterns.name: Prepare/send two-phase request lifecycle
patterns.description: Request → PreparedRequest separates the user-facing API from the wire format. Request is a user-friendly container with optional fields. PreparedRequest is the immutable-ish internal representation with fully resolved URL, encoded body, merged headers, and attached auth. The prepare() method is a multi-step pipeline: prepare_method → prepare_url → prepare_headers → prepare_cookies → prepare_body → prepare_auth → prepare_hooks, each operating on the PreparedRequest in sequence.
patterns.rationale: Users think in terms of 'GET this URL with these params and this auth', but the wire needs a fully resolved URL string, encoded body bytes, and merged headers. Separating the two phases means: (1) Session can merge its own settings (default headers, cookies, auth) with per-request overrides during preparation; (2) PreparedRequest can be serialized/pickled and sent later; (3) The prepare pipeline makes the transformation steps explicit and individually testable. Auth must be last because it may depend on the fully prepared request (e.g. signing the body).

patterns.name: merge_setting — request-level override with None-removal semantics
patterns.description: Session-level defaults are merged with per-request overrides. For dict settings (headers, params), session defaults are the base, request values update on top. Keys explicitly set to None in the request are deleted from the merged result — None is a sentinel meaning 'remove this default', not 'leave unspecified'. For non-dict settings (verify, cert, stream), request value wins if non-None.
patterns.rationale: Sessions carry persistent defaults (auth, headers, proxies) that most requests inherit. But users need per-request overrides and, critically, per-request removals — 'use the session's headers but NOT its Authorization'. Without None-as-removal, there's no way to say 'remove this default for this request only' without mutating the session. The function also handles the case where only one of session/request setting exists, bypassing merge entirely.

patterns.name: LookupDict — attribute-accessible dict for enumerated constants
patterns.description: A dict subclass that overrides __getattr__ and __getitem__ to return None for missing keys instead of raising KeyError. Used to build the 'codes' object where HTTP status codes are accessible as both attributes (codes.ok) and items (codes['ok']), with case-insensitive aliases (codes.OK == codes.ok). Multiple names map to the same code (codes.moved == codes.moved_permanently == 301).
patterns.rationale: HTTP status codes have many common names (200 = 'ok' = 'okay' = 'all_good'), and users want to access them as attributes (codes.not_found) not dict lookups (codes['not_found']). By overriding __getattr__ to fall through to None, the API is forgiving — typos return None instead of crashing. The _init() function iterates a code→names mapping and sets attributes bidirectionally, so every alias works. This is a lightweight alternative to enums for cases with many aliases.

patterns.name: Response hook chain — dispatch as post-processing pipeline
patterns.description: Hooks are registered as {event: [callable]} dicts. dispatch_hook() iterates the hook list for a given event, calling each hook with the current data. If a hook returns non-None, its return value replaces the data for subsequent hooks. This creates a transformation chain where each hook can inspect, modify, or replace the response.
patterns.rationale: Post-processing needs vary widely (auth retry on 401, redirect following, custom logging) and users need to inject their own logic without subclassing Session. The hook chain is simpler than a plugin system: no registration lifecycle, no hook specs, just callables that transform data. The 'return replaces data' contract means hooks naturally compose — the last hook's output is the final result. Auth handlers use this to register response hooks (e.g. HTTPDigestAuth registers handle_401 as a response hook).

patterns.name: Lazy content property with consumed-state guard
patterns.description: Response._content starts as False (sentinel for 'not yet read'). The content property reads the raw stream on first access, caches the result, and sets _content_consumed = True. Subsequent accesses return the cached bytes. If iter_content() was used first (streaming), _content_consumed is already True and accessing .content raises StreamConsumedError — the two access modes are mutually exclusive.
patterns.rationale: HTTP responses can be large, so content should only be read when needed. But once read, it should be cached (no re-reading the socket). The False sentinel (not None, because None might be a valid response body for status 0) distinguishes 'never accessed' from 'accessed and got None'. The consumed guard prevents the common bug of streaming part of a response then accidentally reading .content (which would return empty or hang).

patterns.name: Convenience-function layer over session-based API
patterns.description: Module-level functions (requests.get, requests.post, etc.) are thin wrappers that create a Session, call the corresponding method, and return the response. Each verb function accepts the same kwargs as Session.request() plus verb-specific defaults (e.g. head sets allow_redirects=False). The convenience layer eliminates boilerplate for one-off requests while the Session API handles persistent connections.
patterns.rationale: Most HTTP requests are one-off — the user wants 'GET this URL' without managing session lifecycle. But the implementation must still use a Session (for connection pooling, default headers, cookie handling). The convenience functions bridge this: they create a Session in a with-block (ensuring cleanup), delegate, and return. This is the 'small interface, deep implementation' pattern — the top-level API is 8 one-liner functions, but each delegates to the full Session machinery.

patterns.name: __getstate__/__setstate__ for pickleable objects with non-pickleable internals
patterns.description: Session, PreparedRequest, Response, and HTTPAdapter all define __getstate__ and __setstate__ using a __attrs__ class attribute that lists the serializable field names. __getstate__ extracts only those fields; __setstate__ restores them, often re-initializing non-pickleable internals (like urllib3 PoolManager) from the stored config. This whitelisting approach controls exactly what survives pickling.
patterns.rationale: HTTP clients contain non-pickleable objects (socket connections, urllib3 PoolManager, threading.local). But users need to pickle requests for multiprocessing, caching, or testing. The __attrs__ whitelist ensures only serializable state (config, headers, cookies, body bytes) survives, while __setstate__ reconstructs the non-serializable parts from stored config. HTTPAdapter's __setstate__ re-initializes the pool manager from stored _pool_connections/_pool_maxsize values. [Merged from P169: Tracebacks cannot be pickled — they contain frame references that don't survive serialization. When logs cross process boundaries (via multiprocessing queue with enqueue=True), the exception record must be serialized. Rather than failing, __reduce__ degrades gracefully: it preserves the exception type and tries to preserve the value, dropping what can't be pickled. The custom reduce protocol (returning a different reconstruction callable) allows the round-trip to use a cached pickle blob for efficiency.]

def __getstate__(self):
    state = self.__dict__.copy()
    state["thread_locals"] = None
    state["lock"] = None
    return state

def __setstate__(self, state):
    self.__dict__.update(state)
    self.thread_locals = threading.local()
    self.lock = create_logger_lock()

        return self.__class__, (self.message, self.lineno, self.name, self.filename)

patterns.name: Adapter-level exception translation — wrapping third-party errors
patterns.description: HTTPAdapter.send() wraps all urllib3 exceptions in a try/except, translating each urllib3 error type to the corresponding requests exception. The translation is a mapping from third-party exception classes to domain-specific exceptions, preserving the original error as the cause (via raise NewError(e, request=request)). This isolates the domain error hierarchy from the transport implementation.
patterns.rationale: urllib3 is an implementation detail — users should catch requests.exceptions.ConnectionError, not urllib3.exceptions.MaxRetryError. The adapter is the boundary where third-party errors are translated to domain errors. By catching specific urllib3 types and mapping them individually (MaxRetryError→RetryError, SSLError→SSLError, ReadTimeoutError→ReadTimeout), the translation preserves semantic meaning. The request=request kwarg attaches context to every translated error.

patterns.name: Mixin-based interface composition for model classes
patterns.description: Request and PreparedRequest are assembled from focused mixins: RequestEncodingMixin (URL/body encoding), RequestHooksMixin (hook registration/dispatch). Each mixin provides a cohesive set of methods and carries its own type annotations. The main class inherits multiple mixins to compose the full interface without a monolithic base class.
patterns.rationale: Encoding logic (params, files, multipart) and hook logic (register, dispatch) are independent concerns. Putting them in mixins lets each be tested in isolation and reused in other contexts (e.g. PreparedRequest needs encoding but also hooks). This is the pre-Protocol era approach to interface composition — mixins define method bundles, and classes assemble them via multiple inheritance. Modern Python would use Protocol composition, but mixins remain useful when shared implementation (not just interface) is needed.

patterns.rationale: All HTTP verbs share most kwargs (headers, cookies, auth, timeout) but differ in specifics: GET has no body but has params; POST has data and json; HEAD defaults allow_redirects to False. Without TypedDict + Unpack, **kwargs is untyped and type checkers can't catch mistakes. By modeling each verb's kwargs as a TypedDict, the type checker knows that requests.get(url, data=...) is suspicious (GET shouldn't have a body) while requests.post(url, data=...) is fine.

patterns.name: Virtual base class with __new__ dispatching to backend factory
patterns.description: Base classes (Event, Lock, Semaphore, CapacityLimiter, CancelScope) define the interface with all methods raising NotImplementedError. __new__ calls get_async_backend().create_X() to return a backend-specific implementation. Callers never instantiate the base — they get a concrete backend subclass transparently. This is the factory method pattern realized through __new__, so the constructor itself is the dispatch point.
patterns.rationale: Allows user code to write Event() without knowing or caring which async backend (asyncio, trio) is active. The base class serves as a typed interface (type hints, docstrings, __slots__) while never being instantiated. Backend selection happens at runtime via sniffio, and the appropriate concrete class is returned. This eliminates the need for users to import backend-specific classes. [Merged from P109: Without the adapter, constructing Event() outside an event loop would crash. The adapter provides graceful degradation: it captures intent (set/wait) and replays it once a backend is available. This is essential for module-level or class-level initialization patterns where the event loop hasn't started yet.]

patterns.name: Lazy backend loading with module-level cache
patterns.description: Backend classes are loaded on demand via import_module(f'anyio._backends._{name}') and cached in a module-level dict (loaded_backends). The backend module exposes a 'backend_class' attribute that the loader reads. This avoids importing trio when only asyncio is used.
patterns.rationale: Importing trio unconditionally would add startup overhead and require trio as a hard dependency. By lazy-loading, anyio only imports the backend the user actually needs. The cache dict avoids repeated import_module calls. Using a custom dict instead of sys.modules handles partially-initialized modules safely.

patterns.name: Abstract backend as classmethod-only interface
patterns.description: AsyncBackend defines the entire backend contract as @classmethod @abstractmethod methods. No instance state — backends are never instantiated. All operations are class-level: run(), sleep(), current_time(), create_event(), create_task_group(), etc. Concrete backends (AsyncIOBackend, TrioBackend) implement these as classmethods operating on their respective event loop APIs.
patterns.rationale: Backends are stateless namespaces — there is no per-instance data to hold. Making everything a classmethod means no allocation overhead for backend 'instances', and the backend class itself serves as both the interface and the namespace. This also enables get_async_backend() to return the class (type[AsyncBackend]) rather than an instance, simplifying the dispatch chain.

patterns.name: Stream hierarchy with variance-directed generics
patterns.description: Stream interfaces form a layered hierarchy using Generic with carefully chosen variance: UnreliableObjectReceiveStream[T_co] (covariant — you read T), UnreliableObjectSendStream[T_contra] (contravariant — you send T), ObjectStream[T_Item] (invariant — both directions). Reliability layers compose via inheritance: ObjectReceiveStream extends UnreliableObjectReceiveStream adding ordering guarantees.
patterns.rationale: Variance annotations encode the read/write contract at the type level. A function accepting ObjectSendStream[bytes] can safely accept ObjectSendStream[bytes | str] (contravariance). The layered hierarchy (unreliable → reliable → bidirectional) lets implementations declare exactly what guarantees they provide. Type aliases (AnyByteStream, AnyByteReceiveStream) union the object-stream and byte-stream variants for consumer flexibility.

patterns.name: Stapled stream — composable bidirectional from two unidirectional
patterns.description: StapledByteStream and StapledObjectStream combine a send stream and receive stream into a single bidirectional stream via @dataclass(eq=False) composition. Each method delegates to the appropriate side. Extra attributes are merged from both with receive taking precedence on conflicts.
patterns.rationale: Many transport protocols (TCP, Unix sockets) provide separate send and receive channels that need to be used as a single bidirectional stream. Rather than requiring a new class for each combination, the Stapled pattern composes any send+receive pair into a bidirectional stream. Using @dataclass(eq=False) gives automatic __init__ from fields while avoiding identity-based equality.

patterns.name: TypedAttributeSet with __init_subclass__ annotation enforcement
patterns.description: TypedAttributeSet uses __init_subclass__ to enforce that every public attribute in subclasses has a type annotation. Unannotated public attributes raise TypeError at class-definition time. typed_attribute() returns unique sentinel objects used as keys in a Mapping, and TypedAttributeProvider.extra(attr) looks them up via callables.
patterns.rationale: Typed attributes provide type-safe extra metadata on objects (streams, listeners) without polluting the class hierarchy. __init_subclass__ validation catches missing annotations at definition time, not runtime. The sentinel-object pattern (typed_attribute()) ensures keys are unique and can't collide with string keys. The callable-getter design allows lazy evaluation of attribute values.

patterns.name: ResourceGuard — context manager for single-task exclusive access
patterns.description: ResourceGuard is a lightweight context manager that raises BusyResourceError if entered while already guarded. Uses __slots__ with just 'action' (string for error message) and '_guarded' (bool flag). Provides mutual exclusion without locks — it's a programming error detector, not a synchronization primitive.
patterns.rationale: Async resources like streams can be corrupted if two tasks read/write concurrently. ResourceGuard detects this programming error eagerly (raises immediately on concurrent entry) rather than silently producing corrupted data. It's deliberately not a lock — concurrent access to these resources is a bug, not a contention scenario. The 'action' string makes error messages actionable ('Another task is already reading this resource').

patterns.name: TaskHandle with status enum and __await__ for awaitable tasks
patterns.description: TaskHandle wraps a spawned coroutine with a Status enum (PENDING, CANCELLING, CANCELLED, FINISHED, FAILED), an Event for completion signaling, and __await__ implementation that delegates to the event's wait(). Properties (status, exception, return_value) use match/case on Status to provide type-safe access with appropriate exceptions for each state. Uses @final and __slots__.
patterns.rationale: Decouples task spawning from task awaiting. Unlike asyncio.Task (which is both the handle and the awaitable), TaskHandle allows checking status, canceling, and awaiting independently. The Status enum makes all states explicit and prevents the 'await a cancelled task' ambiguity. __await__ makes the handle directly awaitable while __slots__ + @final signal it's a fixed-shape value object that shouldn't be subclassed.

patterns.name: BlockingPortal — sync-to-async bridge with Future-based result transport
patterns.description: BlockingPortal runs an event loop in a separate thread and exposes synchronous methods (call, start_task_soon) that bridge to async via concurrent.futures.Future. The portal holds a token for cross-thread dispatch, a task group for spawned tasks, and a stop event for shutdown. Results from async code are transported back via Future.set_result/set_exception.
patterns.rationale: Synchronous code in other threads needs to call into an async event loop. BlockingPortal provides this bridge: from a sync thread, you call portal.call(func) which spawns the coroutine in the event loop thread and blocks on a Future until completion. The Future serves as a cross-thread result container. The task group ensures all spawned tasks are cleaned up when the portal stops. [Merged from P378: Allows testing async ASGI apps with standard sync httpx.Client API. The portal manages the event loop lifecycle; the transport translates between sync httpx and async ASGI. No need for async test framework.]

patterns.name: BlockingPortalProvider — reference-counted portal lifecycle
patterns.description: BlockingPortalProvider is a @dataclass that manages a single BlockingPortal shared across multiple threads via reference counting. First __enter__ starts the portal; last __exit__ shuts it down. Uses a Lock for thread-safe lease management. Fields use field(init=False, default_factory=...) for non-init mutable state.
patterns.rationale: Multiple sync threads may need to call into the same event loop. Creating a portal per thread would spawn multiple event loops, wasting resources and preventing cross-thread coordination. Reference counting ensures exactly one portal exists as long as at least one thread needs it, and it's torn down when the last thread exits. The Lock makes the refcount safe for concurrent access.
