class BlockingPortalProvider:
    backend: str = "asyncio"
    backend_options: dict[str, Any] | None = None
    _lock: Lock = field(init=False, default_factory=Lock)
    _leases: int = field(init=False, default=0)
    _portal: BlockingPortal = field(init=False)
    _portal_cm: AbstractContextManager[BlockingPortal] | None = field(init=False, default=None)

    def __enter__(self) -> BlockingPortal:
        with self._lock:
            if self._portal_cm is None:
                self._portal_cm = start_blocking_portal(self.backend, self.backend_options)
                self._portal = self._portal_cm.__enter__()
            self._leases += 1
            return self._portal

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> None:
        portal_cm: AbstractContextManager[BlockingPortal] | None = None
        with self._lock:
            assert self._leases > 0
            self._leases -= 1
            if not self._leases:
                portal_cm = self._portal_cm
                self._portal_cm = None
        if portal_cm:
            portal_cm.__exit__(None, None, None)

patterns.name: RunVar — event-loop-scoped context variable
patterns.description: RunVar is like contextvars.ContextVar but scoped to the running event loop instead of the current context. Uses a WeakKeyDictionary keyed by the native token (event loop identity) to store per-loop values. Supports get/set/reset with default values, and can be used as a context manager for scoped overrides.
patterns.rationale: contextvars.ContextVar is scoped to the current execution context (task), not the event loop. But some state (like thread pools, caches) should be shared across all tasks in the same event loop, not duplicated per task. RunVar fills this gap: it's per-loop, not per-task. Using WeakKeyDictionary avoids preventing event loop garbage collection when the loop ends.

patterns.name: CapacityLimiter with on-behalf-of borrower tracking
patterns.description: CapacityLimiter tracks borrowed tokens as a set of borrower objects, not just a count. acquire_on_behalf_of(borrower) and release_on_behalf_of(borrower) allow delegating capacity to a specific task/object. The wait queue is an OrderedDict mapping borrowers to Events for FIFO fairness. total_tokens is a writable property that proactively wakes waiters when increased.
patterns.rationale: Tracking borrowers by identity (not count) enables: (1) detecting double-acquire by the same borrower (raises RuntimeError), (2) releasing on behalf of a different task than acquired (useful for worker thread patterns where the acquiring task differs from the releasing one), (3) proper cleanup when tasks are cancelled. The writable total_tokens with proactive wake-up allows dynamic capacity scaling at runtime.

patterns.name: Shared mutable state object as dataclass with statistics method
patterns.description: _MemoryObjectStreamState is a @dataclass(eq=False) holding all mutable state for a paired memory stream (buffer, open channel counts, waiting senders/receivers). Both MemoryObjectSendStream and MemoryObjectReceiveStream reference the same state object. A statistics() method returns an immutable NamedTuple snapshot of current state for observability.
patterns.rationale: Memory object streams come in send/receive pairs that share state. Rather than synchronizing two separate objects, a shared state dataclass is the single source of truth. Both stream ends reference it and modify it through their respective methods. The statistics() NamedTuple provides a safe immutable snapshot for monitoring — callers can't accidentally corrupt internal state by inspecting it. eq=False prevents identity-based comparison of state objects.

occurrences.snippet:
@dataclass(eq=False)
class _MemoryObjectStreamState(Generic[T_Item]):
    max_buffer_size: float = field()
    buffer: deque[T_Item] = field(init=False, default_factory=deque)
    open_send_channels: int = field(init=False, default=0)
    open_receive_channels: int = field(init=False, default=0)
    waiting_receivers: OrderedDict[Event, _MemoryObjectItemReceiver[T_Item]] = field(init=False, default_factory=OrderedDict)
    waiting_senders: OrderedDict[Event, T_Item] = field(init=False, default_factory=OrderedDict)

    def statistics(self) -> MemoryObjectStreamStatistics:
        return MemoryObjectStreamStatistics(
            len(self.buffer), self.max_buffer_size,
            self.open_send_channels, self.open_receive_channels,
            len(self.waiting_senders), len(self.waiting_receivers))

class MemoryObjectStreamStatistics(NamedTuple):
    current_buffer_used: int
    max_buffer_size: float
    open_send_streams: int
    open_receive_streams: int
    tasks_waiting_send: int
    tasks_waiting_receive: int

patterns.name: fail_after / move_on_after — deadline-derived cancel scope factories
patterns.description: fail_after(delay) and move_on_after(delay) are convenience functions that create CancelScopes with computed deadlines. fail_after raises TimeoutError if the deadline passes; move_on_after silently exits. Both use current_time() + delay to compute an absolute deadline, then delegate to the backend's create_cancel_scope.
patterns.rationale: CancelScopes use absolute deadlines, but users think in relative durations. These functions bridge that gap with two semantic variants: fail_after for hard timeouts (raise on expiry) and move_on_after for soft timeouts (silently continue). By delegating to create_cancel_scope, they work across all backends. The factory-function pattern (rather than CancelScope methods) keeps CancelScope's interface minimal.

patterns.name: Backend-agnostic exception class via cancelled_exception_class()
patterns.description: Each async backend raises a different cancellation exception (asyncio.CancelledError vs trio.Cancelled). anyio abstracts this via get_cancelled_exc_class() which returns the backend-specific class. Code that needs to catch cancellation uses this function instead of hardcoding the exception class.
patterns.rationale: Catching cancellation is fundamental to structured concurrency — you need to know when a task was cancelled vs failed for another reason. But hardcoding asyncio.CancelledError breaks on trio. By providing a single function that returns the correct class per backend, anyio lets user code write `except get_cancelled_exc_class()` that works everywhere. This is an example of abstracting over exception type, not just API shape.

patterns.name: AsyncResource as async context manager base with aclose contract
patterns.description: AsyncResource is an ABC with __slots__=() that implements __aenter__/__aexit__ to delegate to aclose(). Subclasses only need to implement aclose(). The __aenter__ returns self, enabling `async with resource:` patterns. All async resources in anyio (streams, listeners, sockets) inherit this contract.
patterns.rationale: Every async resource needs cleanup, but the cleanup is always 'close it'. By centralizing __aenter__/__aexit__ in the base class, subclasses only implement aclose() — one method instead of three. __slots__=() signals that subclasses should define their own __slots__. This is the async equivalent of contextlib.closing but as a base class, giving type safety and IDE completion for the async with pattern.

occurrences.snippet:
class AsyncResource(metaclass=ABCMeta):
    __slots__ = ()

    async def __aenter__(self: T) -> T:
        return self

    async def __aexit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> None:
        await self.aclose()

    @abstractmethod
    async def aclose(self) -> None:
        """Close the resource."""

patterns.name: iterate_exceptions — recursive BaseExceptionGroup flattener
patterns.description: iterate_exceptions() is a generator that recursively yields individual exceptions from a BaseException or BaseExceptionGroup. If the input is a group, it recurses into each sub-exception. This flattens nested exception groups into a flat sequence of leaf exceptions.
patterns.rationale: Python 3.11+ introduced BaseExceptionGroup, and anyio's TaskGroup raises them when multiple tasks fail. Code that needs to inspect individual failures (e.g., for error reporting, retry logic) must flatten the group tree. This utility provides that flattening as a single reusable generator, handling arbitrarily nested groups. It's used in the pytest plugin to extract test failures from exception groups.

patterns.name: Decorator-stacked parameter accumulation via __click_params__
patterns.description: Parameter decorators (@option, @argument) don't create parameters immediately — they append to a hidden __click_params__ list on the function object. When @command is applied, it reads __click_params__ (reversed), deletes it, and passes the collected parameters to the Command constructor. This decouples parameter declaration from command creation, allowing arbitrary stacking order.
patterns.rationale: Allows users to stack @option and @argument decorators in any order above @command without worrying about constructor arguments. The function object itself serves as a temporary accumulator, so the decorators stay stateless and composable — each one just appends to the list and returns the function unchanged.

patterns.name: Context as execution scope with parent chain inheritance
patterns.description: Context objects form a parent chain (ctx.parent). Each context inherits settings from its parent: terminal_width, color, help_option_names, token_normalize_func, auto_envvar_prefix, default_map, obj. Inheritance is resolved in __init__, not lazily — if a value is None, it's pulled from the parent. The context doubles as a context manager (__enter__/__exit__) that pushes itself onto a thread-local stack for global access via get_current_context().
patterns.rationale: CLI commands nest (groups contain subcommands). Each subcommand needs its own parameter values but inherits configuration (terminal width, color, envvar prefix) from the parent. Resolving inheritance in __init__ (not lazily) means downstream code never needs to walk the parent chain for configuration — it's already resolved. The thread-local stack makes the current context accessible from anywhere without passing it through every function.

patterns.name: ExitStack as per-invocation resource lifecycle manager
patterns.description: Context holds an ExitStack (_exit_stack) that manages all resources registered during a command's execution. with_resource() enters a context manager and registers it for cleanup. call_on_close() registers a plain callback. On context teardown (__exit__), the ExitStack unwinds everything in LIFO order, passing exception info to allow suppression. The stack is recreated after close to support context reuse.
patterns.rationale: CLI commands often open resources (file handles, DB connections) during execution that must be cleaned up regardless of success or failure. ExitStack provides uniform cleanup for both context managers and plain callbacks, and handles exception propagation correctly. Storing it on the Context (not the Command) means cleanup scope matches invocation scope, not declaration scope.

patterns.name: Eager parameter flag for pre-callback processing
patterns.description: Parameters have an is_eager flag. During processing, iter_params_for_processing() sorts parameters so eager ones are processed before non-eager ones, regardless of declaration order. Within each eagerness group, invocation order (the order the user passed them on the CLI) takes precedence. This allows --version and --help to short-circuit before other parameters are even evaluated.
patterns.rationale: Some parameters need to act before others — --version should print and exit before any other parameter's callback runs. The eager flag is a declarative way to control processing order without requiring the user to understand the internal callback pipeline. Combined with invocation-order sorting within groups, this gives predictable, user-expected behavior.

patterns.name: Value source tracking with ordered IntEnum
patterns.description: ParameterSource is an IntEnum ordered from most explicit (PROMPT=1) to least explicit (DEFAULT=5). Values are recorded during parsing via set_parameter_source(). The ordering enables comparison: source < ParameterSource.DEFAULT_MAP checks if a value was explicitly provided by the user. This drives feature-switch arbitration when multiple options target the same parameter name.
patterns.rationale: When multiple options write to the same parameter slot (e.g. --upper/--lower both set 'case'), the framework needs to know which source is more authoritative. The IntEnum ordering makes this a simple comparison — COMMANDLINE beats ENVIRONMENT beats DEFAULT_MAP beats DEFAULT. Without source tracking, the framework couldn't distinguish 'user passed --foo=bar' from 'foo defaulted to bar'.

occurrences.snippet:
class ParameterSource(enum.IntEnum):
    PROMPT = enum.auto()
    COMMANDLINE = enum.auto()
    ENVIRONMENT = enum.auto()
    DEFAULT_MAP = enum.auto()
    DEFAULT = enum.auto()

# Usage in arbitration:
more_explicit = existing_source is not None and source < existing_source
# If existing was DEFAULT (4) and new is COMMANDLINE (2), new wins

patterns.name: ParamType as generic ABC with __call__ as convert dispatch
patterns.description: ParamType is a Generic ABC parameterized by the converted value type (ParamType[int]). Its __call__ method delegates to convert(), returning None for None input. Subclasses implement convert(value, param, ctx) → T. FuncParamType wraps any callable into a ParamType. convert_type() maps Python types (str, int, float, bool) to singleton ParamType instances (STRING, INT, FLOAT, BOOL).
patterns.rationale: Making ParamType __call__ the dispatch point means parameters can apply type conversion by simply calling self.type(value, param=self, ctx=ctx) — uniform whether the type is a built-in singleton, a custom class, or a wrapped function. The Generic parameterization lets type checkers track the return type through the conversion, so downstream code knows the value is int after IntParamType converts it.

patterns.name: Exception as exit signal with exit_code class attribute
patterns.description: ClickException carries an exit_code class attribute (default 1, UsageError=2). Exit is a RuntimeError with __slots__=('exit_code',) that signals the application should stop. The main() method catches ClickException subclasses, calls show() for user-facing output, then sys.exit(e.exit_code). Abort is another RuntimeError that maps to exit code 1. This replaces sys.exit() calls inside command logic with exception-based control flow.
patterns.rationale: Commands deep in the call chain need to signal 'stop the program with this code' without knowing whether they're running in standalone mode or being invoked from another command. Exceptions bubble naturally through the call stack. The exit_code on the exception class means different error types map to different codes (usage error=2, general error=1) without the caller needing to interpret the error type.

class NoHandler(Exception):

class Finish(Exception):
    """An exception that ends the request without producing an error response."""
    pass

class MissingArgumentError(HTTPError):
    """Exception raised by RequestHandler.get_argument.
    This is a subclass of HTTPError, so if it is uncaught a 400 response
    code will be used instead of 500."""

# In _execute():
# except Finish as e:

class Return(Exception):
    """Special exception to return a value from a coroutine.

    This exception exists for compatibility with older versions of
    Python (before 3.3). In newer code use the ``return`` statement instead.
    """
    def __init__(self, value: Any = None) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.value = value
        self.args = (value,)

patterns.name: augment_usage_errors context manager for error enrichment
patterns.description: A context manager that wraps parameter processing. If a BadParameter or UsageError escapes, it attaches the current context (ctx) and parameter (param) to the exception before re-raising. This means error-throwing code (like type converters) doesn't need to know which context or parameter it's operating under — the context manager fills it in retroactively.
patterns.rationale: Type conversion and validation code raises BadParameter without knowing which parameter or context triggered it. The augment_usage_errors context manager wraps the call site, catching the exception and enriching it with ctx/param before re-raising. This separates error generation (in types.py, deep in the call chain) from error context (known at the call site), keeping the type system decoupled from the command structure.

patterns.name: Group as command registry with decorator-based registration
patterns.description: Group extends Command with a commands dict. The @group.command() decorator creates a Command from a function and immediately registers it via add_command(). @group.group() creates nested groups. command_class and group_class attributes allow customizing the Command/Group class used by the decorators. CommandCollection extends Group to look up commands across multiple source groups, flattening many groups into one.
patterns.rationale: CLI applications are naturally tree-structured (groups contain commands). The decorator pattern (@cli.command()) makes registration declarative — each command function is annotated with its parent group, and the group builds the command tree at import time. command_class/group_class provide a customization point without requiring users to manually construct Command objects.

patterns.name: result_callback chaining for post-processing pipeline results
patterns.description: Group holds a _result_callback. When subcommands complete, their return values flow through _process_result() which invokes the callback with the return value(s). Multiple result_callback decorators chain: each wraps the previous, so the inner callback gets the original value and the outer gets the inner's result. In chain mode, the callback receives a list of all subcommand results.
patterns.rationale: Groups often need to post-process subcommand output — logging, cleanup, aggregation. Rather than forcing this into the group's own callback, result_callback separates post-processing from setup. Chaining (not replacing) means multiple decorators can each add a layer of processing, similar to middleware.

patterns.name: Dual-mode decorator: bare or parenthesized via callable detection
patterns.description: The @command and @option decorators detect whether they were called bare (@command) or with arguments (@command(name='foo')). If the first positional argument is callable, it's treated as the function being decorated (bare mode). Otherwise, a decorator factory is returned. Group.command() and Group.group() use the same pattern.
patterns.rationale: Users want to write @click.command for simple cases and @click.command(name='foo', cls=MyCommand) for complex ones. Supporting both in one function eliminates the need for a separate bare decorator. The callable check is the simplest possible dispatch — no sentinel, no optional bracket convention.

patterns.name: Help generation as formatter-feeding method chain
patterns.description: Command.format_help() orchestrates help generation by calling a sequence of format_* methods (format_usage, format_help_text, format_options, format_epilog), each writing to a HelpFormatter. The formatter is created by Context.make_formatter() (allowing customization via formatter_class attribute). HelpFormatter accumulates output in a buffer with indentation control, and section()/indentation() are context managers for scoped formatting.
patterns.rationale: Help output has many parts (usage, description, options, commands, epilog) that each need different formatting logic. Splitting into format_* methods lets subclasses override one part without reimplementing the whole. The formatter as a separate object (not string concatenation) handles width measurement, indentation, and paragraph wrapping uniformly. Context managers for sections ensure indentation is always balanced.

patterns.name: Feature-switch arbitration for shared parameter slots
patterns.description: When multiple options target the same parameter name (e.g. --upper/--lower both write to 'case'), handle_parse_result arbitrates based on ParameterSource ordering and _default_explicit tracking. The winner is determined by: slot empty, more explicit source, same source but not auto-downgrading-explicit. Losers restore the winning option's source. This prevents a non-explicit default from overriding an explicit default of another option.
patterns.rationale: Feature switches (--upper/--lower, --json/--yaml) are a common CLI pattern where multiple flags map to one variable. Without arbitration, whichever option is processed last wins, which may be the default of a non-selected option. The arbitration ensures the most explicitly-set value wins, falling back to the most explicitly-set default, providing predictable behavior for mutually exclusive options.

occurrences.snippet:
slot_empty = existing_value is UNSET
        more_explicit = existing_source is not None and source < existing_source
        same_source = existing_source is not None and source == existing_source
        auto_would_downgrade_explicit = (
            same_source
            and source == ParameterSource.DEFAULT
            and existing_default_explicit
            and not self._default_explicit
        )
        is_winner = (
            slot_empty
            or more_explicit
            or (same_source and not auto_would_downgrade_explicit)
        )
        if is_winner:
            ctx.params[self.name] = value
        elif existing_source is not None:
            ctx.set_parameter_source(self.name, existing_source)

patterns.name: Resilient parsing mode for non-interactive operations
patterns.description: Context.resilient_parsing flag disables interactivity (prompts), callbacks, and error raising during parsing. Type conversion errors are caught and values reset to UNSET. Used for shell completion: the parser needs to identify which command/option is being completed without actually executing or prompting. make_context() is called with resilient_parsing=True during shell completion.
patterns.rationale: Shell completion needs to parse partial input without side effects — no prompts, no callbacks, no type errors. A single flag disables all interactive behavior rather than threading if-not-interactive checks through every code path. Type conversion failures are silently swallowed because the completion system doesn't need valid values, just structure.

patterns.name: Thread-local context stack for implicit access
patterns.description: A threading.local() object holds a stack of Context objects. push_context()/pop_context() manage the stack. get_current_context() returns the top of the stack (or raises RuntimeError if empty). This allows any function in the call chain to access the current context without explicit parameter passing. The Context.__enter__/__exit__ methods push/pop automatically.
patterns.rationale: Helper functions like echo() or style() need to know the current context (for color settings) but shouldn't require callers to pass ctx through every layer. The thread-local stack makes the context implicitly available without polluting function signatures. The stack (not just a single value) supports nested command invocation where each level has its own context.

patterns.name: to_info_dict as introspection protocol for tooling
patterns.description: Context, Command, Parameter, and ParamType all implement to_info_dict() returning a plain dict of their public attributes. Context.to_info_dict() traverses the entire CLI structure recursively (commands contain sub-commands, params contain their type info). This provides a serializable snapshot of the CLI definition for documentation generators and other tools.
patterns.rationale: External tools (documentation generators, GUI builders, test harnesses) need to inspect the CLI structure without executing it. to_info_dict() provides a stable, serializable interface that decouples tooling from Click's internal class hierarchy. The recursive traversal (Context → Command → params → ParamType) means one call from the root gives the full structure.

patterns.name: Strategy as composable monadic generator (map / filter / flatmap)
patterns.description: A SearchStrategy[T] is a generator object that composes via .map(f), .filter(pred), and .flatmap(f). Each combinator returns a new strategy object, building a tree of strategies declaratively. The actual generation happens lazily via do_draw(data) when a value is needed. The __or__ operator composes alternatives (one_of). Identity functions short-circuit: map(identity) returns self.
patterns.rationale: Declarative composition separates strategy definition from execution. Users build complex generators from simple primitives without touching the generation engine. The monadic interface (map/filter/flatmap) is already familiar from functional programming, lowering the cognitive barrier. Lazy evaluation via do_draw means the strategy tree is cheap to build and can be introspected (is_empty, has_reusable_values) before any values are generated.

patterns.name: Decorator transforming function into parameterized test engine
patterns.description: @given(*strategies, **strategies) is a decorator factory that wraps a test function into a function that runs the test multiple times with generated inputs. The wrapper inspects the original signature, maps strategies to parameters, generates a new signature (minus strategy-filled params), and delegates to a ConjectureRunner engine. The wrapped function preserves the original function's name, doc, and signature via @impersonate + @define_function_signature so that pytest and other tools see the original function.
patterns.rationale: The decorator pattern lets users write property-based tests with zero boilerplate — just annotate. Preserving the original signature is critical for framework integration (pytest fixture resolution, unittest discovery). The @given decorator is the sole entry point; everything else (generation, shrinking, database) is hidden behind it.

patterns.name: Recursive fixed-point property computation for mutually recursive structures
patterns.description: recursive_property() computes properties (is_empty, has_reusable_values, is_cacheable) on strategy trees that may be mutually recursive. It starts with a default value, does a first pass with recursion blocking (returns default on self-reference), then if recursion was hit, iterates a fixed-point computation with listener tracking until values stabilize. Results are cached on the objects.
patterns.rationale: Strategy trees can be self-referential via st.deferred (e.g., recursive data types). Naive recursive computation would infinite-loop. The fixed-point approach handles arbitrary mutual recursion while converging to correct values. The two-phase strategy (fast first pass + careful fixed point only if needed) optimizes for the common case where no recursion exists.

patterns.name: Settings inheritance via sentinel-default with parent fallback
patterns.description: settings(parent=None, *, max_examples=not_set, deadline=not_set, ...) uses a not_set sentinel (UniqueIdentifier) as default for every parameter. In __init__, each parameter checks `if value is not_set: value = self._fallback.attr`. The fallback is either the explicit parent or the current global default profile. This creates a chain of settings objects where unspecified fields inherit from parent.
patterns.rationale: The sentinel pattern cleanly distinguishes 'user did not pass this argument' from 'user passed None'. This is essential because None is a valid value for several settings (e.g., database=None means no database). The fallback chain enables layered configuration: global default → CI profile → local settings → per-test decorator, each overriding only what they specify.

patterns.name: Named profile registry with DynamicVariable context switching
patterns.description: Settings profiles are registered by name (register_profile, get_profile, load_profile). The currently active profile is stored in a DynamicVariable — a thread-local variable with a context manager (with_value). local_settings(s) temporarily replaces the active settings within a context block, restoring the old value on exit. The metaclass settingsMeta makes settings.default a property that reads the DynamicVariable.
patterns.rationale: Thread-local DynamicVariable enables per-test settings overrides without global mutation. The profile registry provides named, reusable configurations (e.g., 'default' vs 'ci') that can be switched at runtime. The context manager pattern ensures settings changes are scoped and automatically reverted, preventing state leakage between tests.

patterns.name: DynamicVariable: thread-local with context manager override
patterns.description: A Generic[T] wrapper around threading.local that provides a .value property (with getter/setter) and a .with_value(v) context manager. The context manager saves the old value, sets the new one, and restores on exit. Used for thread-safe global-ish state that can be temporarily overridden within a code block.
patterns.rationale: Many parts of Hypothesis need contextual state (current settings, current build context, current data observer) that should be thread-local but also support scoped overrides. DynamicVariable provides this with minimal API surface — just .value and .with_value() — replacing what would otherwise be manual try/finally boilerplate at every call site.

patterns.name: Decorator as lazy wrapper with deferred evaluation
patterns.description: @defines_strategy wraps strategy factory functions in LazyStrategy, deferring evaluation of the underlying function until a value is actually drawn. The eager='try' variant attempts immediate evaluation, falling back to lazy on exception. The @cacheable decorator adds LRU caching of strategy results keyed by (function, args, kwargs). Combined, these two decorators make strategy construction both lazy and cached.
patterns.rationale: Many strategy definitions are recursive (e.g., from_type resolving through MRO). Lazy evaluation prevents infinite recursion at definition time. Caching avoids redundant computation when the same strategy is constructed repeatedly (common in parametrized tests). The 'try' eager mode is an optimization for simple strategies where immediate evaluation is safe and avoids LazyStrategy overhead.

class LazyFrame:
    """Representation of a Lazy computation graph/query against a DataFrame.

    This allows for whole-query optimisation in addition to parallelism, and
    is the preferred (and highest-performance) mode of operation for polars.
    """
    _pylf: PyLazyFrame = None

patterns.name: Composite draw function as first-parameter protocol
patterns.description: @composite decorates a function that receives a `draw` callable as its first parameter. The function calls draw(strategy) to generate values and returns a result. CompositeStrategy.do_draw simply calls self.definition(data.draw, *args, **kwargs). DrawFn is a Protocol (callback with optional label param) so type checkers understand the draw interface. The composite function is just regular Python — no generator/async needed.
patterns.rationale: The draw-first-parameter pattern is more readable than flatmap chains for multi-step generation. Users write imperative code with draw() calls, which is natural and debuggable. The Protocol type for DrawFn enables static type checking of composite strategies. By delegating to data.draw at runtime, composite strategies participate in the same shrinking and choice-recording pipeline as built-in strategies.

patterns.name: Three-method ABC with decorator wrapper for extension
patterns.description: ExampleDatabase is an ABC with three abstract methods (save, fetch, delete) and one default method (move). Concrete implementations: DirectoryBasedExampleDatabase (filesystem), InMemoryExampleDatabase (dict), GitHubArtifactDatabase (CI artifact). Wrapper decorators compose: ReadOnlyDatabase wraps and silences writes, MultiplexedDatabase fans out to multiple backends with deduplication. The metaclass _EDMeta intercepts class creation to warn about missing methods.
patterns.rationale: The three-method interface (save/fetch/delete) is the minimal contract for a key→set-of-values store. Keeping move as a default method (delete+save) means backends only need to implement 3 methods. The wrapper pattern (ReadOnly, Multiplexed) allows composing database behavior without subclassing each backend — a form of decorator pattern applied to the database itself.

class Provider(ABC):
    """Base class for command palette command providers."""

    async def startup(self) -> None:
        """Called after the Provider is initialized."""

    @abstractmethod
    async def search(self, query: str) -> Hits:
        """A request to search for commands."""
        yield NotImplemented

    async def discover(self) -> Hits:
        yield NotImplemented

    async def shutdown(self) -> None:
        """Called when the provider is no longer needed."""

    def matcher(self, user_input: str, case_sensitive: bool = False) -> Matcher:
        return Matcher(user_input, match_style=self.match_style, case_sensitive=case_sensitive)

patterns.name: Shrinker as multi-pass minimization engine with deterministic passes
patterns.description: The Shrinker takes a failing test case (ConjectureResult) and repeatedly applies shrink passes — methods that try transformations (delete choices, reduce integers, simplify strings) and update shrink_target if the predicate still holds. Each pass must be deterministic in whether it makes progress (not in which shrinks it finds). The shrinker runs passes in rounds until no pass makes progress. consider_new_nodes() evaluates a candidate and updates the target.
patterns.rationale: Finding a minimal failing example is the core value of property-based testing. The multi-pass design with deterministic progress ensures termination: each pass either shrinks or doesn't, and when none shrinks, we stop. Keeping passes independent allows adding new passes without affecting existing ones. The shortlex sort_key provides a total ordering that makes 'smaller' unambiguous.

patterns.name: Provider backend abstraction with lifetime control
patterns.description: PrimitiveProvider is an ABC with abstract draw_boolean/draw_integer/draw_float/draw_string/draw_bytes methods. Backends register via AVAILABLE_PROVIDERS dict (name → class). Each provider declares a lifetime: 'test_function' (one instance per @given test) or 'test_case' (new instance per generated input). The default HypothesisProvider uses random generation; third-party providers like crosshair use SMT solvers. Provider instances receive ConjectureData for stateful interaction.
patterns.rationale: Separating the generation backend from the engine allows plugging in fundamentally different approaches (random, symbolic, SMT) behind the same interface. The lifetime classvar lets backends choose their statefulness: a stateless random backend uses test_function lifetime, while a stateful SMT solver tracking constraints per-input uses test_case lifetime. This is dependency injection via class-level declaration rather than constructor parameters.

patterns.name: Rule-based stateful testing via decorator accumulation
patterns.description: RuleBasedStateMachine uses @rule and @initialize decorators that stamp marker attributes on functions (RULE_MARKER, INITIALIZE_RULE_MARKER). The setup_state() classmethod collects all rules from the class hierarchy into _setup_state_per_class cache. Rules specify targets (Bundles to push results to) and arguments (strategies or Bundle references). Bundles grow during test execution, enabling data flow between rules. @invariant marks functions checked after every step.
patterns.rationale: Stateful testing requires generating sequences of operations, not just isolated inputs. The decorator-accumulation pattern lets users declare rules as regular methods, with the framework collecting them automatically. Bundles provide a data-flow mechanism: rule A produces a value, rule B consumes it. This models stateful systems (databases, APIs, state machines) declaratively without manual sequence construction.

patterns.name: Pareto front for multi-objective optimization guidance
patterns.description: ParetoFront maintains an approximate Pareto-optimal set of test cases based on target_observations (user-provided metrics via target()). When a new test case is added, it's compared against a random sample (currently 10) of the front. Dominated entries are evicted. The front is sorted by shortlex key for deterministic shrink target selection. ParetoOptimiser uses the front to guide mutation toward higher-scoring inputs.
patterns.rationale: Single-objective optimization can miss bugs that only appear at specific trade-off points between competing metrics. The Pareto front preserves diverse test cases that are each optimal along some dimension. The randomized eviction (sampling 10) is an approximation — exact Pareto maintenance is quadratic — but works well in practice because max_examples bounds the front size.

patterns.name: Function impersonation for transparent framework integration
patterns.description: impersonate(target) is a decorator that overwrites a wrapper function's __code__ (filename, firstlineno), __name__, __module__, __doc__ to match the target. This makes the wrapper invisible to introspection tools — pytest sees the original test function, not the hypothesis wrapper. proxies(target) combines impersonate + wraps + define_function_signature to create a proxy with the exact signature of the target.
patterns.rationale: Testing frameworks (pytest, unittest) use function introspection for discovery, fixture resolution, and traceback presentation. If the @given wrapper doesn't look like the original function, these frameworks break. Impersonation is a pragmatic hack: lie about where the code comes from so that error messages point to the user's test, not hypothesis internals. A __hypothesistracebackhide__ breadcrumb is left for hypothesis' own introspection.

patterns.name: Metaclass-enforced immutability with helpful error messages
patterns.description: settingsMeta overrides __setattr__ on the settings class (not instances) to raise AttributeError with actionable guidance when users try to assign to settings attributes. The error message explains what to do instead ('use settings.load_profile' or '@settings decorator'). StateMachineMeta similarly intercepts settings assignment on state machine classes.
patterns.rationale: Settings objects are immutable by design — mutation would break the inheritance chain. But users naturally try `settings.max_examples = 10`, which would silently do nothing on instances (properties are read-only) or corrupt class state. The metaclass intercepts at the class level and provides actionable error messages, guiding users to the correct API instead of leaving them confused by a generic AttributeError.

patterns.name: Pre-instantiated singleton module object
patterns.description: A module exports a single pre-configured instance of its main class, created at import time with sensible defaults. Users import the instance directly rather than constructing their own. The class itself is still importable for advanced use, but the singleton is the primary entry point. Auto-initialization (e.g. adding a default stderr handler) happens at module load, controllable via environment variable.
patterns.rationale: Eliminates boilerplate of logger = getLogger(); logger.setLevel(); logger.addHandler(). Users get a working logger with `from loguru import logger`. The singleton pattern works for logging because there is conceptually one global logging pipeline. This contrasts with structlog's factory pattern where each module creates its own bound logger. The trade-off: simpler for users, less flexible for multi-tenant scenarios.

patterns.name: Sink type-dispatch: polymorphic add() by sink argument type
patterns.description: A single add() method accepts heterogeneous sink types (file path string, file-like object with .write(), stdlib logging.Handler, coroutine function, plain callable) and dispatches to the appropriate wrapper class via isinstance/hasattr checks. Each sink type is wrapped in a uniform adapter (StreamSink, StandardSink, AsyncSink, CallableSink, FileSink) that implements a common write/stop/tasks_to_complete interface.
patterns.rationale: One entry point for all sink types means users don't need to learn different APIs for different output destinations. The type-dispatch happens once at registration time, not per-log-call, so the runtime path is clean. The adapter classes normalize the interface so the Handler doesn't care what kind of sink it's writing to. This is the Strategy pattern with type-based selection rather than explicit strategy objects.

patterns.name: Immutable option tuple as per-call configuration
patterns.description: The Logger class stores all per-call configuration as a plain tuple (_options) rather than individual attributes. Methods like opt(), bind(), patch() create new Logger instances sharing the same _core but with modified option tuples. This makes each logger instance effectively immutable — methods return new configured loggers rather than mutating state.
patterns.rationale: Tuples are immutable and cheap to copy. By storing options as a tuple, methods like bind() and opt() can create derived loggers with O(1) tuple creation, sharing the same core. This is a lightweight alternative to frozen dataclasses for per-instance configuration. The Logger constructor takes the tuple elements as separate params, and methods destructure/reconstruct: `*options, extra = __self._options; return Logger(__self._core, *options, {**extra, **kwargs})`.

patterns.name: Patcher chain: list of record-mutating callables
patterns.description: Record patching is a chain of callables, each receiving the record dict and mutating it in-place. The chain is accumulated via patch() calls that append to a list. At log time, the global patcher (if any) runs first, then each per-logger patcher runs in order. Patchers are stored in the options tuple and propagated to derived loggers.
patterns.rationale: Patchers allow injecting dynamic context (e.g. request_id, hostname) into every log record without modifying the logging call site. The list accumulation means multiple patchers compose naturally — each sees the modifications of the previous. This is structlog's processor chain pattern applied to record mutation rather than log entry transformation. The in-place mutation avoids creating intermediate dicts.

patterns.name: ContextVar-backed contextualize for thread-safe context
patterns.description: The contextualize() context manager uses a module-level ContextVar to store a per-context extra dict. Entering the context sets a new dict (merging with existing), exiting resets to the previous value via the token. At log time, the record's extra dict merges core defaults, context-local values, and per-logger bound values. This makes context propagation safe across threads and async tasks.
patterns.rationale: contextvars.ContextVar provides automatic isolation across threads and asyncio tasks — each task sees its own copy. This is superior to thread-local storage for async code where multiple tasks share a thread. The token-based reset ensures clean teardown even with exceptions. The three-layer merge (core.extra → context.get() → logger.extra) creates a clear precedence: global defaults < contextual < per-logger.

patterns.name: Error interceptor as configurable catch-and-report guard
patterns.description: A dedicated ErrorInterceptor class wraps sink errors. When catch=True (default), sink exceptions are caught, printed to stderr with context (handler id, record repr), and the logger continues operating. The interceptor has a should_catch() method that handlers check before raising, making the catch/no-catch decision configurable per-handler.
patterns.rationale: Logging should never crash the application. A logging framework that lets sink errors propagate defeats its own purpose. But silent failure is also bad — operators need to know when sinks fail. The ErrorInterceptor pattern balances both: errors are reported (to stderr, not the sink) but not propagated. The per-handler configuration allows critical sinks to opt out of catching if needed.

patterns.name: Re-entrancy guard via thread-local flag
patterns.description: A thread-local boolean flag prevents infinite recursion when logging an exception triggers another exception that is also caught by the logger. The flag is set before logging the exception and cleared after. If the flag is already set when entering the catch block, the exception is re-raised instead of logged.
patterns.rationale: Without this guard, a broken __repr__ on an exception value could cause infinite recursion: logger formats exception → calls repr on value → repr raises → logger catches and formats the new exception → calls repr again. The thread-local flag breaks the cycle by detecting re-entrant logging and falling back to letting the exception propagate. Thread-local (not global) ensures independent threads don't interfere.

occurrences.snippet:
if getattr(logger._core.thread_locals, "already_logging_exception", False):
    return False
# ... log the exception ...
logger._core.thread_locals.already_logging_exception = True
try:
    logger._log(level, from_decorator, catch_options, message, (), {})
finally:
    logger._core.thread_locals.already_logging_exception = False

patterns.name: Deadlock-aware lock with thread-local acquisition flag
patterns.description: The handler's _protected_lock() context manager checks a thread-local flag before acquiring. If the lock is already held by the current thread (e.g. because a sink called logger internally), it raises RuntimeError with a descriptive message instead of deadlocking. The flag is set on acquisition and cleared on release.
patterns.rationale: Loguru is not re-entrant — calling the logger from within a sink would deadlock on the handler lock. Rather than deadlocking silently, the lock detects the re-entrant attempt and raises a clear error explaining the cause. This is more helpful than a hang because the user immediately knows what went wrong. The thread-local flag is necessary because the lock itself doesn't track which thread holds it in Python's threading.Lock.

patterns.name: Message as str subclass with record attribute
patterns.description: The formatted log message is a str subclass (Message) with a single __slots__ attribute 'record' holding the log record dict. The message can be used as a plain string (it IS a string) but sinks that need context can access message.record. The __slots__ prevents adding arbitrary attributes.
patterns.rationale: Sinks receive a single object that is both the formatted string (for simple sinks that just write it) and carries the full record (for complex sinks that need context). Making it a str subclass means callable sinks and file-like sinks work without any adaptation — they just receive a string. The record attribute is opt-in: only sinks that explicitly access it pay the cost of knowing about it. __slots__ keeps the memory footprint minimal.

occurrences.snippet:
class Message(str):
    __slots__ = ("record",)

patterns.name: Record attribute objects with custom __format__ for template formatting
patterns.description: Record fields like level, file, process, thread are represented as custom objects with __slots__ and custom __format__ methods. The __format__ method returns the default attribute (e.g. level.name, file.name) when no format spec is given, but the object also carries secondary attributes (level.no, level.icon, file.path) accessible via dot notation in format strings. This enables {level} → 'INFO' and {level.no} → 20 in the same template.
patterns.rationale: str.format() calls __format__ on the value. By implementing __format__ to return the primary attribute, the format string '{level}' works naturally. For secondary attributes, str.format's dot notation ('{level.no}') calls getattr on the object. This dual access pattern (primary via __format__, secondary via getattr) lets a single object serve both as a formatted display value and as a structured data container, without the overhead of dict lookups.

patterns.name: Fork-safe lock registration via os.register_at_fork
patterns.description: Locks are tracked in WeakSets and registered with os.register_at_fork. Before fork, all locks are acquired. After fork (in both parent and child), all locks are released. This prevents deadlocks in child processes that inherit locked mutexes from the parent. Logger locks are acquired before handler locks to maintain acquisition order.
patterns.rationale: When a process forks while a lock is held, the child process inherits the locked state but not the thread that holds it — guaranteed deadlock. os.register_at_fork provides hooks to sanitize locks across fork. The WeakSet tracking avoids preventing garbage collection of locks. The ordering (logger locks before handler locks) prevents deadlock between the two lock categories during the before-fork acquisition phase.

patterns.name: Enqueue-based multiprocessing-safe log dispatch
patterns.description: When enqueue=True, the handler puts Message objects on a multiprocessing.SimpleQueue instead of writing directly to the sink. A daemon thread (_queued_writer) reads from the queue and writes to the sink under a separate queue lock. The queue uses a sentinel (None) for shutdown and (True) for confirmation. complete_queue() blocks until all pending messages are processed.
patterns.rationale: Multiprocessing.SimpleQueue is process-safe, so child processes can log through the same handler without corrupting sink state. The daemon thread ensures writes happen in one process, avoiding the need for process-safe file operations. The confirmation mechanism (putting True, waiting for event) lets complete() guarantee all messages are flushed. The trade-off: messages are delayed by queue serialization, but logging calls return immediately (non-blocking).

patterns.name: String parser chain: multi-format type coercion with fallback
patterns.description: File sink configuration parameters (rotation, retention) accept multiple input types (str, int, timedelta, time, callable). Each is parsed by trying a chain of parser functions (parse_size → parse_duration → parse_frequency → parse_daytime) until one succeeds. If none match, a ValueError is raised. Each parser returns None on failure (not exception), enabling the chain.
patterns.rationale: Human-friendly configuration strings like '100 MB', '1 week', '18:00', 'sunday' are far more usable than raw integers or timedeltas. The chain pattern lets each parser handle only its domain and return None otherwise, avoiding complex if-else trees. The factory method (_make_rotation_function) converts the parsed value into a callable, normalizing all inputs to a uniform (message, file) → bool interface.

patterns.name: Environment variable defaults with typed coercion
patterns.description: All default configuration values are read from environment variables with type coercion. A single env() helper function handles str, bool, and int types with appropriate parsing and validation. Each config parameter has a sensible fallback default if the env var is not set.
patterns.rationale: Environment variables enable configuration without code changes — useful for Docker, CI, and 12-factor apps. The typed coercion ensures bool env vars are actually booleans (not strings 'true'/'false'), preventing subtle bugs. Centralizing the env-reading logic in one function avoids scattered os.environ.get() calls with inconsistent parsing. The naming convention (LOGURU_PARAM) is discoverable.

patterns.name: Markup tag parser as token stream with nesting validation
patterns.description: Color markup tags (e.g. <red>, </>, <level>) are parsed into a token stream of (TokenType, value) pairs. The parser maintains a stack of open tags, validates nesting rules, and supports escaping (\<red> prints literally). Three token types: TEXT, ANSI (color code), LEVEL (deferred level color), CLOSING (reset). The same token stream can be stripped (for non-color output) or colorized (with a specific level color).
patterns.rationale: Separating parsing from rendering allows the same format string to produce both colored and plain output without re-parsing. The token stream is produced once and reused for every log message. The LEVEL token type defers the level-specific color until render time, so a single format string works for all levels. The nesting validation catches user errors (mismatched tags) at parse time, not at render time.

patterns.name: Cached format preparation with lru_cache for dynamic formatters
patterns.description: When the format is a dynamic function (not a string), the handler memoizes the colorization/stripping of the returned format string using functools.lru_cache(maxsize=64). The cache key is the format string itself. This avoids re-parsing and re-colorizing the same format on every log call, which is common because dynamic formatters typically return one of a small set of format strings based on level.
patterns.rationale: Dynamic format functions add flexibility but risk performance — every log call runs the formatter and then colorizes the result. In practice, formatters return a small set of strings (one per level), so caching by format string value eliminates redundant work. lru_cache(maxsize=64) bounds memory and handles the common case (a few levels × a few formatters). The cache is rebuilt on __setstate__ (post-pickle) because the cached functions are closures.

patterns.name: Interceptor as decorator + context manager dual-mode object
patterns.description: The catch() method returns a Catcher object that works as both a decorator (via __call__) and a context manager (via __enter__/__exit__). The __call__ method detects whether it's being used as a bare decorator (catch, without parens) or a parameterized decorator (catch(...), returning Catcher). It wraps sync, async, and generator functions differently.
patterns.rationale: Users want to use exception catching in multiple ways: @logger.catch (bare decorator), @logger.catch(reraise=True) (parameterized decorator), and with logger.catch(): (context manager). A single object supporting all three modes reduces the API surface. The async/generator detection ensures the wrapped function's protocol is preserved — an async function stays async, a generator stays a generator.

patterns.name: opt() as immutable configuration overlay returning new instance
patterns.description: The opt() method creates a new Logger instance sharing the same _core but with modified per-call options (exception, depth, record, lazy, colors, raw, capture, depth). It does not chain — the last opt() call takes precedence because it resets all options to defaults except the specified ones. The bind() and patch() methods work similarly but only modify their respective tuple positions.
patterns.rationale: opt() enables per-call customization without polluting the global logger state. By returning a new Logger with the same core, the configuration is scoped to the returned instance. The 'last wins' rule (not chaining) keeps the mental model simple — you don't have to reason about accumulated options from multiple opt() calls. The shared _core means all loggers write to the same sinks — the options only affect how the record is created.

patterns.name: Module-level activation list for per-module log filtering
patterns.description: Log enablement/disablement is tracked as a list of (dotted_name_prefix, status) tuples, sorted by module depth (deepest first). When a module logs for the first time, its name is checked against this list — the first matching prefix determines the status. Results are cached in an enabled dict for O(1) subsequent checks. disable()/enable() prune conflicting entries before adding new ones.
patterns.rationale: Library authors need to disable logging for their module without affecting the host application. The prefix-based matching (dotted name + '.') naturally handles module hierarchies: disabling 'mylib' also disables 'mylib.sub'. The depth-sorted list ensures the most specific rule wins (child module rules override parent). The cache avoids repeated list scanning on every log call — once a module's status is determined, it's stored in the enabled dict.

patterns.name: Thread-first/thread-last: reduce-based value threading with form dispatch
patterns.description: Thread a value through a sequence of functions/forms using reduce. Each form is either a callable (applied directly) or a tuple (func, *args) where the value is inserted at the front (thread_first) or back (thread_last) of the args. This enables a UNIX-pipe-like syntax in pure Python where the value flows left-to-right through transformations.
patterns.rationale: Makes multi-step transformation chains readable as a flat sequence rather than nested function calls. The tuple form allows multi-argument functions to participate without partial application. Using reduce means the threading logic is a single expression, not a loop with mutable state.

patterns.name: Curry as callable class with introspection and partial merging
patterns.description: A curry class wraps a callable, storing accumulated partial arguments. On __call__, it attempts to invoke the underlying function; if a TypeError occurs and insufficient args were provided, it returns a new curry with the additional args merged. The class exposes .func, .args, .keywords as properties (delegating to functools.partial), implements __eq__/__hash__ for comparability, and __getstate__/__setstate__ for pickling (since functools.partial itself is not picklable).
patterns.rationale: Unlike functools.partial which requires all arguments upfront, curry allows progressive partial application with automatic detection of when enough arguments have been accumulated. The introspection properties (func/args/keywords) make curried functions transparent to debugging and testing. The pickle protocol override is necessary because the internal functools.partial is not picklable.

patterns.name: Curried decorator for auto-partial application namespace
patterns.description: A parallel 'curried' module that applies curry() to every multi-argument function in the main module. It introspects the main module's __dict__, identifies functions with >1 argument via inspect.getargspec, wraps them in curry(), and builds a new namespace where all functions support implicit partial application. Functions with 0-1 args pass through unchanged.
patterns.rationale: Provides a complete alternative API surface where every function is curried, without duplicating any function definitions. Users import from toolz.curried instead of toolz to get the partial-application-friendly versions. This is a module-level transformation pattern: one source of truth (the original functions), two API surfaces (eager and curried).

patterns.name: Memoize with pluggable key function and arity-aware caching strategy
patterns.description: memoize caches function results with a customizable key function. It inspects the wrapped function's signature to choose an optimal cache key strategy: for unary functions (single arg, no *args/**kwargs), the arg itself is the key; for functions that may have keyword arguments, the key is (args, frozenset(kwargs.items())); for the general case, just args. A user-provided key(args, kwargs) function overrides all of this.
patterns.rationale: The arity-aware key strategy avoids unnecessary tuple/frozenset overhead for the common case of unary functions, while correctly handling the complex case of mixed positional and keyword arguments. The pluggable key function lets users handle non-hashable arguments or implement custom cache eviction logic. memoize itself is curried, so @memoize(cache={...}) works as a decorator factory.

patterns.name: Compose as callable class with __slots__ and pickle protocol
patterns.description: A Compose class stores a tuple of functions in __slots__=['funcs']. __call__ applies them right-to-left. The factory function compose() returns identity for 0 args, the function itself for 1 arg, and a Compose instance for 2+. The class implements __getstate__/__setstate__ for pickling.
patterns.rationale: Using a class with __slots__ instead of a closure allows the composed function to be introspected (you can access .funcs), pickled, and compared. The factory function's special-casing of 0 and 1 args avoids unnecessary wrapper objects. Right-to-left application matches mathematical function composition notation f(g(h(x))).

patterns.name: Pipe: left-to-right value threading via sequential application
patterns.description: pipe(data, f, g, h) applies functions left-to-right: h(g(f(data))). Unlike compose (right-to-left) or thread_first (tuple-based), pipe is the simplest possible form: a for loop that reassigns data = func(data) for each function in sequence.
patterns.rationale: Left-to-right reading order matches the mental model of data flowing through a pipeline (like UNIX pipes). The implementation is deliberately trivial — a for loop, not reduce — because the operation is sequential by nature. This is the minimal viable pipeline: no metadata, no names, no type boundaries, just function application in order.

patterns.name: juxt: parallel function application with tuple collection
patterns.description: juxt(*funcs) returns a callable that applies all functions to the same arguments and collects results as a tuple. Accepts either multiple callable arguments or a single list of callables. Uses __slots__=['funcs'] and implements pickle protocol.
patterns.rationale: Juxtaposition (applying multiple functions to the same input) is a common pattern in data analysis — e.g., computing min/max/mean simultaneously. Making it a first-class callable means it composes with map, pipe, and other higher-order functions. The tuple return type is immutable and hashable, suitable for use as dict keys.

patterns.name: Functional dict operations: map/filter over keys/values/items
patterns.description: A family of functions (valmap, keymap, itemmap, valfilter, keyfilter, itemfilter) that treat dictionaries as functional data structures. map variants apply a function to keys/values/items and return a new dict. filter variants select items by predicate on keys/values/items. All return new dicts — no mutation.
patterns.rationale: Python's built-in dict comprehensions handle these cases, but named functions are more composable — they can be passed to pipe, compose, or juxt without a lambda. The symmetric naming (val*/key*/item*) creates a discoverable API surface where the operation and target are immediately clear from the name. Returning new dicts rather than mutating preserves the functional contract.

patterns.name: assoc/dissoc: non-mutating dict update returning new dict
patterns.description: assoc(d, key, value) returns a new dict with the key set — implemented as merge(d, {key: value}). dissoc(d, key) returns a new dict with key removed — copies then deletes. update_in(d, keys, func) recursively navigates nested dicts, applies func, and returns a new nested dict via assoc.
patterns.rationale: Clojure-style non-mutating dict updates. The original dict is never modified, enabling safe sharing of dicts across contexts. update_in's recursive implementation with assoc at each level means nested updates are expressed as a path + function, not manual nested copying. This is the immutable data pattern applied to Python's mutable dicts.

patterns.name: Iterator-first design: everything lazy, materialize on demand
patterns.description: All sequence functions return generators/iterators, never lists. Functions like mapcat, concat, interleave, unique, accumulate, sliding_window, partition, partition_all, pluck, and interpose use yield or return iterator-producing constructs (itertools.islice, itertools.chain.from_iterable). The caller materializes with list(), tuple(), or iterates directly. Even groupby returns a dict of lists only because the grouping operation requires materialization.
patterns.rationale: Lazy evaluation enables working with infinite sequences and large datasets without memory pressure. Functions compose without intermediate materialization — pipe(data, map(f), filter(g), unique) processes each element through the full chain before the next element is read. This is the functional programming contract: functions transform streams, they don't collect results.

patterns.name: Callable-or-index dual-mode key parameter
patterns.description: Functions that accept a 'key' parameter check `if not callable(key): key = getter(key)`. This allows the caller to pass either a function (e.g., lambda x: x['name']) or a raw index/attribute name (e.g., 'name' or 0). The getter() helper converts indices to operator.itemgetter calls and lists to multi-index getters.
patterns.rationale: Eliminates the need for callers to wrap simple indexing in lambdas. groupby('gender', data) is more readable than groupby(lambda x: x['gender'], data). The dual-mode parameter is a convenience layer that costs one callable() check at call time. This pattern recurs across groupby, reduceby, countby, join, and pluck — all sequence operations that need to extract a value from each element.

patterns.name: get_in: generalized nested access with reduce + default fallback
patterns.description: get_in(keys, coll, default) navigates nested data structures by reducing operator.getitem over the keys path. On KeyError/IndexError/TypeError, returns the default (or re-raises if no_default=True). This is a generalization of dict.get() to arbitrary-depth nested structures.
patterns.rationale: Nested data (JSON, nested dicts) access with manual try/except at each level is verbose and error-prone. get_in encapsulates the entire traversal + error handling into one call. The no_default flag lets callers distinguish 'return None because missing' from 'return None because the value IS None'. The reduce implementation is the minimal expression of sequential indexing.

patterns.name: merge_with: combine dicts via per-key function application
patterns.description: merge_with(func, *dicts) merges multiple dicts, collecting all values for each key into a list, then applying func to each list. This is a generalized merge that handles conflicting keys by transformation rather than last-wins overwriting.
patterns.rationale: Standard dict merge (update) uses last-wins semantics, losing data from earlier dicts. merge_with preserves all values by collecting them into lists and applying a combining function. This supports common patterns like sum-merge (merge_with(sum, ...)), first-merge (merge_with(first, ...)), or custom aggregation. The two-pass implementation (collect then apply) is clearer than interleaving collection and combination.

patterns.name: complement: predicate negation via function composition
patterns.description: complement(func) returns a function that returns the logical NOT of func's result. Implemented as compose(operator.not_, func). This is a higher-order function that transforms predicates.
patterns.rationale: Instead of writing lambda x: not iseven(x), you write complement(iseven). The composed function is inspectable (it's a Compose instance with .funcs), picklable, and works with any predicate. This is the functional programming approach to boolean operations: transform the function, not the data.

occurrences.snippet:
def complement(func):
    return compose(operator.not_, func)

patterns.name: do: side-effect injection in a pure pipeline
patterns.description: do(func, x) calls func(x) for its side effects, then returns x unchanged. This allows injecting logging, tracing, or debugging into a pipe/compose chain without affecting the data flow.
patterns.rationale: In a pure pipeline (pipe(data, f, g, h)), there's no way to observe intermediate values without breaking the chain. do solves this by being a transparent pass-through that executes a side effect. Composed with other functions, it becomes: compose(inc, do(log.append)) — the value flows through, is logged, and continues. This is the functional equivalent of a debugger watchpoint.

patterns.name: reduceby: fused groupby + reduce in single pass
patterns.description: reduceby(key, binop, seq, init) performs a simultaneous groupby and reduction in a single pass over the sequence. Instead of building intermediate groups (groupby then valmap(reduce)), it applies binop incrementally to each group's accumulator as elements are encountered. Supports both constant and callable init values.
patterns.rationale: The naive approach (groupby then valmap(reduce)) materializes all groups in memory before reducing. reduceby processes one element at a time, keeping only the running accumulator per group — O(groups) memory instead of O(elements). This makes it suitable for datasets larger than memory. The fused operation is also faster: one pass over the data instead of two.

patterns.name: fold: parallel reduce via chunked map + recursive combine
patterns.description: fold(binop, seq, map=map, chunksize=128, combine=None) partitions the sequence into chunks, reduces each chunk independently via map (which may be parallel), then recursively folds the intermediate results. The combine operator defaults to binop for associative operations.
patterns.rationale: Standard reduce is inherently sequential. fold decouples the reduction strategy from the binary operator: by accepting an injected map function, the same code works with sequential map, multiprocessing.Pool.map, or distributed map. The chunk size and combine operator are configurable, making fold a general-purpose parallel reduction framework. The recursive self-call on intermediate results handles arbitrary numbers of chunks.

patterns.name: EqualityHashKey: adapter for unhashable types in hash containers
patterns.description: EqualityHashKey wraps an unhashable item with a hashable adapter. The hash is computed from a key function (or a default sentinel), while equality delegates to the wrapped item's __eq__. This allows lists, dicts, and other unhashable types to be used in sets and dict keys.
patterns.rationale: Python's hash/eq contract prevents unhashable types from being used in hash containers. EqualityHashKey breaks this barrier by separating the hash (from a distinguishing key function) from equality (from the item itself). The __slots__ design and the warning about O(N²) scaling in the docstring show deliberate engineering: the adapter is a convenience, not a performance solution. The key function lets users optimize by choosing a good hash discriminator.

patterns.name: Sentinel string as module-level default marker
patterns.description: Module-level sentinel strings like no_default = '__no__default__' distinguish 'no value provided' from None (which is a valid default). Functions check `if default is no_default` to detect whether the caller passed a default at all, versus passing None as the intended default.
patterns.rationale: Python's convention of using None as a default sentinel breaks when None is a valid value. The string sentinel is simple, picklable, and visible in tracebacks. Unlike object() sentinels (which require module-level singletons and are not picklable), string sentinels are self-describing and survive serialization. The pattern recurs across itertoolz.py and utils.py.

patterns.name: Compatibility shim: version-conditional imports with __all__
patterns.description: A compatibility.py module centralizes Python 2/3 differences. It uses runtime version checks to assign the correct implementations (e.g., imap vs map) and exports them via __all__. Other modules import from compatibility rather than using conditional imports scattered throughout.
patterns.rationale: Centralizing version differences in one module means the rest of the codebase is version-agnostic. The __all__ list documents the compatibility surface. When Python 2 support is eventually dropped, only compatibility.py needs updating. This is the adapter pattern at the module level: one indirection layer absorbs environmental variation.

patterns.name: groupby via defaultdict append trick
patterns.description: groupby uses a defaultdict(lambda: [].append) to group items. Each key maps to the bound append method of a fresh list. After iteration, the actual lists are recovered via v.__self__ on each bound method. This avoids per-item isinstance checks or explicit list creation.
patterns.rationale: The defaultdict normally creates a list and then you'd append to it. By storing the bound append method directly as the defaultdict value, the hot loop (`d[key(item)](item)`) is a single dict lookup + method call — no attribute lookup for .append, no list construction check. The __self__ attribute of a bound method recovers the original list. This is a performance-oriented micro-pattern that trades readability for speed in the inner loop.

patterns.name: Semi-streaming join: materialize left, stream right
patterns.description: join(leftkey, leftseq, rightkey, rightseq) fully materializes the left sequence into a groupby dict, then streams the right sequence element by element, yielding matches as they are found. The left side is O(n) memory, the right side is O(1) per element. Outer joins are supported via left_default/right_default sentinels.
patterns.rationale: A full hash join requires both sides in memory. A streaming join (merge join) requires both sides sorted. This semi-streaming approach is the practical middle ground: the smaller side (left) is materialized for O(1) lookup, the larger side (right) is streamed. This pattern is common in database engines and data processing frameworks. The asymmetry is documented in the docstring: 'The LEFT sequence is fully evaluated and placed into memory. The RIGHT sequence is evaluated lazily and so can be arbitrarily large.'

patterns.name: iterate: infinite generator from repeated function application
patterns.description: iterate(func, x) yields x, then func(x), then func(func(x)), ad infinitum. It's a generator that never terminates unless the caller stops consuming. The implementation is a while True loop with yield.
patterns.rationale: Infinite sequences are a core FP concept (Haskell's iterate, Clojure's iterate). In Python, they're practical for generating test data, building power sequences, or implementing fixed-point iteration. The generator contract (lazy, pull-based) means the consumer controls termination. This complements take/drop which can extract finite prefixes from infinite sequences.

patterns.name: interleave: round-robin iteration with live iterator filtering
patterns.description: interleave(seqs) yields elements from multiple sequences in round-robin order. On each pass, it tries to get the next element from each iterator; exhausted iterators are filtered out of the newiters list. The loop continues until no iterators remain.
patterns.rationale: Standard itertools round-robin solutions often use sentinel values or zip_longest. This implementation cleanly filters exhausted iterators without sentinels: each pass builds a newiters list of still-alive iterators. The pass_exceptions parameter allows certain exceptions (like timeouts in async contexts) to be treated as 'skip this iterator' rather than errors. This is a generator that manages multiple sub-iterators as first-class objects.

patterns.name: Pure Python + Cython acceleration via separate package (toolz/cytoolz)
patterns.description: toolz is pure Python with no compiled dependencies. A separate package (cytoolz) provides Cython-accelerated implementations of the same API. The pure Python version is the reference implementation; cytoolz is a drop-in replacement that can be installed independently. The codebase is structured so that hot paths (groupby, reduceby, unique) have clear Cython equivalents.
patterns.rationale: Keeping the reference implementation in pure Python ensures maximum portability (any Python, any platform, no compiler). The Cython acceleration is an optional optimization, not a dependency. This separation means the library works everywhere out of the box, and performance-sensitive users can opt into cytoolz. The API contract is identical, so code written against toolz works with cytoolz without modification.
