patterns.name: Self-caching immutable config via __new__ + __slots__ + precomputed hash
patterns.description: Configuration object caches itself at construction time. __new__ (not __init__) builds a hashable tuple of all params, checks a module-level dict for a prior instance with same params, returns that cached instance if found, otherwise creates and caches a new one. All attributes stored in __slots__. Hash is precomputed once at construction. __eq__ compares the param tuple. __repr__ is lazily computed and cached. A module-level Lock guards the cache dict for thread safety.
patterns.rationale: Config objects are used as dict keys for memoizing decorators. Without caching, BeartypeConf(strategy=X) is BeartypeConf(strategy=X) would be False, breaking memoization. __new__ is used instead of __init__ because Python unconditionally calls __init__ even when __new__ returns a cached instance — __init__ would redundantly re-initialize. __slots__ reduces memory and attribute access time by ~10%, critical for a config object accessed on every type-check.

patterns.name: Exception with weakref culprits and __reduce__ pickle protocol
patterns.description: Type-checking violation exceptions store weak references (not strong references) to the offending objects ('culprits') to avoid memory leaks. A culprits property dereferences weakrefs on access, falling back to the stored repr string if the object has been garbage-collected. __reduce__ and __getstate__ are overridden to replace unpickleable weakrefs with their repr strings during pickling, enabling multiprocessing-safe exception propagation.
patterns.rationale: Exceptions often outlive the call stack that created them. Storing strong references to large user objects in exceptions would prevent garbage collection and cause memory leaks. Weakrefs allow the exception to hold a reference without extending the object's lifetime. The pickle protocol override is necessary because weakref objects are unpickleable, and multiprocessing transmits exceptions via pickle.

patterns.name: PEP-dispatched code generation by type hint kind
patterns.description: Code generation is dispatched by the PEP number of the type hint. A central make_check_expr() function inspects the type of the hint (e.g., typing.List → PEP 484/585, typing.Literal → PEP 586, typing.Annotated → PEP 593) and delegates to a PEP-specific code factory. Each PEP factory generates a boolean expression string that checks the pith against that hint. Factories are memoized per (hint, conf) pair.
patterns.rationale: Python's type hint system spans 30+ PEPs, each with different subscriptation semantics. A single monolithic function would be unmaintainable. PEP-specific dispatch keeps each generator small and testable, and memoization ensures each unique hint is compiled only once across all decorated callables.

patterns.name: Decorator dual-mode: decoration vs configuration via obj=None sentinel
patterns.description: A decorator supports two modes: (1) decoration mode (@beartype def f()) where obj is the callable, and (2) configuration mode (beartype(conf=BeartypeConf(strategy=On))) where obj is None and a new configured decorator closure is returned. The closure is cached by configuration in a module-level dict keyed by the BeartypeConf instance (which is itself cached).
patterns.rationale: Users need both @beartype (default config, most common) and @beartype(conf=...) (custom config, less common). The dual-mode pattern handles both with a single entry point. The configuration-mode closure cache ensures that repeated calls with the same config return the same decorator, avoiding redundant closure creation.

patterns.name: Optimization-aware decorator: identity noop under -O flag
patterns.description: At module load time, check if the Python interpreter is running in optimized mode (python -O or PYTHONOPTIMIZE). If so, replace the decorator with an identity function that returns the object unchanged. The check uses __debug__ / is_python_optimized() at import time, not at call time — zero runtime overhead when optimized.
patterns.rationale: Type-checking is development-time tooling. In production with -O, users expect zero overhead. By swapping the decorator at import time, there is no per-call cost — the wrapper function is never created. The TYPE_CHECKING guard ensures static type checkers still see the real implementation.

patterns.name: Exception-to-warning degradation for robust batch processing
patterns.description: A decorator factory accepts a warning_cls_on_decorator_exception config. When set (non-None), decoration failures are caught and converted to warnings instead of raising exceptions. The original object is returned unmodified. This is used by import hooks that process entire packages — one undecorable function should not crash the entire import.
patterns.rationale: Import hooks (beartype.claw) automatically decorate all functions in a package. Real-world packages have functions beartype can't handle (C extensions, exotic signatures). Fail-fast would make import hooks practically useless — one bad function kills the entire import. Warning degradation allows the import to continue, type-checking what it can and warning about what it can't.

patterns.name: Strategy enum for algorithm complexity selection
patterns.description: An Enum (BeartypeStrategy) with members named by Big-O notation (O0, O1, Ologn, On) selects the type-checking algorithm. O1 (default) checks one randomly-selected container item; On checks all items. The strategy is set per-decoration via config, and code generation branches on the strategy value.
patterns.rationale: Different use cases need different tradeoffs between type-checking coverage and runtime overhead. O(1) is the safe default — negligible overhead, catches most violations. O(n) is for development/debugging — full coverage at cost of performance. Naming by Big-O makes the tradeoff immediately obvious to users.

patterns.name: Custom memoization with exception caching (not functools.lru_cache)
patterns.description: A custom @callable_cached decorator caches both return values AND exceptions by argument tuple. Unlike functools.lru_cache, it: (1) has no size limit (unbounded), (2) skips statistics tracking, (3) caches exceptions so re-raising is O(1), (4) gracefully handles unhashable arguments by skipping cache. Single-argument calls flatten the tuple to the argument itself for faster dict lookup.
patterns.rationale: functools.lru_cache with maxsize=None still tracks hit/miss statistics, adding ~15% overhead. For a type-checking library where memoized functions are called thousands of times per decoration, this overhead is significant. Exception caching ensures that a type hint that caused an error once doesn't re-trigger the full error-handling path on every subsequent use.

patterns.name: linecache injection for debuggable generated code
patterns.description: When dynamically generating functions, inject the generated source code into the standard linecache module under the synthetic filename. This makes tracebacks through generated functions readable (pdb, traceback.print_exc show actual source lines). A weakref.finalize callback removes the linecache entry when the generated function is garbage-collected.
patterns.rationale: Dynamically generated functions have no source file. Without linecache injection, tracebacks show '<string>' with no source context, making debugging impossible. linecache.cache is a dict mapping filename → (size, mtime, lines, fullname). Injecting there makes the source available to pdb, traceback, and profilers. The finalize callback prevents memory leaks from accumulating dead function sources.

patterns.name: String template constants as code generation building blocks
patterns.description: Code generation uses triple-quoted string constants as reusable templates, stored in a dedicated module (_checksnip.py). Each template has named interpolation slots ({var_name}, {arg_random_int}). Factories format these templates with .format() and concatenate with f-strings to build complete function bodies. Templates are documented with their expected interpolation parameters.
patterns.rationale: Generating Python code by concatenating raw strings is error-prone. Named template constants separate the code structure from the interpolation logic, making both testable. Storing all templates in one module provides a single source of truth for the generated code's structure, while the formatting logic lives in the factory functions.

patterns.name: Exception hierarchy with PEP-numbered leaf exceptions
patterns.description: A deep exception hierarchy with a single root (BeartypeException), domain branches (BeartypeDecorException, BeartypeCallException, BeartypeConfException), and PEP-numbered leaves (BeartypeDecorHintPep484Exception, BeartypeDecorHintPep593Exception, etc.). Users can catch broad categories (except BeartypeDecorHintPepException) or specific PEPs. Mixins (_BeartypeHintForwardRefExceptionMixin) add cross-cutting concerns without inheritance coupling.
patterns.rationale: Type hint errors are inherently PEP-specific — a PEP 484 TypeVar error is different from a PEP 593 Annotated error. PEP-numbered exceptions let users catch exactly the errors they care about. The mixin pattern allows forward-reference handling to be applied across multiple branches without diamond inheritance.

patterns.name: Import hook + AST transformation for zero-config adoption
patterns.description: PEP 302/451-compliant import hooks (beartype.claw) intercept module imports, parse the module source to AST, inject @beartype decorators onto all annotated functions/classes/assignments, compile the modified AST, and execute the result. Users call beartype_all() once to type-check entire packages without modifying any source code.
patterns.rationale: Manual @beartype decoration of every function is tedious and error-prone. Import hooks enable zero-config adoption — one line enables type-checking across an entire codebase. AST transformation (rather than source string manipulation) preserves line numbers and is robust to formatting. The hook respects a skip list (claw_skip_package_names) for packages that shouldn't be type-checked.

patterns.name: Exception placeholder string for deferred error context
patterns.description: A magic placeholder constant (EXCEPTION_PLACEHOLDER) is passed through the code generation pipeline as the exception_prefix parameter. The real exception context (function name, parameter name) is only known at the outer call site. The placeholder is replaced at the end via reraise_exception_placeholder() which catches the exception, string-replaces the placeholder with the real context, and re-raises. This allows memoization — the generated code is identical regardless of which callable uses it.
patterns.rationale: Code generation factories are memoized by (hint, conf). If the exception prefix (which contains the callable name) were baked into the generated code, each callable would generate unique code, defeating memoization. The placeholder defers context injection to runtime, keeping the generated function reusable across all callables.

patterns.name: Configurable violation type: exception or warning per context
patterns.description: The config accepts violation_door_type, violation_param_type, and violation_return_type parameters, each accepting an exception OR warning class. Code generation checks at generation time (not call time) whether the violation type is a warning subclass, and generates either a raise statement or a warnings.warn() call accordingly. This is stored as precomputed booleans (_is_violation_param_warn, _is_violation_return_warn) on the config.
patterns.rationale: Some users want type violations as warnings (non-fatal, logged) rather than exceptions (fatal, halting). Different contexts (door checks vs parameter checks vs return checks) may want different severity. Precomputing the warning/exception decision at code generation time avoids a runtime branch in the hot path — the generated code directly contains either raise or warn() with no conditional.

patterns.name: FrozenDict: immutable dict for hashable config values
patterns.description: A FrozenDict class wraps a regular dict, exposing read-only access (keys, values, items, __getitem__) but no mutation. It implements __hash__ by hashing a frozenset of items. Used in config (hint_overrides=FrozenDict({...})) so config objects remain hashable and cacheable.
patterns.rationale: Python has no stdlib frozen dict. Config objects must be hashable for the self-caching __new__ pattern. Mutable dicts break hashing. FrozenDict provides immutability + hashability without requiring users to pass frozensets of tuples (which have awkward API for key-value access).

patterns.name: Lazy __repr__ with first-access computation and caching
patterns.description: The config's __repr__ method initializes self._repr = None at construction. On first call, it computes the repr string by iterating over all kwargs, omitting those matching default values (diff against BEARTYPE_CONF_DEFAULT._conf_kwargs), and caches the result in self._repr. Subsequent calls return the cached string.
patterns.rationale: Computing repr on every call is wasteful for a config object that might be repr'd thousands of times in debug output. The diff-against-defaults logic ensures repr only shows non-default parameters, keeping output concise. The None sentinel distinguishes 'never computed' from 'computed and empty string'.

patterns.name: Module-level deprecation via __getattr__ with name remapping
patterns.description: A module defines __getattr__(attr_name) (PEP 562) that intercepts access to deprecated attribute names. It looks up the deprecated name in a remapping dict (old → new name), imports the new attribute from globals(), emits a DeprecationWarning, and returns it. Unknown names raise AttributeError.
patterns.rationale: Renaming public API attributes breaks downstream code. PEP 562 module __getattr__ provides a clean deprecation path: old names still work but emit warnings, guiding users to new names. The remapping dict is the single source of truth for old→new name mappings. Isolating imports inside __getattr__ avoids polluting the module namespace.

patterns.name: Factory function generating a configured class
patterns.description: A plain function (not a metaclass, not a builder) that assembles and returns a new class from a configuration dict. The function body defines an attrs-decorated class inline, wires class-level constants (VALIDATORS, META_SCHEMA, TYPE_CHECKER) from the function's parameters, then returns the class. Callers invoke the factory to produce variant classes without subclassing.
patterns.rationale: Avoids metaclass complexity while still generating classes at runtime from configuration. The factory closure captures configuration (meta_schema, validators, type_checker) as class-level constants, so each generated class is self-contained. Enables creating draft-specific validator classes declaratively — each draft is just a function call with different arguments, not a subclass.

occurrences.snippet:
def create(
    meta_schema,
    validators=(),
    version=None,
    type_checker=_types.draft202012_type_checker,
    format_checker=_format.draft202012_format_checker,
    id_of=referencing.jsonschema.DRAFT202012.id_of,
    applicable_validators=methodcaller("items"),
):
    format_checker_arg = format_checker
    specification = referencing.jsonschema.specification_with(
        dialect_id=id_of(meta_schema) or "urn:unknown-dialect",
        default=referencing.Specification.OPAQUE,
    )

    @define
    class Validator:
        VALIDATORS = dict(validators)
        META_SCHEMA = dict(meta_schema)
        TYPE_CHECKER = type_checker
        FORMAT_CHECKER = format_checker_arg
        ID_OF = staticmethod(id_of)
        _APPLICABLE_VALIDATORS = applicable_validators
        # ... methods ...

    if version is not None:
        safe = version.title().replace(" ", "").replace("-", "")
        Validator.__name__ = Validator.__qualname__ = f"{safe}Validator"
        Validator = validates(version)(Validator)
    return Validator

patterns.name: Dual-registry decorator for version-keyed class registration
patterns.description: A decorator `validates(version)` that registers a class in TWO registries simultaneously: one keyed by version name (`_VALIDATORS`), one keyed by meta-schema ID (`_META_SCHEMAS`). The decorator returns the class unmodified. Later, `validator_for(schema)` looks up the appropriate class by reading the schema's `$schema` keyword and consulting the meta-schema registry.
patterns.rationale: Two registries serve two lookup paths: version name for explicit selection, meta-schema ID for automatic detection from schema content. The decorator pattern keeps registration at the class definition site, and the dual registration ensures both lookup paths stay in sync without manual bookkeeping.

occurrences.snippet:
def validates(version):
    def _validates(cls):
        _VALIDATORS[version] = cls
        meta_schema_id = cls.ID_OF(cls.META_SCHEMA)
        _META_SCHEMAS[meta_schema_id] = cls
        return cls
    return _validates

# Usage:
# Draft7Validator = create(meta_schema=..., version="draft7", ...)
# Inside create(): Validator = validates(version)(Validator)

patterns.name: ErrorTree via defaultdict recursion
patterns.description: Build a tree structure from a flat list of errors using `defaultdict(self.__class__)` as the children container. Each error's path (deque of keys/indices) navigates into the tree, creating child nodes lazily. The tree mirrors the validated instance's structure, allowing `tree[key]` to access the subtree of errors at that path.
patterns.rationale: Converting flat error lists into a tree that mirrors the instance structure lets consumers query 'does path X have errors?' in O(1) without scanning all errors. The `defaultdict(self.__class__)` trick makes the tree self-building — any access to a missing key creates a new subtree of the same type, so the tree grows organically as errors are inserted.

patterns.name: best_match: multi-criteria heuristic error selection
patterns.description: When multiple validation errors exist (possibly nested as context), select the most relevant one using a multi-criteria sort key. The key considers: error depth (deeper = more specific), path order, weak vs strong keywords, and type matching. Uses `heapq.nsmallest` to descend into error context, stopping when all children have equal relevance.
patterns.rationale: Validation produces trees of errors where parent errors (e.g., anyOf failed) contain child errors (e.g., type mismatch). Showing all errors is overwhelming; showing the first is often wrong. A heuristic that prefers deeper, more specific, non-weak-keyword errors gives users the most actionable error. The nsmallest approach efficiently finds the minimum without full sorting.

patterns.name: extend() for composition over inheritance
patterns.description: A standalone function that creates a new validator class by merging an existing validator's keyword handlers with additional ones. Explicitly documents that subclassing is unsupported and composition is the extension path. The function copies the parent's VALIDATORS dict, updates with new entries, then calls the factory to create a fresh class.
patterns.rationale: Subclassing creates fragile coupling to internal implementation details. extend() provides a controlled extension point: callers add or override keyword handlers without touching the parent class's internals. The result is a new independent class, not a subclass — no MRO issues, no fragile super() calls, no accidental method inheritance.

patterns.name: Cross-class evolve with registry-based dispatch
patterns.description: evolve() creates a copy of the current object with modifications, but may return a DIFFERENT concrete class. The new class is determined by calling `validator_for(new_schema)` which looks up a registry based on the schema's `$schema` keyword. This allows an object to transform into a different implementation when its schema changes to a different version/draft.
patterns.rationale: When a $ref resolves to a schema declaring a different draft version, the validator must switch to the appropriate draft's keyword set. Hard-coding the class would break cross-draft references. By consulting a registry inside evolve(), the switch is automatic and transparent — callers just call evolve() and get back the right type.

patterns.name: Generator-based lazy error collection
patterns.description: All validation keyword handlers are generator functions that `yield ValidationError` objects. iter_errors() chains generators lazily — errors are produced on demand, not collected upfront. is_valid() checks only `next(iter_errors(...), None)` — short-circuits on first error without computing the rest. validate() raises the first error.
patterns.rationale: Lazy generation means validation can short-circuit for is_valid() (stop at first error) while still supporting full enumeration via iter_errors() for error reporting. No separate code paths for 'check' vs 'collect' — the same generator serves both. Memory efficient for large instances with many errors.

patterns.name: Error parent chain for absolute path computation
patterns.description: ValidationError stores relative_path (local path segment) and a parent pointer. absolute_path is computed lazily by walking the parent chain and prepending each ancestor's relative_path. This allows errors from deeply nested validation to report their full path without storing it at creation time.
patterns.rationale: Storing absolute paths at error creation time would require each validation level to know its full context, creating tight coupling between nesting levels. The parent chain pattern lets each level only know its local segment; absolute paths are assembled on demand. This also means the same error object can be reparented without recalculating paths.

patterns.name: Deferred attribute population with sentinel guard
patterns.description: Error objects are created by keyword validators with minimal info (just message + local path). After the generator yields them, the caller fills in shared context (validator name, instance, schema, type_checker) via `_set()`. The `_set()` method only fills attributes that are still the Unset sentinel — it won't overwrite explicitly set values. This separates per-keyword error creation from shared context injection.
patterns.rationale: Keyword validator functions shouldn't need to know about the schema, instance, or type_checker — those are shared context. But error objects need all of it for reporting. _set() bridges this gap: keyword functions create errors with what they know, the framework fills in the rest post-hoc. The Unset sentinel prevents overwriting values that keyword functions explicitly set (e.g., a custom validator value).

patterns.name: Frozen checker with persistent data structure and redefine/remove
patterns.description: TypeChecker is a frozen (immutable) attrs class backed by HashTrieMap (a persistent/immutable map). redefine() and remove() return NEW TypeChecker instances with updated maps, never mutating. Draft-specific checkers are built by chaining: `draft4 = draft3.remove('any')`, `draft6 = draft4.redefine('integer', new_fn)`. Each draft's checker is a derivative of the previous.
patterns.rationale: Immutable checkers are safe to share across validators without copy-on-write concerns. The chained construction (draft4 from draft3, draft6 from draft4) makes the evolution of type rules across JSON Schema drafts explicit and auditable. HashTrieMap provides efficient structural sharing — draft7_type_checker and draft6_type_checker share most internal nodes.

patterns.name: Multi-target decorator for cross-instance registration
patterns.description: A decorator factory `_checks_drafts(draft3='ipv4', draft4='ipv4', ...)` that registers the same function across multiple FormatChecker instances simultaneously, each with a potentially different format name. The decorator iterates over draft-specific FormatChecker instances, calling `.checks(name)` on each. This enables a single function to serve as the validator for the same logical format across multiple schema draft versions.
patterns.rationale: Format validation functions (is_ipv4, is_email, etc.) are conceptually the same across draft versions but may have different names (e.g., 'ip-address' in draft3 vs 'ipv4' in draft4). Without the multi-target decorator, each function would need 6 separate @checks decorators. The decorator captures the mapping from draft to format name, making the registration declarative and DRY.

patterns.name: suppress(ImportError) for optional dependency registration
patterns.description: Optional format checkers (rfc3987, fqdn, webcolors, etc.) are registered inside `with suppress(ImportError):` blocks. If the optional library is installed, the format checker function is defined and registered. If not, the block is silently skipped — the format is simply not checked. No error, no warning, graceful degradation.
patterns.rationale: Format validation for specific formats (URI, hostname, color) requires third-party libraries that may not be installed. Making them hard dependencies would bloat the install. try/except ImportError at import time is the standard pattern, but `with suppress(ImportError):` is cleaner — it scopes the optional registration to a block, making it visually clear which functions are optional and which library they need.

from sys import hexversion

try:
    from uvicorn.supervisors.watchfilesreload import WatchFilesReload as ChangeReload
except ImportError:  # pragma: no cover

patterns.name: Namespace accessor via property returning namespace object
patterns.description: A large API surface is organized into logical groups by exposing properties (e.g. expr.bin, expr.cat, expr.dt) that return namespace objects (ExprBinaryNameSpace, ExprDateTimeNameSpace). Each namespace holds a reference to the parent object and delegates operations to it. This keeps the main class focused on core operations while domain-specific methods live in separate modules.
patterns.rationale: Expr has 12,000+ lines of methods. Without namespaces, the class would be unmaintainable and autocomplete would be useless. Namespaces group related methods (all string ops under .str, all datetime ops under .dt) while keeping them on the same object. New namespaces can be registered by users via register_expr_namespace.

patterns.name: Lazy proxy module for optional dependencies
patterns.description: A ModuleType subclass acts as both a lazy-loader and a proxy. On first attribute access, it imports the real module, replaces itself in globals, and forwards the attribute. If the module is not installed, attribute access raises a helpful ModuleNotFoundError naming the required package. The proxy is NOT registered in sys.modules — it lives exclusively within the project.
patterns.rationale: Heavy optional dependencies (pyarrow, numpy, pandas) should not be imported at module load time. A simple 'try: import numpy' either fails or loads eagerly. The proxy module pattern allows code to 'import polars._dependencies import numpy as np' and use np freely — if numpy is never accessed, it's never imported; if it is accessed without being installed, the error message tells the user exactly what to install.

patterns.name: Re-export module to break circular imports
patterns.description: A dedicated _reexport.py module imports and re-exports core types (DataFrame, Expr, LazyFrame, Series, etc.) with explicit __all__. Other modules import from _reexport instead of from the defining module, breaking circular dependency chains that arise when core types reference each other.
patterns.rationale: In a large codebase, Expr references DataFrame (for return types), DataFrame references Expr (for operations), LazyFrame references both. Direct imports create circular dependencies. The _reexport module is a single indirection point: it imports from the defining modules, and all other modules import from it. The cycle is broken because _reexport has no dependencies on the modules that import from it.

"""Re-export Polars functionality to avoid cyclical imports."""

from polars.dataframe import DataFrame
from polars.datatype_expr import DataTypeExpr
from polars.datatypes import DataType, DataTypeClass
from polars.expr import Expr, When
from polars.lazyframe import LazyFrame
from polars.schema import Schema
from polars.selectors import Selector
from polars.series import Series

__all__ = [
    "DataFrame", "DataTypeExpr", "DataType", "DataTypeClass",
    "Expr", "LazyFrame", "Schema", "Selector", "Series", "When",
]

patterns.name: classinstmethod: dual class/instance method descriptor
patterns.description: A custom descriptor that allows a method to be called on both the class and an instance. When accessed on an instance, it binds to the instance; when accessed on the class, it binds to the class. Uses __get__ to dispatch: if instance is not None, bind to instance; otherwise bind to the type.
patterns.rationale: DataType methods like base_type(), is_numeric(), is_integer() should work both as pl.Int64.base_type() (class method) and pl.Int64().base_type() (instance method). @classmethod doesn't work on instances properly for this use case, and @staticmethod loses the type context. The classinstmethod descriptor provides the right binding in both cases without duplicating the method.

patterns.name: DataTypeClass metaclass with dual-mode equality
patterns.description: A metaclass (DataTypeClass(type)) provides class-level type-checking methods (is_numeric, is_integer, is_temporal) via issubclass checks. The base DataType class implements __eq__ with overloads: comparing with a DataTypeExpr returns an Expr (for query building), comparing with a DataTypeClass checks issubclass, comparing with an instance checks isinstance. __hash__ uses hash(self.__class__) so instances of the same type are equal.
patterns.rationale: Polars data types exist in two forms: as classes (pl.Int64) and as instances (pl.Int64(), pl.List(pl.Int32)). Both should be comparable. The metaclass enables class-level checks (pl.Int64.is_numeric()) without instantiation. The dual-mode __eq__ allows types to participate in query expressions (pl.col('x') == pl.Int64) while also working in plain Python comparisons (pl.Int64() == pl.Int64()).

patterns.name: Schema as typed OrderedDict subclass with construction validation
patterns.description: Schema inherits from OrderedDict[str, DataType] and validates all values at construction time. A _check_dtype function ensures every type is a DataType instance, not just a DataTypeClass — nested/parameterized types must be fully instantiated. Accepts multiple input formats (dict, list of tuples, pyarrow schema via __arrow_c_schema__ protocol).
patterns.rationale: A schema is fundamentally an ordered mapping of names to types. By subclassing OrderedDict, Schema gets all dict operations for free while adding type safety. Construction-time validation catches errors early — e.g., passing pl.List instead of pl.List(pl.Int32) raises immediately, not when the schema is used in a query. The OrderedDict base preserves column order, which is semantically meaningful for DataFrames.

patterns.name: Exception dual-definition: compiled import or Python fallback
patterns.description: Exceptions are imported from a compiled extension module (polars._plr) when available. If the import fails (e.g., building docs without the binary), pure Python fallback classes with the same hierarchy are defined. The TYPE_CHECKING branch imports from the binary for type checkers; the else branch tries the import and falls back to stubs.
patterns.rationale: Exceptions in polars are defined in Rust and exported to Python via the C extension. But the Python code must still work when the extension isn't available (doc building, type checking, CI on non-target platforms). The dual-definition pattern ensures the exception hierarchy is always importable, with the real Rust-backed exceptions taking priority when available. The fallback classes carry docstrings so documentation generation works.

patterns.name: Unstable feature decorator with env-var gate
patterns.description: A @unstable() decorator marks functions as experimental. When called, it checks the POLARS_WARN_UNSTABLE environment variable — if set, it issues an UnstableWarning; if not set, the function runs silently. The decorator preserves the original signature via inspect.signature for tooling compatibility.
patterns.rationale: Polars ships APIs that work but may change. Users who want early access can opt in by setting POLARS_WARN_UNSTABLE=1 to discover which APIs are unstable. Users who don't set the flag are not bothered with warnings for APIs they're already using. This is gentler than @deprecated (which always warns) and more visible than a docstring note. The env-var gate means CI can run with warnings on, production can run without.

patterns.name: Config as reusable context manager + decorator with deferred application
patterns.description: Config can be used as a context manager (with pl.Config(...)) or decorator (@pl.Config(...)). It saves original state on __enter__, applies new options, and restores on __exit__ via save()/load(). The apply_on_context_enter=True flag defers option setting until context entry, allowing reusable Config instances: create once, apply in multiple scopes independently.
patterns.rationale: Configuration changes should be scoped — you want to temporarily change table formatting for one print, not globally. The context manager pattern handles this. But creating a new Config(...) object every time is wasteful when you reuse the same settings. The apply_on_context_enter flag separates creation from application: you create cfg = pl.Config(verbose=True, apply_on_context_enter=True) once, then use @cfg or with cfg: in multiple places, each getting its own save/restore cycle.

patterns.name: Deferred execution with optimization flag forwarding via decorator
patterns.description: LazyFrame represents a computation graph not executed until collect(). The collect() method accepts both new-style QueryOptFlags and deprecated individual boolean parameters. A @forward_old_opt_flags() decorator intercepts deprecated parameters, translates them to QueryOptFlags mutations via a mapping dict of lambdas, issues deprecation warnings, and passes the merged flags object to the actual function.
patterns.rationale: Query optimization has many flags (predicate_pushdown, projection_pushdown, etc.) that were originally individual parameters. Migrating to a QueryOptFlags object is cleaner but breaks existing code. The decorator translates old parameters to new flags transparently, with deprecation warnings guiding migration. The mapping dict of lambdas keeps the translation logic declarative rather than procedural — each old parameter maps to a one-liner that mutates the flags object.

patterns.name: Selector as Expr subclass with type-preserving set operations
patterns.description: Selector extends Expr and overrides set operators (__and__, __or__, __sub__, __xor__) to return Selector when operating with another Selector (preserving the selector type), but fall back to Expr operations when operating with non-selectors. __invert__ returns all() - self. This enables composable column selection: cs.numeric() - cs.float() selects all numeric except floats.
patterns.rationale: Column selectors need set algebra (union, intersection, difference) to express selections like 'all numeric columns except floats'. If set operations returned Expr, the result couldn't be composed further as a selector. By preserving the Selector type through set operations, complex selections compose naturally: cs.numeric() & cs.temporal() works. The fallthrough to Expr for non-selector operands ensures arithmetic still works: cs.numeric() + 1 adds 1 to all selected numeric columns.

patterns.name: Plugin function registration via dynamic library loading
patterns.description: register_plugin_function() loads a Rust-compiled dynamic library (.so/.dll/.pyd) from a file path or directory, resolves the path relative to the virtual environment, and registers a function from that library as a Polars expression. Uses lru_cache for path resolution. Non-expression arguments are serialized via pickle protocol 5. Capability flags (is_elementwise, changes_length, returns_scalar) tell the query engine how to handle the function.
patterns.rationale: Polars' expression system is extensible: users can write Rust functions, compile them to dynamic libraries, and register them as first-class expressions. The plugin system must handle path resolution (relative to venv for portability), serialization of non-expression arguments, and capability declaration so the optimizer can make intelligent decisions. The lru_cache on path resolution avoids repeated filesystem scans. The capability flags are essential — without them, the optimizer cannot safely reorder or parallelize plugin calls.

occurrences.snippet:
def register_plugin_function(
    *, plugin_path: Path | str, function_name: str,
    args: IntoExpr | Iterable[IntoExpr],
    kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    is_elementwise: bool = False,
    changes_length: bool = False,
    returns_scalar: bool = False,
    cast_to_supertype: bool = False,
    input_wildcard_expansion: bool = False,
    pass_name_to_apply: bool = False,
    use_abs_path: bool = False,
) -> Expr:
    pyexprs = parse_into_list_of_expressions(args)
    serialized_kwargs = _serialize_kwargs(kwargs)
    plugin_path = _resolve_plugin_path(plugin_path, use_abs_path=use_abs_path)
    return wrap_expr(plr.register_plugin_function(
        plugin_path=str(plugin_path), function_name=function_name,
        args=pyexprs, kwargs=serialized_kwargs,
        is_elementwise=is_elementwise, ...
    ))

patterns.name: CPU feature check before binary import via inline assembly
patterns.description: A pure-Python module checks CPU capabilities via inline x86 assembly (CPUID instruction) using ctypes memory allocation and mmap, BEFORE importing the compiled Rust binary. Platform-specific opcodes (POSIX 64-bit, Windows 64-bit, cdecl 32-bit) are assembled and executed. If required features are missing, a warning is issued suggesting the compatibility package.
patterns.rationale: The Rust binary may use CPU instructions (AVX2, SSE4.2, etc.) that don't exist on older processors. If the binary is imported first and then executes an illegal instruction, the process crashes with a SIGILL — no opportunity for a helpful error message. By checking CPU features in pure Python before importing the binary, polars can warn the user and suggest installing a compatibility build. The check must be in Python because the Rust compiler may emit SIMD instructions in the check code itself.

occurrences.snippet:
# Determine whether Polars can be run on the current CPU.
# This must be done in pure Python, before the Polars binary is imported. If we
# were to try it on the Rust side the compiler could emit illegal instructions
# before/during the CPU feature check code.

_POSIX_64_OPC = [
    0x53,                    # push   %rbx
    0x89, 0xf0,              # mov    %esi,%eax
    0x89, 0xd1,              # mov    %edx,%ecx
    0x0f, 0xa2,              # cpuid
    0x89, 0x07,              # mov    %eax,(%rdi)
    # ...
    0xc3                     # retq
]

def check_cpu_flags(feature_flags: str) -> None:
    if not expected_cpu_flags or os.environ.get("POLARS_SKIP_CPU_CHECK"):
        return
    missing_features = [f for f in expected_cpu_flags if not supported_cpu_flags.get(f)]
    if missing_features:
        warnings.warn(f"Missing required CPU features: {', '.join(missing_features)}...", RuntimeWarning)

patterns.name: Custom namespace registration via descriptor with caching
patterns.description: A NameSpace descriptor wraps a user-defined class. On first attribute access via __get__, it instantiates the namespace class with the parent object and caches the result via setattr(instance, accessor_name, ns_instance). Subsequent accesses return the cached instance directly. Registration is via decorator: @register_expr_namespace('name') which sets the descriptor as a class attribute and adds the name to _accessors set.
patterns.rationale: Users extend polars with domain-specific operations (e.g. a 'financial' namespace with Black-Scholes calculations). The descriptor pattern allows lazy instantiation — the namespace object is only created when first accessed, not at registration time. The setattr caching means the descriptor's __get__ is called only once per instance; subsequent accesses hit the cached attribute directly. The _accessors set tracks all registered namespaces for introspection and prevents overriding built-in ones.

patterns.name: DataTypeGroup as frozenset subclass with custom __contains__
patterns.description: DataTypeGroup extends frozenset with a _match_base_type flag. When True, __contains__ normalizes the query item to its base_type() before checking membership. This allows 'pl.Int32 in INTEGER_DTYPES' to match even when the group was defined with pl.Int32 (the class) rather than pl.Int32() (the instance). Pre-defined groups (INTEGER_DTYPES, FLOAT_DTYPES, TEMPORAL_DTYPES) are module-level Final constants.
patterns.rationale: Type checking in polars often asks 'is this type in the numeric group?' but the input might be pl.Int32 (class), pl.Int32() (instance), or pl.Datetime('us') (parameterized instance). Without base_type normalization, each form would need separate checking. DataTypeGroup with _match_base_type=True collapses all forms to their root type before comparison. Using frozenset as the base gives O(1) lookup and set operations (INTEGER_DTYPES | FLOAT_DTYPES = NUMERIC_DTYPES) for free.

patterns.name: Message pump as actor-model base class
patterns.description: A base class provides every instance with its own async message queue (asyncio.Queue) and a dispatch loop (_process_messages_loop). Messages are posted to the queue, then dispatched to handler methods via MRO walking. This is the actor model implemented via inheritance: every Widget/Screen/App is an independent actor with its own mailbox.
patterns.rationale: Decouples senders from receivers — any code can post_message() without knowing who handles it. Each node processes its own queue independently, enabling concurrent message processing across the widget tree. The actor model avoids shared-state concurrency bugs by giving each node its own isolated state and message queue.

occurrences.snippet:
class MessagePump(metaclass=_MessagePumpMeta):
    """Base class which supplies a message pump."""

    def __init__(self, parent: MessagePump | None = None) -> None:
        self._parent = parent
        self._running: bool = False
        self._closing: bool = False
        self._closed: bool = False
        self._disabled_messages: set[type[Message]] = set()
        self._pending_message: Message | None = None
        self._task: Task | None = None

patterns.name: Reactive descriptor with watch/compute/validate lifecycle
patterns.description: A descriptor type (Reactive) that intercepts attribute access (__get__) and mutation (__set__) to trigger a lifecycle: validate → store → check watchers → invoke watch_*/compute_* methods → trigger side-effects (layout/repaint/recompose/refresh_bindings). Watchers can be sync or async. Compute methods make attributes read-only derived values that auto-recalculate when dependencies change.
patterns.rationale: Encapsulates the entire reactive data flow (validate → store → notify → compute → refresh) behind a simple attribute assignment. Users write `self.value = 42` and the framework handles validation, notification, layout invalidation, and dependent recomputation. This removes boilerplate for property-change-notification patterns and makes data flow declarative rather than imperative.

patterns.name: Declarative compose via generator + context manager stack
patterns.description: Widgets declare their children by implementing compose() as a generator that yields Widget instances. Container widgets (using `with` context manager protocol) push themselves onto a compose stack; yielded widgets are added to the top of stack as children. The compose engine walks the generator, assigning parent-child relationships based on the stack state.
patterns.rationale: Allows declaring widget trees in a readable, nested, Pythonic way — `with Horizontal(): yield Label("left"); yield Label("right")` — without explicit parent assignment or builder APIs. The generator approach naturally supports conditional and loop-based composition. Error propagation through the generator (via .throw()) produces better tracebacks than exception handling in a builder.

patterns.name: WeakRef parent references to prevent reference cycles
patterns.description: In a parent-child tree structure, the parent reference is stored as weakref.ref() rather than a direct reference. The child holds a strong reference to nothing upward, while the parent holds strong references to children via NodeList. This prevents reference cycles that would otherwise defeat garbage collection.
patterns.rationale: In a DOM-like tree where children reference parents and parents reference children, direct references in both directions create reference cycles that the garbage collector must handle specially (and may leak). WeakRef on the parent direction breaks the cycle while still allowing children to access their parent. The property getter transparently dereferences the weakref.

patterns.name: Message coalescing via can_replace
patterns.description: The message processing loop peeks the queue before dispatching. If the next pending message can_replace() the current one (returns True), the pending message replaces the current one and is dispatched instead. This collapses redundant messages (e.g., multiple resize/refresh events) into a single dispatch.
patterns.rationale: High-frequency events (resize, refresh, scroll) can flood the message queue with redundant updates. Coalescing prevents the UI from lagging behind by processing only the latest state. The can_replace() method on Message is the extension point — subclasses override it to define coalescing rules, keeping the base loop generic.

patterns.name: Prevent context manager for message suppression
patterns.description: A context manager pushes a set of message types onto a ContextVar stack. While inside the block, post_message() checks the stack and silently drops messages of prevented types. The stack is per-async-context (ContextVar), so different tasks have independent prevention states.
patterns.rationale: Allows temporarily suppressing specific message types during programmatic state changes. For example, setting Input.value programmatically inside `with self.prevent(Input.Changed):` prevents the Changed message that would normally fire, avoiding feedback loops. Using a ContextVar stack (rather than instance state) ensures correct behavior with concurrent async tasks and proper cleanup via try/finally.

patterns.name: Optionally-awaitable return objects via __await__ + __call__
patterns.description: Methods return objects that implement both __await__ (for `await result`) and __call__` (for `result()` without await). The object wraps a Future; if awaited, it waits for completion; if not awaited, the work proceeds in the background. This allows callers to choose whether to wait.
patterns.rationale: In an async framework, some operations (mount, remove) should work both synchronously (fire-and-forget) and asynchronously (wait for completion). Returning an optionally-awaitable object avoids forcing callers to await when they don't need to, while still supporting awaiting when they do. This is more ergonomic than requiring `asyncio.create_task()` or returning a bare Future.

patterns.name: CSS cascade via class-level DEFAULT_CSS + __init_subclass__ inheritance control
patterns.description: Each widget class declares DEFAULT_CSS as a class variable string. __init_subclass__(inherit_css=True) controls whether subclasses inherit parent CSS. The _css_bases method walks the MRO collecting all classes that contribute CSS, respecting the inherit_css flag. CSS is scoped to the widget type name by default (SCOPED_CSS=True).
patterns.rationale: Allows widgets to carry their own styling as a class-level declaration — no external CSS file needed for default appearance. The inheritance flag lets subclasses opt out of parent styles when they want a completely different look. MRO walking ensures multi-level inheritance accumulates CSS from all ancestors. Type-name scoping prevents CSS from leaking to unrelated widgets.

occurrences.snippet:
def __init_subclass__(
        cls,
        inherit_css: bool = True,
        inherit_bindings: bool = True,
        inherit_component_classes: bool = True,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__()
        cls._inherit_css = inherit_css
        cls._inherit_bindings = inherit_bindings
        cls._inherit_component_classes = inherit_component_classes
        css_type_names: set[str] = set()
        bases = cls._css_bases(cls)
        cls._css_type_name = bases[0].__name__
        for base in bases:
            css_type_names.add(base.__name__)
        cls._merged_bindings = cls._merge_bindings()
        cls._css_type_names = frozenset(css_type_names)

patterns.name: Worker decorator with group/exclusive/thread semantics
patterns.description: A @work decorator wraps methods on DOMNode to return Worker objects instead of their original return type. Workers support named groups (for categorization), exclusive mode (cancels existing workers in the same group), thread mode (runs sync code in a thread), and exit_on_error (controls whether exceptions crash the app). A WorkerManager on the App tracks all workers.
patterns.rationale: Async tasks in a GUI framework need lifecycle management — cancellation when widgets unmount, grouping for mutual exclusion, and error handling that doesn't crash the app. The decorator approach integrates task management into the method declaration, making it obvious which methods are workers. Group/exclusive semantics handle common concurrency patterns (only one file load at a time) without manual task tracking.

occurrences.snippet:
@wraps(method)
        def decorated(*args, **kwargs) -> Worker[ReturnType]:
            self = args[0]
            assert isinstance(self, DOMNode)
            worker = cast(
                "Worker[ReturnType]",
                self.run_worker(
                    partial(method, *args, **kwargs),
                    name=name or method.__name__,
                    group=group,
                    description=debug_description,
                    exclusive=exclusive,
                    exit_on_error=exit_on_error,
                    thread=thread,
                ),
            )
            return worker

patterns.name: Signal as weak pub-sub with deferred callback option
patterns.description: A Signal object holds subscriptions in a WeakKeyDictionary keyed by DOMNode. Subscribers register callbacks that can be invoked immediately (direct call) or deferred (posted to the subscriber's message queue via call_next). Publishing checks all subscribers for liveness (is_running, is_attached) and auto-removes dead ones.
patterns.rationale: Provides a lightweight pub-sub mechanism that doesn't create strong reference cycles between signal owners and subscribers. WeakKeyDictionary auto-cleans when subscribers are garbage collected. The immediate vs deferred choice lets subscribers choose between low-latency direct calls and safe message-queue-based execution that won't interrupt current processing.

patterns.name: ContextVar-based implicit context propagation
patterns.description: Framework-wide context (active_app, active_message_pump, prevent_message_types_stack, message_hook) is propagated via contextvars.ContextVar, set and reset via context managers. This provides implicit access to the current app/message pump without passing it through every function parameter. Each async task gets its own copy of the context.
patterns.rationale: In a deeply nested call chain (widget method → reactive watcher → message handler), threading explicit 'app' and 'message_pump' parameters through every call would be extremely verbose. ContextVars provide per-async-task implicit context that works correctly with asyncio. The context manager pattern (_context) ensures proper cleanup on task exit, and ContextVars are async-safe (no thread issues within one event loop).

occurrences.snippet:
active_app: ContextVar["App[Any]"] = ContextVar("active_app")
active_message_pump: ContextVar["MessagePump"] = ContextVar("active_message_pump")
prevent_message_types_stack: ContextVar[list[set[type[Message]]]] = ContextVar("prevent_message_types_stack")
visible_screen_stack: ContextVar[list[Screen[object]]] = ContextVar("visible_screen_stack")
message_hook: ContextVar[Callable[[Message], None]] = ContextVar("message_hook")

patterns.name: Dual-indexed collection (list + set + dict-by-key)
patterns.description: A collection type maintains three internal data structures simultaneously: a list (for ordered iteration), a set (for O(1) membership checks), and a dict (for O(1) lookup by string key). Writes update all three atomically. Cached views (e.g. displayed_nodes) are lazily computed and invalidated by an update counter.
patterns.rationale: Widget children need ordered access (for layout), fast membership tests (to prevent duplicates), and fast id-based lookup (for CSS selector queries). Maintaining three indices costs O(n) memory overhead but gives O(1) for all three access patterns. The update counter allows downstream caches to invalidate only when the collection actually changes, avoiding redundant recomputation.

patterns.name: Metaclass-collected decorated handlers at class definition time
patterns.description: A metaclass scans class_dict at class creation time, finding methods with a specific attribute (_textual_on) stamped by a decorator (@on). It collects these into a class-level _decorated_handlers dict mapping message types to handler methods. This registry is used at dispatch time for O(1) handler lookup instead of runtime reflection.
patterns.rationale: Decorator-based handler registration (@on(Button.Pressed, '#save')) is ergonomic but would be slow if the framework had to scan every method on every message dispatch. The metaclass collects handlers once at class definition, building a lookup table. The decorator itself doesn't wrap the function — it only stamps metadata, so the function remains directly callable and inspectable. This separates registration (decorator) from discovery (metaclass) from dispatch (MRO walk with registry lookup).

patterns.name: Event bubbling with stop/prevent propagation control
patterns.description: After a message is dispatched to its target, if message.bubble is True and the target has a parent, the message is reposted to the parent's queue (_bubble_to). The message carries _stop_propagation and _no_default_action flags that handlers can set via message.stop() and message.prevent_default(). Bubbling continues up the DOM until stopped or the root is reached.
patterns.rationale: Enables a delegation pattern where parent widgets can handle events from children without the children knowing about their parents. A ScrollableContainer can handle key events from its children uniformly. The stop() and prevent_default() flags give fine-grained control: stop() halts bubbling, prevent_default() skips base-class handlers but continues bubbling. This mirrors DOM event semantics, making the behavior familiar to web developers.

patterns.name: Configurable: __new__ as factory for implementation subclasses
patterns.description: An abstract base class whose __new__ acts as a factory: when the base is instantiated, it creates an instance of a configured implementation subclass and calls initialize() instead of __init__. The implementation class is set globally at runtime via configure(). This lets the interface look like a normal class (isinstance works) while the actual implementation is swappable.
patterns.rationale: When the choice of implementation is a global decision (e.g. epoll vs select, or asyncio vs custom loop), a factory-class pattern lets callers write IOLoop() without knowing which subclass they get. Unlike dependency injection, this works at the class level without passing instances around. The initialize() method replaces __init__ because __new__ already chose the subclass — __init__ would run on the wrong class.

patterns.name: Template-to-Python compilation pipeline (Lexer → Parser → AST → CodeGen → exec)
patterns.description: A template system that compiles template strings directly into Python source code. The pipeline: _TemplateReader (lexer/tokenizer) → _parse (parser producing _Node AST) → _CodeWriter (code generator emitting Python source) → compile() (bytecode) → exec (runtime). Each _Node subclass has a generate(writer) method that writes Python lines, producing a function _tt_execute() that returns the rendered bytes.
patterns.rationale: Compiling templates to Python source (rather than interpreting them) gives maximum performance: the template runs as native Python code with no parsing overhead at render time. The _Node AST with generate() methods lets each template construct own its code generation, keeping the compiler extensible. The _CodeWriter tracks indentation and template source annotations for debugging.

patterns.name: Request lifecycle hooks: prepare → method → on_finish with exception interception
patterns.description: A request handler defines an ordered lifecycle: prepare() (common init, may be async) → HTTP method dispatch (get/post/etc, may be async) → finish() (cleanup). The framework's _execute() orchestrates this sequence, awaiting async steps, and intercepting all exceptions via _handle_request_exception. Subclasses override individual hooks rather than the orchestrator.
patterns.rationale: Separating the lifecycle into named hooks lets subclasses customize one phase (e.g. prepare for auth) without re-implementing the request dispatch flow. The framework handles error interception centrally, so handler code doesn't need try/except boilerplate. Making hooks optionally async (return Awaitable) allows gradual migration from sync to async without breaking the interface.

patterns.name: Exception as control flow: Finish exception for non-error request termination
patterns.description: A dedicated exception (Finish) that terminates request processing without triggering error-handling paths. Raising Finish ends the request immediately, calls finish() if not already called, but skips write_error and error logging. This lets handler code abort early from nested calls without returning through the normal call stack.
patterns.rationale: In a request handler, deep call stacks (handler → helper → auth check) may need to abort the request early. Throwing an exception is cleaner than threading return values or flags through multiple layers. Distinguishing Finish from HTTPError lets the framework know this is intentional termination, not an error — so it doesn't log or generate error pages.

patterns.name: Rule-based router with Matcher/Target separation
patterns.description: Routing separates matchers (PathMatches, HostMatches, AnyMatches — each implements match(request) → Optional[dict]) from targets (RequestHandler, nested Router, callable). A Rule pairs a matcher with a target and optional kwargs. RuleRouter iterates rules in order, first match wins. Tuples are auto-wrapped into Rules, and string patterns auto-wrapped into PathMatches.
patterns.rationale: Separating matching from handling allows orthogonal composition: any matcher can route to any target type. Matchers can extract path params (returned as dict), which flow to the target. Auto-wrapping tuples and strings keeps the common case ergonomic while allowing full Rule objects for complex cases. Nested routers enable hierarchical routing without the router knowing about its parent.

patterns.name: singledispatch for extensible type conversion
patterns.description: Using functools.singledispatch on a conversion function (convert_yielded) allows third-party types to register their own conversion to Future without modifying the original function. The base implementation handles built-in types (lists, dicts, Futures, awaitables); external code registers new types via @convert_yielded.register(SomeType).
patterns.rationale: When a function must accept many different input types and convert them to a common form, singledispatch is cleaner than a chain of isinstance checks. It follows the open/closed principle: open for extension (register new types), closed for modification (don't touch the original function). Tornado uses this to let tornado.platform.twisted register Deferred support without gen.py knowing about Twisted.

patterns.name: OutputTransform as response middleware with first-chunk/chunk split
patterns.description: Response transforms implement two methods: transform_first_chunk(status_code, headers, chunk, finishing) for the initial response (can modify status and headers), and transform_chunk(chunk, finishing) for subsequent chunks. The framework applies all transforms in order before writing. The base class is a no-op pass-through.
patterns.rationale: HTTP response transformation (e.g. gzip encoding) needs to modify headers on the first chunk but only transform body on subsequent chunks. Splitting the interface into first-chunk and chunk methods makes this natural. The base class being a no-op means transforms are opt-in — the framework can run with zero transforms. GZipContentEncoding adds content-encoding header and compresses, while also checking minimum length and content type before engaging.

patterns.name: with_timeout: non-canceling timeout wrapper for Futures
patterns.description: A function that wraps a Future with a timeout without canceling the underlying Future. On timeout, it sets an exception on the result Future but leaves the original running. A quiet_exceptions parameter suppresses error logging for specific exception types from the wrapped Future arriving late. The timeout handle is removed if the wrapped Future completes first.
patterns.rationale: Canceling a Future on timeout is unsafe — other code may be waiting on the same Future, and concurrent.futures.Future can only be canceled while queued. Instead, with_timeout creates a separate result Future, chains the original to it, and sets TimeoutError on the result if the deadline passes. This is composable: the original Future can be reused or awaited elsewhere. quiet_exceptions handles the common case where a late-arriving error after timeout is expected, not a bug.

occurrences.snippet:
def with_timeout(timeout, future, quiet_exceptions=()):
    future_converted = convert_yielded(future)
    result = _create_future()
    chain_future(future_converted, result)
    io_loop = IOLoop.current()

    def timeout_callback():
        if not result.done():
            result.set_exception(TimeoutError("Timeout"))
        future_add_done_callback(future_converted, error_callback)

    timeout_handle = io_loop.add_timeout(timeout, timeout_callback)
    future_add_done_callback(
        future_converted, lambda f: io_loop.remove_timeout(timeout_handle))
    return result

patterns.name: ObjectDict: dict with attribute-style access via __getattr__/__setattr__
patterns.description: A Dict subclass that delegates attribute access to key lookup via __getattr__ and __setattr__. Provides ergonomic d.key syntax alongside d['key'] without requiring a full dataclass. KeyError is translated to AttributeError for proper attribute semantics.
patterns.rationale: For configuration namespaces, template contexts, and settings — where keys are dynamic and a full dataclass would be overkill — attribute access is more ergonomic than dict indexing. Subclassing Dict preserves all dict operations (iteration, .get(), .items()) while adding .key sugar. Translating KeyError to AttributeError ensures hasattr() and try/except AttributeError work correctly.

patterns.name: OptionParser: global singleton with object-like access and caller-tracking
patterns.description: A global OptionParser singleton stores command-line options as _Option objects. Options are accessed as attributes (options.port) or items (options['port']). The define() method uses sys._getframe() to auto-detect which file defined each option, creating natural groupings. Options have type coercion (str/int/float/bool/datetime), callbacks on change, and a 'final' flag to freeze configuration after parsing.
patterns.rationale: Command-line options are inherently global state. A singleton with attribute access keeps usage ergonomic (options.port vs options.get('port')). Auto-tracking the defining file creates natural documentation groups without explicit group= arguments. The 'final' flag prevents late configuration changes from accidentally overriding intentional settings — once parse_command_line(final=True) runs, further define() calls are rejected.

patterns.name: UIModule: component with render + asset hooks
patterns.description: A UI component base class with a primary render() method that must be overridden, plus optional hooks for declaring assets: embedded_javascript(), javascript_files(), embedded_css(), css_files(), html_head(), html_body(). The framework collects assets from all modules on a page and injects them into the response. Modules are registered on the Application and instantiated per-request.
patterns.rationale: Web UI components need to declare both their rendered output and their dependencies (JS/CSS). Splitting these into separate hook methods lets the framework aggregate all module assets at page level — one script tag per unique file, not per module instance. render() as the only required method keeps the barrier low; asset hooks are opt-in. The per-request instantiation (module(handler)) gives modules access to the request context without global state.

patterns.name: chain_future: one-directional Future linking with thread-safety
patterns.description: A utility that links two Futures: when Future A completes, its result or exception is copied to Future B (unless B is already done). Handles both asyncio.Future (uses add_done_callback directly) and concurrent.futures.Future (routes through IOLoop.add_future for thread-safety). This bridges sync and async worlds without blocking.
patterns.rationale: When wrapping blocking code (run_on_executor) or converting between Future types (asyncio vs concurrent.futures), you need to propagate results without blocking. chain_future does this with callbacks, not await. The thread-safety branch (IOLoop.add_future for concurrent.futures.Future) ensures the callback runs on the right thread — concurrent.futures.Future can complete on any thread, while asyncio.Future must be modified on its event loop.

patterns.name: Safe API layer wrapping hazardous low-level primitives
patterns.description: A high-level 'safe' API module (e.g. Fernet) sits on top of a 'hazmat' (hazardous materials) layer containing low-level primitives. The safe API encapsulates correct cryptographic composition (encrypt-then-MAC, proper padding, key derivation) behind a simple interface, while hazmat exposes raw algorithms for experts who need fine-grained control.
patterns.rationale: Cryptographic APIs are dangerous when used incorrectly — wrong mode, missing authentication, improper padding. Separating safe recipes from raw ingredients lets most users never touch the dangerous layer, while still exposing it for experts. The module name 'hazmat' itself is a warning.

patterns.name: ABC interface with Rust implementation registration
patterns.description: Python ABC interfaces define the contract (abstract methods with docstrings), then Rust implementations are registered as virtual subclasses via ABC.register(). The ABC serves as documentation and type-checking target, while the actual implementation lives in compiled Rust. No Python subclassing of the ABC exists — registration is purely nominal.
patterns.rationale: Lets the Python interface serve as human-readable API documentation and type-checker target, while the high-performance implementation lives in Rust. register() avoids requiring the Rust type to inherit from the Python ABC, which would be impossible across the language boundary.

occurrences.snippet:
CipherContext.register(rust_openssl.ciphers.CipherContext)
AEADEncryptionContext.register(rust_openssl.ciphers.AEADEncryptionContext)
AEADDecryptionContext.register(rust_openssl.ciphers.AEADDecryptionContext)

patterns.name: Immutable builder with copy-on-modify returning new builder instance
patterns.description: Builder objects are immutable — each setter method validates the input, then returns a NEW builder instance with the updated field. The original builder is unchanged. A final sign()/build() method consumes the builder and produces the immutable result. Each setter also enforces 'set once' semantics (raises if already set).
patterns.rationale: Immutable builders are thread-safe by construction, allow branching (build multiple certificates from a common base by calling different setters), and make the construction history auditable. Copy-on-modify means you can partially configure a builder and reuse it as a template for multiple final objects.

patterns.name: Mode-algorithm cross-validation via validate_for_algorithm
patterns.description: Cipher modes implement a validate_for_algorithm(algorithm) method that checks mode-algorithm compatibility (e.g. IV length matches block size, key size restrictions). The Cipher constructor calls this method, providing a single validation point for cross-cutting constraints that neither the mode nor algorithm can validate alone.
patterns.rationale: Cipher mode correctness depends on the specific algorithm it's paired with (e.g. CTR nonce length must equal block size, XTS requires specific key sizes). Neither the mode nor algorithm has enough information to validate alone. The validate_for_algorithm method provides a clean seam for this cross-cutting validation without coupling the two hierarchies.

occurrences.snippet:
if mode is not None:
    assert isinstance(mode, modes.Mode)
    mode.validate_for_algorithm(algorithm)

self.algorithm = algorithm
self.mode = mode

patterns.name: Module-with-deprecations wrapper for lazy deprecation warnings
patterns.description: A _ModuleWithDeprecations wrapper replaces the real module in sys.modules. It intercepts attribute access via __getattr__, checks if the attribute is a _DeprecatedValue, and emits a deprecation warning before returning the underlying value. Non-deprecated attributes are cached in __dict__ for O(1) subsequent access.
patterns.rationale: Deprecation warnings need to fire on attribute access, not just at import time, because users may access deprecated symbols long after import. Wrapping the module transparently intercepts all access without modifying the original module's code. The caching mechanism ensures the deprecation cost is paid only once per attribute.

patterns.name: Versioned deprecation warning classes as migration timeline
patterns.description: DeprecatedIn36, DeprecatedIn40, DeprecatedIn41, etc. are all aliases of CryptographyDeprecationWarning. The class name encodes the version when deprecation was introduced, serving as a migration timeline. Users can filter by specific version class to suppress warnings they've already addressed.
patterns.rationale: A deprecation timeline encoded in class names lets users programmatically track which deprecations are new since their last upgrade. Filtering `warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=DeprecatedIn43)` suppresses everything deprecated in 43 and earlier, surfacing only new deprecations. This is more maintainable than version strings in messages.

occurrences.snippet:
class CryptographyDeprecationWarning(UserWarning):
    pass

DeprecatedIn36 = CryptographyDeprecationWarning
DeprecatedIn40 = CryptographyDeprecationWarning
DeprecatedIn41 = CryptographyDeprecationWarning
DeprecatedIn42 = CryptographyDeprecationWarning
DeprecatedIn43 = CryptographyDeprecationWarning
DeprecatedIn47 = CryptographyDeprecationWarning
DeprecatedIn50 = CryptographyDeprecationWarning

patterns.name: Capability query backend with FIPS-aware feature gating
patterns.description: A Backend class exposes *_supported() methods (hash_supported, cipher_supported, elliptic_curve_supported, etc.) that check both runtime capabilities (via Rust bindings) and policy constraints (FIPS mode). FIPS mode restricts the allowed algorithm set via class-level frozensets (_fips_ciphers, _fips_hashes, _fips_ecdh_curves) and minimum key sizes.
patterns.rationale: Cryptographic backends must enforce policy constraints (FIPS 140-3) that vary at runtime. Rather than scattering if-fips checks throughout algorithm code, the backend centralizes all capability queries. Callers ask 'is this supported?' before attempting an operation, getting a clean boolean rather than a cryptic OpenSSL error.

patterns.name: Sentinel class objects for named constant values
patterns.description: Instead of using string or integer sentinels, dedicated empty class objects serve as named sentinel values (e.g. _MaxLength, _Auto, _DigestLength). These are used as class-level constants on a parameter class, accepting either concrete values or sentinel objects.
patterns.rationale: Sentinel class objects have unique identity (isinstance check is unambiguous), readable repr, and cannot be confused with legitimate values. Using 'PSS.MAX_LENGTH' is more readable than passing -1 or 'max', and the type system can express the union of int | _MaxLength | _Auto | _DigestLength.

patterns.name: Generic class parameterized by mode type for overload-based return typing
patterns.description: A Cipher class is Generic[Mode] where Mode is bounded by Optional[Mode]. Overloaded methods use the type parameter to narrow return types: encryptor() on Cipher[ModeWithAuthenticationTag] returns AEADEncryptionContext, while on other modes returns CipherContext. The runtime implementation checks isinstance to dispatch.
patterns.rationale: Static type checkers can distinguish AEAD from non-AEAD cipher contexts based on the mode type parameter, preventing users from calling .tag() on a non-AEAD context or .authenticate_additional_data() on a plain context. The overloads make the type-level distinction visible without runtime cost.

patterns.name: Key rotation via multi-key decryption with single-key encryption
patterns.description: A MultiFernet wrapper holds a list of Fernet keys. Encryption always uses the first key. Decryption tries each key in order until one succeeds. The rotate() method decrypts with any valid key and re-encrypts with the first (newest) key, preserving the original timestamp.
patterns.rationale: Key rotation is a common operational need — old keys must still decrypt existing data while new encryption uses the new key. MultiFernet makes this transparent: decrypt tries all keys (parse token once, try each), and rotate re-encrypts without changing the timestamp so existing TTL logic still works.

patterns.name: Pre-instantiated module-level constants for hot-path objects
patterns.description: Expensive-to-construct objects used in hot paths are pre-instantiated at module level and reused across calls. The comment explains: 'Hoisted to module level so each operation doesn't reconstruct them.'
patterns.rationale: Cryptographic padding objects and hash algorithm objects are stateless after construction but carry configuration. Constructing them per-call adds unnecessary overhead in tight loops (e.g. decrypting many tokens). Module-level singletons amortize the construction cost.

occurrences.snippet:
# Hoisted to module level so each operation doesn't reconstruct them.
_PKCS7_128 = padding.PKCS7(128)
_SHA256 = hashes.SHA256()
DEFAULT_TIMEOUT: Final[ClientTimeout] = ClientTimeout(total=5 * 60, sock_connect=30)

patterns.name: Algorithm as value object with frozenset key_sizes and class-level name
patterns.description: Cryptographic algorithm classes are value objects: name and key_sizes are class-level constants (frozenset for immutability), key_size is an instance property derived from the actual key. The __eq__ method enables algorithm comparison. Constructor validates key size against the allowed set.
patterns.rationale: Algorithms are identified by name and constrained by valid key sizes — these are static properties of the algorithm, not of a particular instance. Making them class-level constants means they serve as both documentation and runtime validation. frozenset signals immutability and enables O(1) membership testing.

patterns.name: Duplicate-rejection guard for accumulated builder extensions
patterns.description: A module-level function _reject_duplicate_extension checks whether a new extension's OID already exists in the accumulated list. The check is explicitly quadratic ('This is quadratic in the number of extensions') — acceptable because extension counts are small (< 20). Called from every builder's add_extension method.
patterns.rationale: Duplicate OID detection prevents ambiguous certificates where the same extension appears twice. The quadratic approach is a deliberate trade-off: extension lists are short (< 20), so O(n²) is negligible, and using a set would require implementing __hash__ on Extension objects. The guard is shared across all builders via a module-level function.

patterns.name: Module-level deprecation via deprecated() helper with _DeprecatedValue wrapper
patterns.description: A deprecated() function wraps a value in _DeprecatedValue (holding value + message + warning_class), sets it on the module via _ModuleWithDeprecations, and returns the wrapper. When accessed, the module's __getattr__ intercepts the _DeprecatedValue and emits the warning. The original value is still returned.
patterns.rationale: Provides a declarative way to deprecate any module attribute — function, class, or constant — without modifying the attribute's code. The deprecation is registered at import time but fires at access time. The _DeprecatedValue wrapper carries all metadata (message, warning class) so the module wrapper knows what to emit.

occurrences.snippet:
utils.deprecated(
    Camellia,
    __name__,
    "Camellia has been moved to "
    "cryptography.hazmat.decrepit.ciphers.algorithms.Camellia and "
    "will be removed from "
    "cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.algorithms in 49.0.0.",
    utils.DeprecatedIn43,
    name="Camellia",
)

patterns.name: Interface hierarchy via mixin composition of abstract capability interfaces
patterns.description: Cipher interfaces are composed by mixin inheritance: CipherContext (update/finalize) → AEADCipherContext (adds authenticate_additional_data) → AEADEncryptionContext (adds tag) / AEADDecryptionContext (adds finalize_with_tag). Each layer adds one capability. Concrete implementations register against the appropriate interface.
patterns.rationale: Cryptographic cipher contexts have progressively more capabilities: plain ciphers update+finalize, AEAD adds authenticated data, encryption adds tag output, decryption adds delayed tag input. Mixin composition lets type checkers and runtime distinguish these capabilities. A user with an AEADDecryptionContext knows they have finalize_with_tag but not tag.
