patterns.name: Key splitting for separate encryption and signing subkeys
patterns.description: A single master key is split into independent subkeys for different purposes: first half for encryption, second half for signing. This ensures a compromise of one subkey doesn't directly compromise the other operation, and that encryption and authentication use different keys (required for some security proofs).
patterns.rationale: Using the same key for encryption and authentication can break security proofs. Splitting the master key into independent subkeys for each purpose is a simple key-separation strategy that doesn't require a KDF. The 32-byte Fernet key splits into 16-byte signing + 16-byte encryption subkeys.

occurrences.snippet:
self._signing_key = key[:16]
self._encryption_key = key[16:]
self._aes = algorithms.AES(self._encryption_key)

patterns.name: Verify-before-decrypt for authenticated encryption with explicit HMAC
patterns.description: Decryption verifies the HMAC signature BEFORE attempting decryption. The token is parsed into unverified parts (version, timestamp, IV, ciphertext, HMAC), the HMAC is verified against everything except the HMAC itself, and only then is decryption attempted. This prevents oracle attacks where decryption errors leak plaintext information.
patterns.rationale: Verifying the MAC before decrypting prevents padding oracle attacks. If decryption fails before MAC verification, the error pattern leaks information about the plaintext. By verifying first, all invalid tokens produce the same InvalidToken error regardless of what's wrong.

patterns.name: Fixed-size algorithm class variant for compile-time key size guarantee
patterns.description: Alongside the general algorithm class (AES with key_sizes={128,192,256,512}), fixed-size variants (AES128, AES256) hardcode a single key_size as a class-level constant. The constructor still validates, but the key_size is known at class-definition time, enabling stronger type-level guarantees.
patterns.rationale: Some cipher modes (e.g. XTS) require a specific key size. The fixed-size variants let APIs express 'I need exactly AES-256' via the type system (isinstance check), rather than runtime key_size inspection. The class name itself documents the key size, and the frozenset with one element is self-documenting.

occurrences.snippet:
class AES128(BlockCipherAlgorithm):
    name = "AES"
    block_size = 128
    key_sizes = frozenset([128])
    key_size = 128

    def __init__(self, key: utils.Buffer):
        self.key = _verify_key_size(self, key)

patterns.name: Deprecated module path with re-export and deprecation warning
patterns.description: When algorithms move from one module to another (e.g. primitives → decrepit), the old module re-exports them with a deprecation wrapper. The old import path continues to work but emits a deprecation warning with the new location and removal version. The re-export uses the deprecated() helper.
patterns.rationale: Module reorganization breaks downstream imports. Re-exporting with a deprecation warning gives users time to update their imports while signaling the removal timeline. The warning message includes both the new path and the version where the old path will be removed.

occurrences.snippet:
warnings.warn(
    "The `uvicorn.workers` module is deprecated. Please use `uvicorn-worker` package instead.\n"
    "For more details, see https://github.com/Kludex/uvicorn-worker.",
    DeprecationWarning,
)

patterns.name: Decorator-based draw pipeline wrapping with capability flags
patterns.description: Draw methods are wrapped by decorators that inject cross-cutting behavior (rasterization control) and stamp capability flags (_supports_rasterization) as attributes. The decorator checks state before delegating, and the attribute serves as a marker to prevent double-wrapping in subclasses.
patterns.rationale: Separates rasterization control from the draw logic itself. Subclasses get rasterization handling automatically via __init_subclass__; explicit override is detected by checking the marker attribute, avoiding double-wrapping.

patterns.name: __init_subclass__ auto-signature generation from introspected properties
patterns.description: Base class uses __init_subclass__ to introspect all get_/set_ property methods via ArtistInspector, then auto-generates a set() method with a proper inspect.Signature and docstring listing all settable properties as keyword-only parameters. A _autogenerated_signature flag prevents overwriting explicit subclass definitions.
patterns.rationale: Eliminates boilerplate: subclasses get a typed set(**kwargs) API for free, with IDE-visible parameter names, without each subclass manually listing its properties. The flag preserves explicitly-defined set() methods.

patterns.name: Inspector class for property introspection and alias discovery
patterns.description: A separate ArtistInspector class introspects Artist subclasses by scanning dir() for get_/set_ method pairs, discovers aliases from docstring patterns, and extracts valid values from ACCEPTS: annotations or numpydoc parameter types. Provides get_setters(), get_aliases(), get_valid_values() as a query API over the class structure.
patterns.rationale: Decouples property discovery from the Artist base class. The inspector pattern allows tooling (GUI, documentation generation) to query the full settable surface of any Artist subclass without the Artist itself carrying inspection logic.

patterns.name: Backend fallback chain: base class provides slow default, subclasses override for optimization
patterns.description: RendererBase defines draw_path as abstract (raise NotImplementedError) but provides fallback implementations for draw_markers, draw_path_collection, draw_quad_mesh that delegate to draw_path in a loop. Backends override the optimized methods if they can do better, but a minimal backend only needs draw_path.
patterns.rationale: Allows new backends to be functional with minimal implementation (just draw_path), while giving established backends optimization hooks. The fallback is correct but slow; the override is optional but fast.

patterns.name: Canvas swap context manager for format-specific rendering
patterns.description: print_figure uses _switch_canvas_and_return_print_method as a context manager that temporarily replaces the figure's canvas with one that supports the requested output format, yields the format-specific print method, then restores the original canvas on exit. This allows saving to any format regardless of the interactive canvas.
patterns.rationale: Decouples output format from display canvas. A figure displayed in a Qt window can still save to PDF/SVG/PGF by temporarily swapping to the appropriate canvas, without the user managing canvas lifecycle.

patterns.name: RcParams as MutableMapping + dict subclass with write-time validation
patterns.description: RcParams inherits from both MutableMapping and dict. __setitem__ looks up a validator function from a class-level validate dict, calls it on the incoming value, and stores the coerced result. __getitem__ has special-case lazy resolution for the backend key. Direct bypass methods _set/_get are provided for internal use with explicit deprecation warnings against dict.__setitem__.
patterns.rationale: Provides dict-like API ergonomics while enforcing type correctness on every write. The dual inheritance gives both the dict storage and the Mapping protocol. The _set/_get escape hatch acknowledges that some internal paths need to bypass validation but should be visible and deprecated for external users. [Merged from P305: Centralizes validation logic per config key in a flat registry. Adding a new config parameter means adding one entry to _validators with its validator function. The validator both coerces types (str→enum, str→float) and validates ranges, so stored values are always pre-validated.]

occurrences.snippet:
_validators = {
    'backend':           validate_backend,
    'backend_fallback':  validate_bool,
    'figure.hooks':      validate_stringlist,
    'toolbar':           _validate_toolbar,
    'interactive':       validate_bool,
    'timezone':          validate_string,
    'lines.linewidth':   validate_float,
    'lines.linestyle':   _validate_linestyle,
    'lines.color':       validate_color,
    'lines.marker':      _validate_marker,
}

patterns.name: Strategy pair: Locator (where) + Formatter (how to display) as swappable axis behavior
patterns.description: TickHelper is the shared base for two parallel strategy hierarchies: Locator (computes tick positions: tick_values(vmin, vmax) → array) and Formatter (converts values to labels: __call__(x, pos) → str). Both are set on an Axis and can be swapped at runtime. Locator has MAXTICKS safety limit; Formatter has context-dependent modes (format_ticks sets up state, __call__ formats individual values).
patterns.rationale: Separates 'where to place ticks' from 'how to label them', allowing independent swapping. A LogLocator works equally with a ScalarFormatter or LogFormatterSciNotation. The shared TickHelper base provides axis binding (set_axis/create_dummy_axis) so both strategies have access to the axis they serve.

patterns.name: Stale flag with upward propagation callback
patterns.description: Artist has a stale property (bool). When set to True, it triggers stale_callback(self, val) which propagates the staleness upward to the parent Axes (via _stale_axes_callback). The Axes in turn marks the Figure stale. This creates a bottom-up invalidation chain: any property change on a leaf Artist automatically marks all ancestors as needing redraw, without the caller knowing the tree structure.
patterns.rationale: Eliminates manual invalidation calls. When a user sets line.set_color('red'), the Line2D becomes stale → Axes becomes stale → Figure becomes stale → canvas schedules a redraw. The propagation is opt-out (animated artists skip it) and the callback is injectable for custom propagation behavior.

patterns.name: Transform tree with lazy invalidation and weakref parent links
patterns.description: TransformNode forms a DAG where each node stores weak references to its parents. When a node changes, invalidate() walks up the parent chain marking each ancestor with an invalidation level (AFFINE_ONLY or FULL). Lazy recomputation: get_points/get_matrix check _invalid flag and recompute only when stale. set_children() registers parent refs automatically during construction.
patterns.rationale: Transform trees can be deep (data→axes→figure→display) and recomputed frequently. Lazy invalidation ensures each node is recomputed at most once per draw cycle. Weakref parent links prevent reference cycles from leaking memory when transforms are replaced.

patterns.name: TransformWrapper: hot-swappable transform node with method delegation
patterns.description: TransformWrapper holds a single child Transform and delegates all transform methods (transform, transform_affine, transform_non_affine, transform_path, get_affine, inverted, get_matrix) by assigning them as instance attributes pointing to the child's methods. set() replaces the child and re-binds all delegated methods, triggering invalidation. Dimension properties are forwarded via property descriptors.
patterns.rationale: Allows replacing a transform at runtime without breaking the transform tree structure — parent nodes still point to the wrapper, not the child. The method rebinding is explicit (not __getattr__ dispatch) for performance: transform calls happen in hot drawing loops.

occurrences.snippet:
class TransformWrapper(Transform):
    def set(self, child):
        if hasattr(self, '_child'):
            self.invalidate()
        self._child = child
        self.set_children(child)
        self.transform = child.transform
        self.transform_affine = child.transform_affine
        self.transform_non_affine = child.transform_non_affine
        self.transform_path = child.transform_path
        self.get_affine = child.get_affine
        self.inverted = child.inverted
        self.get_matrix = child.get_matrix
        self.invalidate()

    input_dims = property(lambda self: self._child.input_dims)
    output_dims = property(lambda self: self._child.output_dims)
    is_affine = property(lambda self: self._child.is_affine)

patterns.name: Descriptor for marking inherited methods as unsupported
patterns.description: unsupported_method is a descriptor that, when assigned in a subclass body, generates a method raising UnsupportedError with a clear message ('SubclassName does not support method_name'). Uses __set_name__ to capture the owner class and method name at class-definition time. Optionally appends custom guidance.
patterns.rationale: Inheritance hierarchies that don't fully satisfy LSP (e.g., 3D axes not supporting twinx) need explicit opt-out. The descriptor pattern is declarative: `twinx = _api.unsupported_method()` reads as intent, not as a method body. The generated error message is always correct because it's built from __set_name__ metadata.

patterns.name: classproperty: property that triggers on class access, not just instance
patterns.description: A property-like descriptor where __get__ calls fget(owner) regardless of whether access is via class or instance. Unlike @property which only fires on instance access, classproperty fires on ClassName.attr access too. Only implements fget (no setter/deleter).
patterns.rationale: Some class-level attributes need computed values (e.g., supports_blit checks hasattr on the class). Regular @property doesn't fire on class access, requiring an instance. classproperty enables clean class-level computed attributes.

patterns.name: define_aliases: class decorator for property alias generation
patterns.description: A class decorator that takes an alias map {property: [alias1, alias2]} and generates get_alias/set_alias methods wrapping the original get_property/set_property. Stores the bidirectional mapping as _alias_to_prop on the class for later use by normalize_kwargs. Detects conflicts with parent class aliases.
patterns.rationale: Matplotlib has a massive set of property names (linewidth, markerfacecolor) with short aliases (lw, mfc). The decorator generates both getter/setter wrappers and a lookup table in one declarative step, avoiding manual alias method definitions. The stored _alias_to_prop enables kwargs normalization (set(lw=2) → set_linewidth(2)).

patterns.name: caching_module_getattr: property-based module-level lazy loading
patterns.description: A decorator that transforms a class named __getattr__ into a module-level __getattr__ function. Each @property in the class becomes a lazily-computed, cached module attribute. The result is cached via functools.cache, and accessing an undefined name raises a proper AttributeError.
patterns.rationale: Module-level __getattr__ is Python's mechanism for lazy module attributes, but writing it as a function with if/elif chains is brittle. The class+property pattern is declarative and self-documenting: each property is a lazy attribute, types are clear, and deprecation decorators can be applied per-attribute.

patterns.name: Deprecation decorator with type-dispatched wrapping (function/class/property)
patterns.description: The @deprecated decorator inspects the decorated object's type and applies different wrapping strategies: for classes it wraps __init__, for properties it subclasses the property type overriding __get__/__set__/__delete__, for functions it wraps directly. All paths emit the same deprecation warning via warn_deprecated and inject a deprecation notice into the docstring.
patterns.rationale: A single decorator handles all deprecation cases with consistent behavior (warning message, docstring update, version tracking). The type-dispatched approach means the caller writes @deprecated('3.0') regardless of what they're deprecating — the decorator figures out the right wrapping strategy.

patterns.name: Context manager for temporary attribute override with class/instance distinction
patterns.description: _setattr_cm(obj, **kwargs) is a context manager that temporarily sets attributes on an object and restores original state on exit. It distinguishes between instance-level attributes (restored via setattr), class-level properties (restored via setattr), and class-level non-property descriptors (restored via delattr). Uses a sentinel object() to detect attributes that didn't exist before.
patterns.rationale: print_figure needs to temporarily change figure DPI, facecolor, canvas, and _is_saving flag, then restore all of them. Manually saving/restoring each attribute is error-prone, especially when some might not pre-exist. The context manager handles the full lifecycle including properties and descriptors.

patterns.name: Backend registry singleton with entry point auto-discovery
patterns.description: BackendRegistry is a singleton with three backend sources: built-in (hardcoded dict mapping name→module+GUI framework), module:// syntax (arbitrary module path), and entry points (importlib.metadata, for third-party backends). Entry points are loaded lazily on first access. resolve_backend() determines the GUI framework by loading the module and checking required_interactive_framework class attribute.
patterns.rationale: Allows third-party packages to register backends without modifying matplotlib. The entry point mechanism is the standard Python packaging way to extend. Lazy loading ensures import time isn't affected by scanning for installed backends. The GUI framework detection (loading module + reading class attribute) defers the cost to first use.

patterns.name: Projection registry with duck-typed _as_mpl_axes protocol
patterns.description: Two registration mechanisms: (1) Axes subclass with a name class attribute → register_projection(cls) stores it in a name→class dict. (2) Any object implementing _as_mpl_axes() → returns (Axes_subclass, kwargs) — used for parameterizable projections. fig.add_subplot(projection=...) checks both: if string, looks up in registry; if object with _as_mpl_axes, calls it.
patterns.rationale: Simple projections (polar, 3D) just need a name and a class. Complex projections (custom geographic with parameters) need a factory. The _as_mpl_axes duck-typed protocol avoids requiring projection authors to subclass a specific base — any object with the method works, enabling composition over inheritance.

patterns.name: Colormap as callable: __call__ with bad/under/over special values
patterns.description: Colormap.__call__(X, alpha=None, bytes=False) maps scalar values in [0,1] to RGBA. Internally handles three special value categories: bad (NaN/masked → transparent), under (< 0 → _rgba_under), over (> 1 → _rgba_over). These are stored as indices N, N+1, N+2 in the lookup table. The callable interface means the colormap is a pure function: data → color.
patterns.rationale: Makes colormaps composable: Normalize maps data to [0,1], Colormap maps [0,1] to RGBA. The __call__ protocol means any function expecting a color mapper can accept a Colormap. Special value handling (bad/under/over) is built into the lookup table, not the caller's responsibility.

occurrences.snippet:
class Colormap:
    def __init__(self, name, N=256, *, bad=None, under=None, over=None):
        self._rgba_bad = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if bad is None else to_rgba(bad)
        self._rgba_under = None if under is None else to_rgba(under)
        self._rgba_over = None if over is None else to_rgba(over)
        self._i_under = self.N
        self._i_over = self.N + 1
        self._i_bad = self.N + 2

    def __call__(self, X, alpha=None, bytes=False):
        ...
        # maps X values to RGBA using lookup table with special indices

patterns.name: Normalize+Colormap two-stage data-to-color pipeline with autoscale
patterns.description: ScalarMappable chains Normalize (data→[0,1]) with Colormap ([0,1]→RGBA). Normalize has autoscale behavior: if vmin/vmax are None, they're computed from the first data array passed. Normalize has property setters that call _changed() to trigger callback, so changing vmin/vmax automatically updates dependent colorbars.
patterns.rationale: Separates the linear/logarithmic scaling decision (Normalize subclass) from the color mapping decision (Colormap instance). Both are independently swappable. The autoscale-on-first-data behavior provides sensible defaults without requiring the user to know data ranges upfront. The callback chain ensures visual consistency.

patterns.name: GraphicsContext as mutable state bag with copy_properties for save/restore
patterns.description: GraphicsContextBase holds rendering state (alpha, linewidth, capstyle, joinstyle, clip rect/path, dashes, hatch, etc.) as plain instance attributes. copy_properties(gc) copies all state from another gc. restore() is a no-op hook for backends that use a graphics context stack. No immutability, no slots — just a mutable state container with bulk copy.
patterns.rationale: Rendering backends need to snapshot and restore graphics state frequently (e.g., when drawing each artist, the renderer saves the current GC, modifies it, draws, then restores). The copy_properties method provides bulk transfer without serialization. The simplicity (mutable attributes) is intentional: GC objects are short-lived and performance-critical.

occurrences.snippet:
class GraphicsContextBase:
    def __init__(self):
        self._alpha = 1.0
        self._antialiased = 1
        self._capstyle = CapStyle('butt')
        self._cliprect = None
        self._linewidth = 1
        self._rgb = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0)

    def copy_properties(self, gc):
        self._alpha = gc._alpha
        self._antialiased = gc._antialiased
        self._capstyle = gc._capstyle
        self._cliprect = gc._cliprect
        self._linewidth = gc._linewidth
        self._rgb = gc._rgb
        ...

    def restore(self):
        pass

patterns.name: _val_or_rc: parameter-or-config fallback helper
patterns.description: A module-level function _val_or_rc(val, *rc_names) that returns val if not None, else the first non-None rcParams value from rc_names, falling back to the last rc_names entry. Used throughout matplotlib for function parameters that default to config values: facecolor=_val_or_rc(facecolor, 'savefig.facecolor').
patterns.rationale: Matplotlib has many function parameters that should default to a config value but also accept explicit overrides and None (meaning 'use config'). Without this helper, every call site needs a 3-line if/else chain. The variadic rc_names allows fallback chains (try this config, then that config).

patterns.name: check_in_list / check_isinstance: positional-first validation helpers with suggestion engine
patterns.description: _api.check_in_list(values, /, **kwargs) validates that each kwarg value is in the allowed set, raising ValueError with close-match suggestions (via difflib.get_close_matches) for string values. _api.check_isinstance(types, /, **kwargs) validates isinstance with friendly type names. Both use positional-only first parameter to allow 'types'/'values' as kwarg keys.
patterns.rationale: Centralizes the most common validation patterns (is this value in the allowed set? is this the right type?) with consistent, helpful error messages. The suggestion engine (difflib) turns 'ValueError: invalid linestyle' into 'ValueError: invalid linestyle; did you mean solid?' — a huge UX improvement for string enums.

patterns.name: Z-order based draw ordering with rasterization splitting
patterns.description: Axes.draw() collects all child artists, sorts them by zorder attribute, then splits the sorted list at a configurable rasterization_zorder boundary. Artists below the boundary are rasterized into a single image (for performance with many small elements); artists above are drawn as vectors. The draw loop interleaves renderer.start_rasterizing/stop_rasterizing calls based on the split.
patterns.rationale: A plot with 10,000 scatter points needs rasterization for performance, but text labels and axes must remain vector for crispness. Z-order splitting allows both: low-zorder artists (scatter points) are rasterized together, high-zorder artists (labels) are drawn as vectors. The boundary is configurable per-Axes.

occurrences.snippet:
artists = sorted(artists, key=attrgetter('zorder'))

rasterization_zorder = self._rasterization_zorder
if (rasterization_zorder is not None and
        artists and artists[0].zorder < rasterization_zorder):
    split_index = np.searchsorted(
        [art.zorder for art in artists],
        rasterization_zorder, side='right'
    )
    # rasterize artists below split_index, vector above

patterns.name: select_matching_signature: try-multiple-overloads function dispatch
patterns.description: Given a list of functions, tries each one with the given args/kwargs in order. Functions that raise TypeError (signature mismatch) are silently skipped. The first function that succeeds returns its result. If all fail, the last TypeError is re-raised. Used to support multiple calling conventions for the same public API.
patterns.rationale: Matplotlib's public API has evolved over 20 years, accumulating multiple calling conventions for the same function. Rather than deprecating old signatures, select_matching_signature allows a function to accept both old and new conventions, trying new first and falling back to old.

patterns.name: Iterator wrapper with internal cache for added capabilities
patterns.description: Wrap an iterator and maintain an internal cache (deque or list) to provide capabilities the underlying iterator lacks: lookahead (peek), prepending (prepend), random access (__getitem__), and rewinding (seek). __next__ checks the cache first before pulling from the source.
patterns.rationale: Plain iterators are forward-only and single-pass. Many algorithms need lookahead, rewind, or indexing. Rather than materializing the entire sequence, the wrapper caches only what's needed and lazily pulls from the source. This avoids copying while enabling non-sequential access patterns.

patterns.name: Seekable iterator with configurable cache window
patterns.description: Wrap an iterator with a cache that supports arbitrary seek positions. The cache grows as items are consumed, or is bounded by maxlen for memory safety. Supports relative_seek, peek, and __getitem__ into the cache. Returns a SequenceView of cached elements for inspection without copying.
patterns.rationale: Some algorithms need to rewind and re-process earlier items. A seekable wrapper caches consumed items so they can be revisited. The maxlen parameter prevents unbounded memory growth on large or infinite iterables, trading rewind range for memory.

patterns.name: Lazy partition via shared source with twin buffer generators
patterns.description: Split an iterable into two lazy sub-iterators based on a predicate, using a single shared source iterator and two deque buffers. Each generator pulls from the shared source, buffering items that belong to the other partition. Neither partition is materialized until consumed.
patterns.rationale: Eager partitioning (e.g., two list comprehensions) requires materializing both halves. Twin lazy generators with shared buffers allow streaming: consuming one partition only pulls enough from the source to satisfy that partition, buffering the other side. This works on infinite iterables and minimizes memory.

patterns.name: Namespace class with only static methods
patterns.description: Use a class with only @staticmethod methods as a namespace to group related encode/decode functions. No __init__, no instance state, no class state — the class is purely a container for related callable names.
patterns.rationale: When two functions are tightly coupled (encode/decode, read/write) but don't share state, a namespace class provides discoverability and grouping without the overhead of a separate module. The class name becomes the namespace: run_length.encode, run_length.decode.

patterns.name: Automatic algorithm selection by parameter threshold
patterns.description: Select between multiple algorithm implementations based on a parameter value, using a simple threshold comparison rather than an explicit strategy enum. The caller sees one function; the internal dispatch is invisible.
patterns.rationale: Different input sizes have different optimal algorithms (islice-based for small n, deque-based for large n). Exposing this as a strategy enum adds API complexity for no user benefit. A threshold-based dispatch keeps the interface simple while optimizing performance automatically.

patterns.name: Time-bounded iterator with state flag
patterns.description: Wrap an iterator to stop yielding after a time limit. Checks monotonic() before each yield. Sets a timed_out attribute to True if the limit was hit, allowing the caller to distinguish between natural exhaustion and timeout.
patterns.rationale: When processing untrusted or unbounded iterators, a time limit prevents runaway computation. The timed_out flag lets the caller distinguish 'iterator finished naturally' from 'iterator was cut short', enabling graceful degradation.

patterns.name: Coroutine auto-prime decorator
patterns.description: Decorator that advances a PEP-342 coroutine generator to its first yield point, so the caller can use .send() immediately without manually calling next(). Wraps the generator function to auto-priming the returned generator.
patterns.rationale: PEP-342 coroutines require priming (calling next() before .send()). This is a common source of bugs — forgetting to prime causes TypeError. The decorator eliminates the boilerplate and the footgun, making coroutines usable as drop-in consumers.

patterns.name: Function-to-decorator adapter via result_index
patterns.description: Convert any iterable-transforming function into a decorator factory. The result_index parameter specifies where the decorated function's result goes in the wrapping function's signature, enabling automatic insertion.
patterns.rationale: Many iterable utilities (chunked, filter, peekable) are functions, not decorators. make_decorator bridges this gap, allowing the same utility to be used at function definition time (as a decorator) or at call time (as a function). This avoids duplicating logic into decorator versions.

patterns.name: Type-preserving defaults via type inference from arguments
patterns.description: When a function accepts numeric arguments of arbitrary type (int, float, Decimal, Fraction, datetime), compute default values using the type of the input arguments themselves: type(self._stop)(0), type(self._stop - self._start)(1). This ensures all internal values match the caller's numeric type.
patterns.rationale: Hardcoding defaults as int (0, 1) breaks when the caller uses Decimal or Fraction — mixing types causes precision loss or TypeError. By inferring the type from the input, the function works transparently across all numeric types without type-checking branches.

patterns.name: Zero-copy read-only view via ABC delegation
patterns.description: Wrap a Sequence object and delegate __getitem__ and __len__ to the target, providing a read-only dynamic view. The view updates when the underlying sequence changes. Constructor validates the target is a Sequence (rejecting iterators). No data is copied.
patterns.rationale: Copying a sequence to provide read-only access is wasteful. A view that delegates indexing to the source gives read-only semantics with near-zero overhead. The ABC type check (isinstance(target, Sequence)) ensures the view only wraps objects that support indexing, failing fast on incompatible types.

patterns.name: Exception-based filtering and mapping
patterns.description: Filter or map an iterable by using try/except on a validator function: filter_except yields items where the validator does NOT raise specified exceptions; map_except yields transformed items unless the function raises specified exceptions. This uses exception propagation as the filtering signal, not boolean predicates.
patterns.rationale: Some validations are naturally exception-based (int('abc') raises ValueError, not returns False). Converting these to boolean predicates requires wrapping every call in try/except boilerplate. filter_except/map_except internalize this pattern, making exception-based filtering as ergonomic as predicate-based filtering.

patterns.name: Transparent observability wrapper with side-effect counter
patterns.description: Wrap an iterator and increment a counter attribute each time __next__ is called, without changing the iterator's behavior. The wrapper is fully transparent — it yields the same items in the same order — but exposes an items_seen attribute for monitoring.
patterns.rationale: Debugging and monitoring iterator consumption requires knowing how many items have been pulled. A transparent wrapper that only adds a counter avoids changing the data flow, making it safe to add or remove without affecting results. The counter is a public attribute, not a callback, keeping the interface simple.

patterns.name: Lock-wrapping decorator for thread-safe iterators
patterns.description: Wrap an iterator-returning function so that each returned iterator is wrapped in a serialize object that holds a non-reentrant Lock around __next__, send, throw, and close. Can also be used as a decorator on generator functions.
patterns.rationale: Standard iterators and generators are not thread-safe — concurrent calls to __next__ can corrupt internal state. Wrapping with a lock makes them safe for multi-consumer scenarios. The decorator form (@synchronized) makes it trivial to add thread-safety to any generator function without modifying its body.

patterns.name: Linked-list tee with lock for concurrent consumption
patterns.description: Implement a thread-safe tee using a mutable two-element linked list [value, next_link] shared between consumers. Each consumer advances the shared iterator under a lock only when its link's value is not yet populated, then detaches to its own next link. Multiple consumers independently traverse the linked structure.
patterns.rationale: itertools.tee is not thread-safe and can deadlock or corrupt when consumed concurrently. A linked-list structure where each node is [value, next_link] allows consumers to independently read cached values while only locking when a new value must be pulled from the source. This minimizes lock contention compared to locking every __next__ call.

patterns.name: Non-destructive split with tee+compress
patterns.description: Split an iterator at the first point where a predicate fails, returning two iterators: one that yields matching items (like takewhile) and one that yields the remainder INCLUDING the first non-matching item. Uses tee to duplicate the source, takewhile for the matching part, and compress to synchronize consumption.
patterns.rationale: takewhile loses the first non-matching item because it's consumed during the predicate check. By using tee to duplicate the source and compress to drive consumption, the boundary item is preserved in the remainder iterator. This enables parsing patterns like 'read header lines, then read body' without losing the first body line.

occurrences.snippet:
def before_and_after(predicate, it):
    trues, after = tee(it)
    trues = compress(takewhile(predicate, trues), zip(after))
    return trues, after

patterns.name: Value normalization to iterator with type exclusion
patterns.description: Normalize any input value to an iterator: None returns empty iterator, non-iterables return single-item iterator, iterables return iter(obj). A base_type parameter excludes specific types (str, bytes by default) from being treated as iterable, preventing character-by-character iteration of strings.
patterns.rationale: Functions that accept 'iterable or single value' need to handle None, scalars, and iterables uniformly. always_iterable provides a single normalization point: callers can write 'for x in always_iterable(obj)' without type-checking. The base_type exclusion prevents the common bug of iterating strings character-by-character.

patterns.name: __class_getitem__ via types.GenericAlias for lightweight generics
patterns.description: Enable class subscript syntax (ClassName[int]) without inheriting from Generic or using typing.TypeVar. Assign __class_getitem__ = classmethod(types.GenericAlias) to support PEP 585 generic aliasing with zero runtime overhead.
patterns.rationale: Inheriting from Generic adds metaclass complexity and runtime overhead. For classes that only need generic alias syntax for type-checker hints (not runtime type enforcement), types.GenericAlias is sufficient. This is the lightest possible way to support subscript notation.

patterns.name: Exception-as-iterator-terminator protocol conversion
patterns.description: Convert a call-until-exception interface (like list.pop raising IndexError) to an iterator interface by wrapping the call in a loop with suppress(exception). Also supports a first callback for initial-state calls. The exception type is the termination signal, not a sentinel value.
patterns.rationale: Many APIs (dict.__getitem__, list.pop, file.readline) signal exhaustion via exceptions, not sentinels. iter_except bridges these to the iterator protocol without requiring a sentinel. Multiple exception types can be specified, making it robust against different failure modes.

patterns.name: Bucket: lazy keyed partitioning with on-demand caching
patterns.description: Wrap an iterable and return an object that lazily partitions items by a key function into child iterables. Items are consumed from the source on demand; non-matching items are cached in a defaultdict(deque) keyed by their bucket. Supports __contains__ and __getitem__ for random bucket access, with an optional validator to limit valid keys.
patterns.rationale: Eager groupby requires sorted input; eager dict-of-lists requires materializing everything. bucket provides lazy, on-demand partitioning: accessing a bucket only pulls enough from the source to satisfy that bucket, caching items for other buckets. The validator parameter prevents unbounded caching when the key space is known and finite.

patterns.name: Callback-to-iterator adapter via threading and Queue
patterns.description: Convert a callback-based function to an iterator by running the function in a background thread, passing a Queue-feeding callback. The iterator polls the Queue for items. Supports context manager protocol for cleanup, and exposes done/result attributes for the function's completion state and return value.
patterns.rationale: Many legacy APIs use callbacks instead of iterators. Converting them to iterators enables use in for-loops and pipeline composition. The threading approach avoids blocking the main thread, and the context manager ensures the background thread is cleaned up even if iteration is abandoned early.

occurrences.snippet:
class callback_iter:
    def __init__(self, func, callback_kwd='callback', wait_seconds=0.1):
        self._func = func
        self._callback_kwd = callback_kwd
        self._aborted = False
        self._future = None
        self._wait_seconds = wait_seconds
        self._module = __import__('concurrent.futures').futures
        self._executor = self._module.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1)
        self._iterator = self._reader()

    def __enter__(self):
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        self._aborted = True
        self._executor.shutdown()

patterns.name: match/case for strategy selection by string mode
patterns.description: Use match/case on a string mode parameter to select between strategies (fill, strict, ignore), each delegating to a different implementation. Invalid values raise ValueError. The match/case replaces if/elif chains and makes the exhaustive set of options visible at a glance.
patterns.rationale: String-mode parameters are common in APIs (incomplete='fill'|'strict'|'ignore'). match/case makes the valid options explicit and provides a clean default case for validation. Compared to an Enum, it avoids requiring the caller to import an Enum type — a plain string is sufficient.

patterns.name: Sentinel-based iteration via iter(callable, sentinel)
patterns.description: Use iter(callable, sentinel) to create an iterator that calls a function repeatedly until it returns the sentinel value. Combined with functools.partial, this creates chunked iteration: iter(partial(take, n, iter(iterable)), []) yields chunks until the source is exhausted and take returns [].
patterns.rationale: iter(callable, sentinel) is a built-in Python idiom that converts a callable-returns-sentinel interface to an iterator. Combined with partial, it enables concise chunked iteration without explicit while-loop boilerplate. The empty list [] is a natural sentinel because take returns [] when the source is exhausted.

occurrences.snippet:
def chunked(iterable, n, strict=False):
    iterator = iter(partial(take, n, iter(iterable)), [])

patterns.name: Registry-based plugin discovery with format identification probes
patterns.description: A central registry maps format IDs to (factory, accept_probe) pairs. The accept_probe function inspects the first N bytes of a file to quickly reject incompatible formats. Image.open() iterates the registry, calling each probe until one accepts. Plugins self-register at import time via register_open(id, factory, accept).
patterns.rationale: Decouples format detection from format implementation — a new format plugin registers itself without modifying any core code. The accept probe avoids full parsing for rejection, making the trial-and-error identification fast. The registry pattern with probe functions is a clean alternative to class hierarchies for format dispatch.

occurrences.snippet:
def register_open(
    id: str,
    factory: Callable[[IO[bytes], str | bytes], ImageFile.ImageFile] | type[ImageFile.ImageFile],
    accept: Callable[[bytes], bool | str] | None = None,
) -> None:
    id = id.upper()
    if id not in ID:
        ID.append(id)
    OPEN[id] = factory, accept

# Usage in PngImagePlugin.py:
# Image.register_open(PngImageFile.format, PngImageFile, _accept)

patterns.name: Lazy loading with deferred file access via _open + load separation
patterns.description: Image.open() identifies the file format and creates an ImageFile object but does NOT read pixel data. The constructor calls _open() which only parses headers and sets mode/size/tile descriptors. Actual pixel data is loaded on first access via load(), which reads tiles from the file pointer. This allows opening large images cheaply and only paying decode cost when pixels are needed.
patterns.rationale: Separating identification from materialization is essential for performance — opening a 100MB image to check its dimensions should not require decoding 100MB of pixels. The tile list acts as a deferred execution plan: load() materializes tiles by seeking to offsets and running decoders on demand.

patterns.name: Mutable core model with immutable operation copies (_new pattern)
patterns.description: The Image class is mutable (pixels can be modified in-place via paste, putpixel). Operations like crop, convert, resize, and filter return NEW Image objects via _new(im), which creates a fresh Image wrapping a new core, copying palette and info dict. This dual model — mutable for in-place editing, copy-on-operation for transformations — gives callers explicit control over memory.
patterns.rationale: Image processing often chains many operations. If every operation mutated in-place, the original would be lost. If every operation required explicit copy(), the API would be verbose. The _new pattern makes operations non-destructive by default while allowing paste() for explicit in-place modification — matching user mental model of 'filter = new image, paste = modify this image'.

patterns.name: Operation modules as free functions returning new Image objects
patterns.description: Image operations (ImageChops, ImageOps, ImageEnhance) are organized as module-level functions that accept Image and return Image, not methods on the Image class. This keeps the Image class focused on core data model (mode, size, pixels) while operations live in separate modules. The pattern: load() → delegate to core.im C method → wrap result in _new().
patterns.rationale: Prevents Image class from becoming a god object with hundreds of methods. Operations are independently importable, testable, and extensible. New operation modules can be added without touching Image.py. The convention 'functions in separate module, return new Image' is a clean alternative to inheritance or mixins for capability composition.

patterns.name: NamedTuple as immutable descriptor for domain types (ModeDescriptor)
patterns.description: ModeDescriptor is a NamedTuple with fields (mode, bands, basemode, basetype, typestr) describing an image mode. getmode() is lru_cache'd, returning the same descriptor for the same mode string. The descriptor is immutable, hashable, and fields are accessible by name. This replaces what would be a class hierarchy of mode types with a simple data record.
patterns.rationale: Image modes are a fixed enumeration (L, RGB, RGBA, P, etc.) with metadata (band names, base type, struct format). A NamedTuple provides field-name access without class hierarchy overhead. lru_cache ensures a single descriptor instance per mode, making identity comparisons fast and reducing allocation.

occurrences.snippet:
class RawRequestMessage(NamedTuple):
    method: str
    path: str
    version: HttpVersion
    headers: "CIMultiDictProxy[str]"
    raw_headers: RawHeaders
    should_close: bool
    compression: str | None
    upgrade: bool
    chunked: bool
    url: URL

patterns.name: DeferredError as lazy exception carrier for closed/invalid resources
patterns.description: DeferredError wraps an exception and raises it on any attribute access via __getattr__. Used to replace _im when an image is closed — instead of setting _im=None and risking AttributeError later, the DeferredError carries a descriptive 'Operation on closed image' ValueError that fires immediately when any method tries to use the core.
patterns.rationale: Setting to None would produce 'NoneType has no attribute X' errors that are unhelpful. DeferredError provides a clear error message at the point of attempted use, not at the point of closure. The pattern is reusable for any resource that should be 'soft closed' — the object still exists but accessing its capabilities raises a meaningful error.

patterns.name: StubImageFile: class morphing via __class__ and __dict__ reassignment
patterns.description: StubImageFile identifies a format but delegates actual loading to an external handler. On load(), it calls the handler which returns a real Image object, then copies that object's __class__ and __dict__ onto itself — effectively morphing into the real implementation at runtime.
patterns.rationale: Allows format identification to be separated from format implementation. A stub can recognize a format (e.g., GRIB) but defer to an external library for actual decoding. The class morphing pattern means callers don't need to know about the indirection — after load(), the object behaves exactly like the real implementation.

patterns.name: Two-tier plugin initialization: preinit for common, init for all
patterns.description: preinit() imports only the 5 most common format plugins (BMP, GIF, JPEG, PPM, PNG). init() imports all ~47 plugins. Image.open() tries preinit first, and only falls back to init() if preinit plugins can't identify the file. This avoids importing 47 modules when 5 cover 99% of use cases.
patterns.rationale: Importing all format plugins at startup is wasteful when most users only need PNG or JPEG. The two-tier approach trades a small code complexity cost for significant startup time savings. The registry pattern makes this safe — plugins self-register on import, so preinit only needs to import the right modules.

patterns.name: ABC as extension point for custom codecs (PyDecoder/PyEncoder)
patterns.description: PyDecoder and PyEncoder are ABCs with abstract decode()/encode() methods. Plugins that need Python-level codec logic subclass these and register via register_decoder/register_encoder. The codec lifecycle is controlled by the framework: setimage/setfd, decode/encode in a loop, cleanup() in finally block.
patterns.rationale: Provides a clean extension point for formats that can't use C-level codecs. The ABC defines the contract (decode returns (bytes_consumed, errcode)), while the framework handles the I/O loop and resource cleanup. This is the Python-level equivalent of the C codec interface, allowing pure-Python format plugins.

patterns.name: IntEnum as parameter type for API stability and discoverability
patterns.description: Pillow uses IntEnum for all enumeric parameters: Resampling (NEAREST, BILINEAR, BICUBIC, LANCZOS), Transform (AFFINE, EXTENT, PERSPECTIVE, MESH), Dither, Palette, Quantize, Transpose. These are IntEnum (not Enum) for backwards compatibility with legacy integer values, but the enum members provide named constants and type hints for discoverability.
patterns.rationale: IntEnum preserves backwards compatibility (old code passing integers still works) while providing named constants for new code. Type hints using these enums make API behavior discoverable in IDEs. The class-level enum also serves as documentation — all valid values for a parameter are visible in one place.

occurrences.snippet:
class Transpose(IntEnum):
    FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT = 0
    FLIP_TOP_BOTTOM = 1
    ROTATE_90 = 2
    ROTATE_180 = 3
    ROTATE_270 = 4
    TRANSPOSE = 5
    TRANSVERSE = 6

class Resampling(IntEnum):
    NEAREST = 0
    BOX = 4
    BILINEAR = 2
    HAMMING = 5
    BICUBIC = 3
    LANCZOS = 1

patterns.name: Chunk-based stream parsing with dynamic dispatch via method name convention
patterns.description: ChunkStream parses binary files by reading chunk headers (id, length), then dispatches to handlers via getattr(self, f'chunk_{cid}') — a naming convention where each chunk type gets its own method. Unknown chunks are silently skipped. CRC verification is separated from parsing.
patterns.rationale: Binary format parsing often involves dozens of chunk types. A dispatch table would require explicit registration; a class hierarchy would be overkill. The method naming convention (chunk_IHDR, chunk_IDAT) is self-documenting — the chunk handler is findable by name, and new chunk types are added by writing a method.

patterns.name: Enhance pattern: degenerate image + blend factor as transformation template
patterns.description: ImageEnhance uses a pattern where each enhancement (Color, Contrast, Brightness, Sharpness) precomputes a 'degenerate' version of the image (the extreme case: grayscale, solid gray, black, blurred). The enhance(factor) method then blends between the degenerate and original: result = blend(degenerate, original, factor). Factor 0 = degenerate, factor 1 = original.
patterns.rationale: Unifies four seemingly different image operations (color, contrast, brightness, sharpness) under a single mathematical framework: interpolation between a degenerate and original image. This pattern is generalizable to any parameterized transformation expressible as a blend between two endpoints.

patterns.name: MutableMapping subclass for structured metadata access (Exif)
patterns.description: Exif subclasses MutableMapping[int, Any] to provide dict-like access to EXIF tags while hiding internal structure (multiple IFDs, hidden data, endian-specific parsing). Users interact with it as exif[274] = 2, while the class manages IFD0, sub-IFDs, and serialization internally.
patterns.rationale: EXIF data is conceptually a key-value mapping but internally complex (tag numbers, IFD hierarchies, type-specific decoding). Subclassing MutableMapping gives users a familiar dict interface while the class encapsulates the complexity. This is preferable to returning a raw dict (which would lose IFD context) or a custom class (which would need to implement all dict methods manually).

patterns.name: Versioned deprecation with scheduled removal date
patterns.description: deprecate() function takes a target Pillow major version number and maps it to a specific calendar date. If the current version has already passed the target, it raises RuntimeError instead of DeprecationWarning. This makes deprecations time-bounded and enforceable — deprecated code is guaranteed to be removed, not left as permanent warnings.
patterns.rationale: Many projects emit DeprecationWarning but never actually remove the deprecated code. By encoding the removal version as a parameter and raising RuntimeError when the version is reached, the deprecation becomes a binding contract. The calendar date in the message helps users plan migrations.

patterns.name: Extension-to-plugin lazy import map for deferred module loading
patterns.description: A dict maps file extensions to plugin module names (_EXTENSION_PLUGIN = {'.dds': 'DdsImagePlugin', ...}). Before importing all plugins, Image.open() checks the file extension and imports only the needed plugin. This avoids importing 47 format modules when only one is needed.
patterns.rationale: Complements preinit/init two-tier system with a more targeted approach: instead of importing 5 common plugins (preinit) or all 47 (init), import exactly the one plugin matching the file extension. For known extensions, this eliminates the trial-and-error identification loop entirely.

patterns.name: ImagePointTransform: value object with overloaded arithmetic operators
patterns.description: ImagePointTransform represents an affine transformation (scale, offset) and implements __add__, __sub__, __mul__, __truediv__, __neg__ with type-aware dispatch (combining two transforms vs. transform + scalar). The _getscaleoffset function evaluates a user-supplied expression by substituting ImagePointTransform(1,0) and reading the result's scale/offset — using Python's operator overloading as a mini-DSL.
patterns.rationale: Allows users to write point operations as mathematical expressions (e.g., lambda x: x * 1.5 + 10) that are transparently converted to affine (scale, offset) pairs. The value object's arithmetic operators make the expression evaluation work naturally — no AST parsing or code generation needed.

patterns.name: Filter ABC hierarchy with single-method contract
patterns.description: ImageFilter defines a minimal ABC hierarchy: Filter (abstract: filter(image) → image), MultibandFilter(Filter) as marker, BuiltinFilter(MultibandFilter) with concrete filter() that delegates to image.filter(*self.filterargs). Subclasses (Kernel, BoxBlur, GaussianBlur) only set class-level attributes (name, filterargs). The entire interface is one method.
patterns.rationale: The single-method ABC makes it trivial to write custom filters — implement filter(). The BuiltinFilter layer provides a shortcut for filters that just pass args to the C engine, avoiding boilerplate. The hierarchy is 3 levels deep but each level adds exactly one concern, keeping it understandable.

patterns.name: NamedTuple tile descriptor for deferred decode plan
patterns.description: _Tile is a NamedTuple with fields (codec_name, extents, offset, args) describing where and how to decode a portion of an image file. The ImageFile.tile list is a deferred decode plan — populated during _open() by parsing headers, consumed during load() by executing each tile. NamedTuple gives field-name access and immutability without class overhead.
patterns.rationale: Image files often store pixel data in multiple non-contiguous chunks. The tile list captures the decode plan as data, not code — it can be sorted, deduplicated, and inspected before execution. Using NamedTuple instead of a class keeps the descriptor lightweight and hashable.

occurrences.snippet:
class _Tile(NamedTuple):
    codec_name: str
    extents: tuple[int, int, int, int] | None
    offset: int = 0
    args: tuple[Any, ...] | str | None = None

patterns.name: Decompression bomb guard with configurable pixel limit
patterns.description: MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS sets a safety limit (~256MB for 24-bit). _decompression_bomb_check() compares image dimensions against this limit and raises DecompressionBombError (hard limit, 2x) or DecompressionBombWarning (soft limit, 1x). The limit is a module-level global that users can override.
patterns.rationale: Malicious image files can claim enormous dimensions, causing decompression to exhaust memory. The bomb guard validates dimensions before decode, not after. The two-tier approach (warning vs error) lets users opt-in to processing large images by suppressing the warning, while the hard error prevents accidental OOM.

patterns.name: Iterator protocol for multi-frame image sequences
patterns.description: ImageSequence.Iterator wraps an image with __getitem__ (seek by index) and __next__ (sequential seek, raising StopIteration on EOFError). This provides Python iteration over multi-frame images (GIF, APNG) without exposing seek/seek internals. The iterator modifies the original image in-place rather than creating copies.
patterns.rationale: Multi-frame images are naturally sequential but Python's iterator protocol (__next__ + StopIteration) maps cleanly onto seek() + EOFError. By adapting the image's native EOF signal to StopIteration, users can use for-loops without knowing about seek semantics.

patterns.name: Type alias as complete protocol contract
patterns.description: The entire application interface is expressed as type aliases: ASGIApp = Callable[[Scope, Receive, Send], Awaitable[None]]. No ABC, no Protocol class, no abstract methods — just a Callable type alias. Anything matching the signature is an ASGI app. The protocol IS the type signature.
patterns.rationale: Type aliases are zero-overhead at runtime — no metaclass, no ABC registration, no isinstance checks. The Callable signature is both the contract and the documentation. Any callable matching the signature satisfies the protocol, enabling maximum duck-typing flexibility.

occurrences.snippet:
Scope = MutableMapping[str, Any]
Message = MutableMapping[str, Any]
Receive = Callable[[], Awaitable[Message]]
Send = Callable[[Message], Awaitable[None]]
ASGIApp = Callable[[Scope, Receive, Send], Awaitable[None]]

ASGI3Application = Callable[[Scope, ASGIReceiveCallable, ASGISendCallable], Awaitable[None]]
ASGIApplication = ASGI2Application | ASGI3Application
Handler = Callable[["Request"], Awaitable["StreamResponse"]]

patterns.name: Middleware as onion wrapping via reversed accumulation
patterns.description: Middleware stack built by wrapping from inside out: iterate reversed(middleware), each middleware takes the current app and returns a wrapped app. The last middleware wraps the router (innermost), the first wraps everything (outermost). Each middleware has signature (app: ASGIApp, ...) -> ASGIApp.
patterns.rationale: Reversed accumulation produces the natural request processing order: outermost middleware sees the request first, innermost last. The same pattern works for building any layered processing pipeline where each layer wraps the next.

patterns.name: Route as polymorphic endpoint adapter
patterns.description: Route constructor detects endpoint type: if it's a function/method, wraps with request_response() to create an ASGI app; if it's a class, uses it directly as ASGI. Single constructor, dual adaptation strategy based on introspection.
patterns.rationale: Allows users to define endpoints as either simple functions (func(request) -> response) or full ASGI classes, without separate registration APIs. The framework adapts to the user's chosen abstraction level.

patterns.name: Match enum for partial matching with fallback dispatch
patterns.description: Route matching returns a Match enum: NONE, PARTIAL, or FULL. PARTIAL means path matched but method didn't — used for 405 Method Not Allowed. Router collects first partial match as fallback if no full match is found.
patterns.rationale: Distinguishes 'path not found' (404) from 'path found but method not allowed' (405) without a second pass. The enum makes the three outcomes explicit and the fallback logic clean.

occurrences.snippet:
class Match(Enum):
    NONE = 0
    PARTIAL = 1
    FULL = 2

# In Router.app():
for route in self.routes:
    match, child_scope = route.matches(scope)
    if match == Match.FULL:
        scope.update(child_scope)
        await route.handle(scope, receive, send)
        return
    elif match == Match.PARTIAL and partial is None:
        partial = route
        partial_scope = child_scope
if partial is not None:
    scope.update(partial_scope)
    await partial.handle(scope, receive, send)
    return

patterns.name: Compiled path triple: regex + format + convertors
patterns.description: compile_path() returns a three-tuple: (compiled regex for matching, format string for URL generation, convertors dict for type conversion). All three are compiled once at route definition time and reused for both incoming matching and outgoing URL generation.
patterns.rationale: A single compilation pass produces artifacts for two directions: request matching (regex) and URL building (format + convertors). Avoids re-parsing path patterns per request. The convertors provide bidirectional str↔type conversion for the same parameter.

occurrences.snippet:
def compile_path(path: str) -> tuple[Pattern[str], str, dict[str, Convertor[Any]]]:
    path_regex = "^"
    path_format = ""
    for match in PARAM_REGEX.finditer(path):
        param_name, convertor_type = match.groups("str")
        convertor = CONVERTOR_TYPES[convertor_type]
        path_regex += f"(?P<{param_name}>{convertor.regex})"
        path_format += "{%s}" % param_name
        param_convertors[param_name] = convertor
    path_regex += re.escape(path[idx:]) + "$"
    return re.compile(path_regex), path_format, param_convertors

patterns.name: Convertor as bidirectional generic with global registry
patterns.description: Convertor[T] is a Generic base with convert(str)->T and to_string(T)->str. Concrete convertors (StringConvertor, IntegerConvertor, UUIDConvertor) register in a global CONVERTOR_TYPES dict. register_url_convertor() allows extension without modifying framework code.
patterns.rationale: Bidirectional conversion (parse for matching, serialize for URL building) in one type-safe object. The registry pattern allows users to add custom path parameter types (e.g. date, slug) without subclassing the router.

patterns.name: Response object as ASGI callable
patterns.description: Response objects implement __call__(scope, receive, send), making them ASGI apps. A response can be returned from an endpoint and then 'called' to send itself: await response(scope, receive, send). Responses are both data containers and executable ASGI apps.
patterns.rationale: Unifies the response lifecycle: the same object holds response data and knows how to send it over ASGI. No separate serializer or response writer needed. Responses can be passed anywhere an ASGI app is expected (middleware, routes, error handlers).

occurrences.snippet:
async def __call__(self, scope: Scope, receive: Receive, send: Send) -> None:
    if scope["type"] == "websocket":
        send = self._wrap_websocket_denial_send(send)
    await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": self.status_code, "headers": self.raw_headers})
    await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": self.body})
    if self.background is not None:
        await self.background()

patterns.name: Response hierarchy via render() override with fixed __call__
patterns.description: Response.__call__ (the ASGI execution) is fixed in the base class. Subclasses customize serialization by overriding render(content) -> bytes. JSONResponse.render returns json.dumps, HTMLResponse just sets media_type. The execution pipeline is stable; only content encoding varies.
patterns.rationale: Template method pattern: the base class owns the response-sending protocol (headers, status, body, background tasks), subclasses own only the content encoding step. This prevents subclasses from accidentally breaking the ASGI message protocol.

patterns.name: BackgroundTask: deferred post-response execution
patterns.description: BackgroundTask wraps a callable + args, executed after the response is sent. BackgroundTasks composes multiple tasks. Both sync and async callables supported via is_async_callable detection. The Response.__call__ checks and awaits self.background after sending the body.
patterns.rationale: Allows cleanup/logging/notifications to run after the client receives the response, without delaying it. The task is attached to the response object, coupling lifecycle naturally. Sync/async detection avoids requiring all callbacks to be async.

patterns.name: wrap_app_handling_exceptions: sender-wrapped closure with response_started guard
patterns.description: Creates a new ASGI app that wraps the original with exception handling. A closure 'sender' function tracks response_started state by intercepting http.response.start messages. If an exception occurs after response started, it raises RuntimeError instead of trying to send a new response.
patterns.rationale: Once the first byte of an HTTP response is sent, the status/headers cannot be changed. The sender closure enforces this invariant: catching an exception after response_started is too late to send an error response, so it must re-raise rather than attempt to send a different response.

patterns.name: Environ as MutableMapping with read-tracking for mutation safety
patterns.description: Environ(MutableMapping) tracks which keys have been read via _has_been_read set. __setitem__ and __delitem__ raise EnvironError if the key has already been read. Prevents subtle bugs where config values are changed after they've been consumed.
patterns.rationale: Environment variables are often read early (at import time) and cached. If later code modifies os.environ, the cached values become stale silently. Read-tracking makes this a loud error instead of a silent bug. The MutableMapping interface means it's a drop-in replacement for os.environ.

patterns.name: HTTPEndpoint as awaitable class with method dispatch
patterns.description: HTTPEndpoint implements __await__ returning self.dispatch().__await__(), making the class instance directly awaitable as an ASGI app. dispatch() inspects the HTTP method and calls the corresponding method (get, post, etc.) via getattr. The class IS the ASGI app.
patterns.rationale: Allows defining endpoints as classes with HTTP method handlers as methods, while remaining ASGI-compatible. The __await__ implementation makes `await endpoint(scope, receive, send)` work without needing a separate wrapper. Method dispatch via getattr is simpler than a method registry.

patterns.name: WebSocket dual state machine with enforced transitions
patterns.description: WebSocket tracks client_state and application_state independently via WebSocketState enum (CONNECTING/CONNECTED/DISCONNECTED/RESPONSE). receive() and send() enforce valid state transitions with explicit RuntimeError messages for invalid transitions. Both sides of the connection are guarded.
patterns.rationale: WebSocket protocol has strict ordering: connect before receive, accept before send, close terminates. Dual state machines (client + app) catch protocol violations early with clear error messages. Without this, invalid sequences would produce confusing ASGI server errors.

patterns.name: Scope as shared mutable context dict
patterns.description: All request context flows through a mutable dict ('scope') passed by reference. Middleware adds keys (scope['app']=self, scope['router']=self), routes update path params (scope.update(child_scope)), and downstream code reads via scope.get(). No immutable request object — the dict IS the context.
patterns.rationale: Mutable dict passing avoids creating new objects at each middleware layer. Each layer can add context without return values. The cost is that any layer can mutate anything — but in a cooperative framework, this simplicity wins over defensive copying.

occurrences.snippet:
# Application adds itself to scope:
async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
    scope["app"] = self
    await self.middleware_stack(scope, receive, send)

# Router updates scope with matched route's child_scope:
if match == Match.FULL:
    scope.update(child_scope)
    await route.handle(scope, receive, send)

patterns.name: AwaitableOrContextManager: dual await/async-with protocol
patterns.description: A Protocol that is simultaneously Awaitable[T] and AbstractAsyncContextManager[T]. The same object can be used as `result = await obj` or `async with obj as result`. A wrapper class implements both __await__ and __aenter__/__aexit__, delegating to the same underlying coroutine.
patterns.rationale: Some resources (e.g. form data) can be used either as a one-shot await or as a context manager that ensures cleanup. Supporting both from one object avoids forcing the user to choose. The wrapper pattern keeps the underlying coroutine lazy until first access.

patterns.name: Exception group unwrapping via collapsing task group
patterns.description: create_collapsing_task_group() is an asynccontextmanager that wraps anyio.create_task_group(). If the task group raises BaseExceptionGroup with exactly one exception, it unwraps and re-raises the original exception directly, preserving __cause__ and __context__. Multi-exception groups are re-raised as-is.
patterns.rationale: anyio task groups always raise BaseExceptionGroup even for single exceptions. This obscures the original traceback and breaks except clauses. Collapsing to the single exception restores normal exception handling semantics while preserving multi-exception behavior when genuinely needed.

patterns.name: CORS middleware with precomputed header dicts
patterns.description: CORSMiddleware precomputes simple_headers and preflight_headers dicts at __init__ time based on configuration. Per-request path is just dict lookup and origin echoing — no regex compilation, no header string building per request.
patterns.rationale: CORS headers are the same for every request given the same configuration. Precomputing at construction time eliminates per-request string building and set operations. The per-request hot path is reduced to a dict update + origin check.

patterns.name: Config as callable with overloaded signatures
patterns.description: Config.__call__ has 5 @overload signatures covering different cast/default combinations: (key), (key, cast), (key, default), (key, cast, default), etc. The callable interface IS the config access API — no .get() needed (though .get() also exists).
patterns.rationale: Overloads provide precise type inference for each combination: config('KEY', cast=int, default=8080) returns int, config('KEY') returns str. The callable form is concise for module-level use: PORT = Config()('PORT', cast=int, default=8080).

patterns.name: StaticFiles as ASGI app with lazy first-request config check
patterns.description: StaticFiles implements __call__(scope, receive, send) directly as an ASGI app. Configuration validation (directory exists, is a directory) is lazy — checked on first request via self.config_checked flag, not in __init__. This allows construction before the filesystem is ready.
patterns.rationale: Eager validation in __init__ would fail when StaticFiles is constructed at import time but the directory is mounted later (e.g. in Docker). Lazy validation defers to first request, when the filesystem is guaranteed to be ready. The flag ensures the check runs exactly once.

occurrences.snippet:
class StaticFiles:
    def __init__(self, *, directory=None, packages=None, html=False, check_dir=True, ...):
        self.config_checked = False
        ...
    async def __call__(self, scope: Scope, receive: Receive, send: Send) -> None:
        assert scope["type"] == "http"
        if not self.config_checked:
            await self.check_config()
            self.config_checked = True
        path = self.get_path(scope)
        response = await self.get_response(path, scope)
        await response(scope, receive, send)

patterns.name: Middleware spec as iterable triple (cls, args, kwargs)
patterns.description: Middleware is a simple data container holding (cls, args, kwargs) that unpacks via __iter__ for tuple unpacking: `for cls, args, kwargs in middleware`. No behavior — just a typed triple that enables `Middleware(CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=['*'])` syntax.
patterns.rationale: Middleware specs need to be both declarative (constructed at config time) and unpackable (consumed at build time). The __iter__ protocol enables clean for-loop unpacking without attribute access. ParamSpec propagates types from constructor to the stored cls/args/kwargs.

patterns.name: AST node metaclass with inherited field accumulation
patterns.description: A custom metaclass (NodeType) intercepts class creation to accumulate 'fields' and 'attributes' tuples from parent classes. Each subclass adds its own fields, which are merged with inherited ones at class-definition time. An 'abstract' flag prevents direct instantiation of base nodes. Fields are positional constructor args, attributes are keyword args. This creates a discriminated union of node types where each node knows its own field layout.
patterns.rationale: AST node hierarchies need declarative field definitions that inherit from parent nodes. The metaclass approach ensures field lists are complete at class-definition time, enabling positional construction (Node(field1, field2)) and generic iteration (iter_fields) without runtime introspection. The abstract flag prevents instantiating base categories (Stmt, Expr) that only exist for type classification.

occurrences.snippet:
class NodeType(type):
    """A metaclass for nodes that handles the field and attribute
    inheritance.  fields and attributes from the parent class are
    automatically forwarded to the child."""

    def __new__(mcs, name, bases, d):
        for attr in "fields", "attributes":
            storage: t.List[t.Tuple[str, ...]] = []
            storage.extend(getattr(bases[0] if bases else object, attr, ()))
            storage.extend(d.get(attr, ()))
            assert len(bases) <= 1, "multiple inheritance not allowed"
            assert len(storage) == len(set(storage)), "layout conflict"
            d[attr] = tuple(storage)
        d.setdefault("abstract", False)
        return type.__new__(mcs, name, bases, d)

patterns.name: Visitor pattern with method-name dispatch via getattr
patterns.description: A NodeVisitor base class dispatches to visit methods by convention: visit_{type(node).__name__}. get_visitor() uses getattr(self, f'visit_{type(node).__name__}', None) to find the handler. If no handler exists, generic_visit() walks child nodes. A NodeTransformer subclass overrides generic_visit to return modified nodes, enabling in-place AST transformation. The visit() method forwards *args/**kwargs, making the visitor signature flexible.
patterns.rationale: Walking an AST with 50+ node types requires a dispatch mechanism. Convention-based method naming (visit_For, visit_If) is more readable than large match/case statements or visitor dictionaries, and scales naturally — adding a node type just means adding a visit_ method. The transformer variant (return value replaces node, None removes it) enables declarative AST rewriting without touching the visit infrastructure.

patterns.name: Undefined behavior variants via subclassing with operator overloading
patterns.description: A base Undefined class represents missing values with configurable behavior via subclassing. The base class allows str() (returns ''), iter() (empty), and bool() (False) but raises UndefinedError on arithmetic, comparison, or call. Subclasses modify behavior: ChainableUndefined returns self from __getattr__/__getitem__ (enabling foo.bar.baz without error), DebugUndefined returns '{{ foo }}' when printed, StrictUndefined raises on ALL operations including str/bool/iter. A factory function make_logging_undefined() dynamically creates a subclass that logs before delegating to the base.
patterns.rationale: Different deployment contexts need different missing-value behavior: production templates should silently ignore undefined vars, debugging should show them, strict mode should fail fast. Subclassing with operator overrides is the Pythonic way to vary behavior — the Environment just stores the undefined class and instantiates it. The factory function adds cross-cutting behavior (logging) without modifying the base hierarchy.

patterns.name: Environment overlay: copy-on-write configuration inheritance
patterns.description: An Environment.overlay() method creates a new environment that shares all data with the current one except for overridden attributes. The overlay copies __dict__, sets overlayed=True and linked_to=self, then applies only the explicitly provided parameters. Extensions are rebound to the new environment via bind(). Cache is copied (not shared). This allows creating scoped configuration variants without duplicating the full environment state.
patterns.rationale: Applications need multiple environment configurations (e.g., different autoescape rules per template directory, different extensions per blueprint) sharing the same filters, tests, and globals. Full copy is wasteful; overlay shares everything by reference and only overrides what changes. The bind() mechanism on extensions ensures each environment has its own extension instances pointing at the right environment.

patterns.name: Pass-arg decorator: implicit context injection via attribute stamping
patterns.description: Three decorators (@pass_context, @pass_eval_context, @pass_environment) stamp a jinja_pass_arg enum attribute on the function. At call time, the runtime inspects _PassArg.from_obj(func) to determine what to inject as the first argument. The function itself is not wrapped — the decorator returns the same object. This avoids wrapper overhead and keeps inspect.signature() clean. The injection point (Context.call) checks the attribute and inserts the appropriate object (context, eval_ctx, or environment).
patterns.rationale: Filters and tests need varying levels of access — some need the full context (to resolve variables), some need just the eval context (for autoescape), some need only the environment (for config). Explicit parameters would pollute the template-facing signature. Attribute stamping (not wrapping) means the function remains directly callable and introspectable, while the runtime injection point handles the dependency. This is the same 'stamp, don't wrap' principle as pluggy's @hookimpl.

patterns.name: LoopContext: one-ahead peeking iterator wrapper with lazy length
patterns.description: LoopContext wraps an iterable to provide loop metadata (index, length, first, last, previtem, nextitem) during iteration. It peeks one item ahead via _peek_next() (cached in _after) to support last/nextitem without consuming the iterator. Length is lazy: tries len() first, falls back to materializing the iterator into a list. The __next__ returns (item, self) so the loop body gets both the value and the loop context. A recursive __call__ enables nested iteration via the _recurse callback.
patterns.rationale: Template for-loops need metadata (am I first? last? what's the next item?) that plain iterators don't provide.
