Peeking one ahead is the minimal cost — it doesn't materialize the entire iterable unless length is requested. Returning (item, self) from __next__ is elegant: the for-loop unpacks both in one step. The lazy length means generators work without pre-materialization unless the template explicitly asks for length/revindex.

patterns.name: Sandboxed subclass: intercepted operators + safe attribute checking
patterns.description: SandboxedEnvironment subclasses Environment to intercept attribute access and operators in untrusted template code. is_safe_attribute() blocks underscore-prefixed and internal Python attributes (gi_frame, mro, __code__). is_safe_callable() checks for unsafe_callable or alters_data markers. Intercepted binops/unops are delegated to call_binop/call_unop via lookup tables (binop_table). The compiler generates sandboxed code (environment.call_binop instead of raw operators) when sandboxed=True. A @unsafe decorator marks specific functions as non-callable from templates.
patterns.rationale: Template execution of untrusted code requires controlling what operations are available. Rather than sandboxing at the Python level (which is hard), Jinja intercepts at the environment level: attribute access is filtered, operators are routed through safe lookup tables, and dangerous callables are marked. The subclass approach means the non-sandboxed path has zero overhead — sandboxing is opt-in via class selection (SandboxedEnvironment vs Environment).

patterns.name: Extension bind: re-targeting plugin instance to new environment
patterns.description: Extension instances are bound to an Environment at construction. When an Environment overlay is created, each extension is re-bound via bind(new_env): a new instance is created via object.__new__ (bypassing __init__), __dict__ is copied, and the environment attribute is updated. This ensures overlay environments have their own extension instances pointing at the right environment, without re-running extension initialization (which might have side effects or require constructor arguments that aren't available).
patterns.rationale: Extensions store a reference to their environment for accessing config and registering callbacks. When creating an overlay, the extensions must point at the new environment, but re-instantiating them is not possible (they take no constructor args — the environment is the only param). The bind() pattern (copy + reassign) creates a shallow clone that shares all state except the environment reference. This is cheaper than re-initialization and preserves any runtime state the extension may have accumulated.

patterns.name: Two-phase template lifecycle: compile-time parse + runtime render
patterns.description: Templates go through distinct phases with clear boundaries: (1) preprocess (extensions transform source string), (2) lex (source → token stream), (3) parse (tokens → AST via parser + extension parse hooks), (4) optimize (AST → constant-folded AST), (5) compile (AST → Python source code via CodeGenerator visitor), (6) execute (compiled code → string output via runtime). Each phase has a well-defined input/output type: string → TokenStream → nodes.Template → nodes.Template → str (source code) → str (output). The compiler writes Python source that imports from jinja2.runtime.
patterns.rationale: Separating compilation from rendering allows caching compiled templates (bytecode cache) and amortizing parse/compile cost across multiple renders. Each phase boundary is a cache point: bytecode cache stores the compiled CodeType, the environment cache stores Template objects. Extensions can hook into preprocess (source), filter_stream (tokens), and parse (AST) — three distinct extension points at three different abstraction levels.

patterns.name: Mutable mapping context with resolve-or-missing sentinel fallback
patterns.description: Context is a Mapping registered via abc.Mapping.register (not a dict subclass) that holds vars (local) and parent (inherited) dicts. resolve_or_missing() checks vars first, then parent, returning the 'missing' sentinel if not found. resolve() wraps this to return an Undefined object instead of the sentinel. The Context is immutable from outside — only generated template code modifies vars. derived() creates a child context sharing the parent dict for loop/block scopes.
patterns.rationale: Template variable resolution needs two-level lookup (local scope + inherited scope) with a fallback to Undefined (not KeyError). The sentinel 'missing' distinguishes 'not found' from 'found but None'. Using abc.Mapping.register instead of dict subclass gives full Mapping protocol without allowing external mutation. The derived() pattern enables nested scopes (loops, blocks) without copying the entire variable space.

patterns.name: Bytecode cache with magic header + checksum validation
patterns.description: A bytecode cache stores compiled Python CodeType objects with a magic header (project identifier + Python version + cache format version) and a source checksum. On load, the magic header is validated first (rejects incompatible Python versions or cache format changes), then the checksum is compared against the current source (rejects stale caches). marshal is used for CodeType serialization. The Bucket abstraction separates cache key management from storage backend (filesystem, memcached).
patterns.rationale: Compiled templates are expensive to regenerate. Caching the compiled bytecode avoids re-parsing and re-compiling on every startup. The magic header prevents loading incompatible bytecode when Python version changes (CodeType is version-specific). The checksum invalidates cache when source changes. The Bucket pattern separates what to cache (key, checksum, code) from where to cache it (subclass provides load_bytecode/dump_bytecode for filesystem, memcached, etc.).

patterns.name: Loader strategy pattern: get_source + uptodate callback
patterns.description: BaseLoader defines a single method get_source() returning (source, filename, uptodate) where uptodate is a zero-arg callable returning bool. The base load() method handles caching, bytecode cache integration, and Template construction — subclasses only implement source retrieval. The uptodate callback (typically a closure capturing mtime) enables auto-reload: the environment checks uptodate() before using a cached template. Multiple loaders (FileSystem, Dict, Package, Choice, Prefix) implement different source strategies while sharing the load() infrastructure.
patterns.rationale: Template sources vary (filesystem, dict, package resources, network) but the caching and compilation pipeline is shared. By putting get_source() as the single extension point, new loaders don't need to understand caching or bytecode. The uptodate callback is a clean way to handle source change detection without the loader knowing about cache internals — it just returns whether the source is still valid. The closure pattern captures state (mtime, hash) at load time.

patterns.name: Constant folding optimizer as AST transformer
patterns.description: An Optimizer subclasses NodeTransformer (which returns modified nodes from visit methods). generic_visit() visits all children first, then tries to call node.as_const() on Expr nodes. If as_const() succeeds (returns a Python value), the node is replaced with a Const node wrapping the value. If as_const() raises Impossible, the original node is kept. This is constant folding — expressions like {{ 2 + 3 }} are replaced with {{ 5 }} at compile time. The optimizer runs via the optimizeconst decorator on each compiler visitor method.
patterns.rationale: Templates often contain constant expressions (arithmetic, string concatenation, comparisons) that don't depend on runtime variables. Folding them at compile time reduces runtime work. Using the transformer pattern means the optimizer plugs into the same visitor infrastructure as the compiler — no separate pass needed. The as_const() method on each node type defines what can be folded: literals trivially, binary ops if both operands fold, etc.

patterns.name: Compile-time Frame stack for scope tracking in code generation
patterns.description: The compiler uses Frame objects to track scope information during code generation. Frames form a parent chain (frame.parent) and carry: Symbols (variable name resolution), buffer (output target — yield vs list append), block (current block name), toplevel/rootlevel flags, loop_frame/block_frame flags, soft_frame (for if-conditions). inner() creates child frames; soft() creates a copy for conditional branches. The Frame is not a runtime object — it's compile-time metadata that guides code generation. The Symbols object within tracks variable load/store operations and scoping levels.
patterns.rationale: Code generation for a template language needs to track which variables are in scope, whether output goes to yield or a buffer (macros use buffers), and whether we're inside a loop or block (affects variable resolution). The Frame stack mirrors the runtime scope chain but exists only at compile time — it guides the compiler to emit correct Python code (e.g., using context.resolve() for outer-scope vars, local vars for loop-scoped). The soft() copy enables conditional branches to tentatively modify scope without affecting the parent.

patterns.name: Versioned deprecation warning with due_date enforcement
patterns.description: A base warning class (SetuptoolsWarning) with a class-level emit() method that accepts a due_date tuple (year, month, day). If due_date has passed and SETUPTOOLS_ENFORCE_DEPRECATION env var is set, the warning is upgraded to an exception. The warning message automatically includes the due date, overdue status, and a URL for migration guidance. Subclasses (SetuptoolsDeprecationWarning) inherit this behavior without overriding emit().
patterns.rationale: Deprecations in widely-used libraries need a predictable enforcement timeline. A due_date makes the transition from warning to error automatic and date-driven, not manual. Users can prepare by filtering PYTHONWARNINGS by class, and CI can set SETUPTOOLS_ENFORCE_DEPRECATION to test readiness. The classmethod emit() keeps the call site clean (one-liner) while the formatting logic is centralized.

patterns.name: Correspondence table: declarative field-to-setter mapping via dict of callables
patterns.description: A module-level dict (PYPROJECT_CORRESPONDENCE) maps normalized config field names to either a callable (custom setter function) or a string (attribute name to setattr). apply() iterates config fields, looks up the correspondence, and either calls the function or does setattr. Separate dicts handle renames (TOOL_TABLE_RENAMES), removals (TOOL_TABLE_REMOVALS), and preprocessing (_PREPROCESS). This replaces a giant if/elif chain with a data-driven dispatch table.
patterns.rationale: Config translation between formats (pyproject.toml → distribution object) requires per-field handling logic. A dict of callables is the simplest data structure that supports both 'just set the attribute' (string value) and 'custom transform then set' (callable value). Adding a new field is a one-line dict entry, not a new branch in a function. Separating renames, removals, and preprocessors into different dicts makes the migration policy explicit and auditable.

patterns.name: Static wrapper types: inherit builtins to mark provenance and prevent mutation
patterns.description: A Static mixin class marks values as originating from config files (not dynamically computed). Subclasses (Str, List, Dict, Tuple) inherit from both Static and the builtin type, so they behave identically to the builtin but carry a _mutated_ flag. Mutation methods are wrapped to emit deprecation warnings and set _mutated_=True. is_static() checks both isinstance and !mutated. This lets the system detect when a plugin overwrites a static config value with a plain builtin.
patterns.rationale: Build systems need to distinguish 'value from config file' (static, should not change) from 'value computed at runtime' (dynamic, can change). Inheriting from builtins means existing code doesn't need to change — Static.List IS a list, just marked. The mutation guard catches accidental in-place modifications that would break PEP 643 (dynamic metadata). The is_static() predicate drives downstream behavior: static values are written to core metadata, dynamic values are left as placeholders.

patterns.name: Meta path finder for stdlib module replacement
patterns.description: A DistutilsMetaFinder registered in sys.meta_path intercepts imports of 'distutils' and redirects them to setuptools._distutils (a vendored copy). It uses find_spec() with per-module dispatch (spec_for_distutils, spec_for_pip, spec_for_sensitive_tests) to apply different policies: replace distutils everywhere except CPython build/test, suppress replacement under pip, and skip for sensitive stdlib tests. The finder self-disables by setting spec_for_distutils = lambda: None after a one-shot policy decision.
patterns.rationale: When a library needs to replace a stdlib module (distutils), it cannot simply monkey-patch — the import system must be intercepted at the finder level. sys.meta_path is the correct hook. Per-module dispatch allows nuanced policy: replace for normal users, but don't interfere with pip's bootstrapping or CPython's own test suite. Self-disabling (lambda: None) prevents repeated policy checks on every import. The shim() context manager makes the replacement scoped and reversible.

patterns.name: Static AST analysis to avoid executing untrusted code
patterns.description: StaticModule parses a Python file with ast.parse() and extracts module-level assignments via ast.literal_eval(), never executing the module. __getattr__ searches for matching ast.Name targets and literal_evals the assigned value. This is used to read version strings, author names, etc. from setup.py without importing it (which would execute arbitrary code). Only falls back to actual import if AST extraction fails.
patterns.rationale: Build tools must read metadata from setup.py, but setup.py can contain arbitrary code — importing it is a security risk. AST parsing + literal_eval extracts constant assignments safely. The fallback to import (only if AST fails) is explicitly marked as a security tradeoff. This pattern enables reading version = '1.0' from setup.py without running setup().

patterns.name: Monkey-patch with unpatched reference: reversible patching via attribute chain
patterns.description: patch_func() replaces a function in a target module and sets replacement.unpatched = original. get_unpatched() retrieves the original via candidate.unpatched. get_unpatched_class() walks the MRO to find the first non-setuptools base class, ensuring the original distutils class is used when setuptools patches are not desired. patch_all() monkeypatches distutils.core.Distribution, distutils.core.Command, distutils.core.Extension across multiple modules.
patterns.rationale: When extending a legacy library (distutils) by monkey-patching, you need (1) reversibility — get the original back, (2) idempotency — don't patch an already-patched class, (3) multi-module consistency — Distribution is referenced from distutils.dist, distutils.core, distutils.cmd. The unpatched attribute chain provides reversibility without a registry. The MRO walk detects double-patching. patch_all() centralizes all patches so the patch set is auditable.

patterns.name: Config directive expansion: file: and attr: string prefixes for deferred value loading
patterns.description: Config values in setup.cfg can use directives: 'file: VERSION.txt' reads the file content, 'attr: mypackage.__version__' reads a module attribute (via StaticModule AST analysis). The expansion functions (read_files, read_attr) are called during config application, not during parsing. This separates 'what the config says' from 'how to compute the value', allowing the same config format to reference external files or code without embedding their content.
patterns.rationale: Config files should be declarative but sometimes need to reference external state (version files, module attributes). Directives (file:, attr:) provide a mini-language for deferred loading: the config parser sees a string, the expansion layer resolves it to a value. This keeps config files DRY (version defined once in VERSION.txt, referenced from setup.cfg) while avoiding arbitrary code execution (attr: uses AST analysis first). The sandbox check (_assert_local) prevents file: from reading outside the project root.

patterns.name: Context manager patch: temporary class replacement for isolated execution
patterns.description: A classmethod @contextmanager patch() temporarily replaces a module-level class (distutils.core.Distribution) with a subclass for the duration of a with block, then restores the original in finally. This allows PEP 517 build functions to run with a modified Distribution class (that raises on setup_requires) without globally affecting the interpreter.
patterns.rationale: Build backends (PEP 517) need to modify global state (distutils.Distribution) only for the duration of a build operation. A context manager is the cleanest scope: patch on __enter__, restore on __exit__. Using finally ensures restoration even on exception. The classmethod form keeps the patch co-located with the class that needs patching, not in a separate utility module.

patterns.name: Layered validation: JSON Schema first, then extra rule functions as pipeline
patterns.description: Validation runs in two layers: (1) JSON Schema validation via compiled fastjsonschema, with custom format functions (trove-classifier, pep440 version, identifier) registered by name. (2) EXTRA_VALIDATIONS — a tuple of functions that each receive the data, apply rules hard to express in JSON Schema (e.g. 'field in dynamic must not also be static'), and return the data. All wrapped in detailed_errors() context manager for enhanced error messages.
patterns.rationale: JSON Schema handles structural validation (types, required fields, patterns) well but cannot express cross-field rules ('if field X is in dynamic, it must not appear as a static key'). Separating the two layers means the schema stays clean and machine-generated, while complex business rules live in readable Python functions. The reduce pipeline (reduce(lambda acc, fn: fn(acc), EXTRA_VALIDATIONS, data)) composes validators without a framework.

patterns.name: PEP 517 backend module: protocol functions as build interface
patterns.description: build_meta.py exports module-level functions (build_wheel, build_sdist, prepare_metadata_for_build_wheel, get_requires_for_build_wheel, etc.) that conform to PEP 517. These functions are the interface — a build frontend (pip, build) imports this module and calls the functions. Internally, they create a Distribution, run setuptools commands, and return results. A _ConfigSettingsTranslator class translates frontend config_settings into distutils command arguments.
patterns.rationale: PEP 517 defines a function-based build backend protocol: the frontend calls module-level functions, not methods on a class. This is the simplest possible interface — no instantiation, no inheritance, just import and call. The functions internally use the command pattern (distutils commands) but expose a clean functional API. _ConfigSettingsTranslator handles the impedance mismatch between PEP 517's config_settings dict and distutils's CLI-style arguments.

patterns.name: Version-conditional import compat modules
patterns.description: A compat/ package contains per-version modules (py39.py, py310.py, py311.py, py312.py). Each module imports stdlib features that were added in that Python version, providing fallbacks for earlier versions. The top-level __init__.py is empty — consumers import directly from the specific version module (e.g. from .compat.py310 import tomllib). This avoids runtime version checks scattered across the codebase.
patterns.rationale: Supporting multiple Python versions requires conditional imports (tomllib in 3.11+, add_note in 3.11+). Rather than scattering if sys.version_info checks, each compat module encapsulates the imports for its version. Consumers import from the lowest version module that provides the feature. This makes version support auditable (check which compat modules exist) and keeps business code clean of version checks.

patterns.name: Error re-export with inheritance: domain-specific errors on top of legacy hierarchy
patterns.description: setuptools/errors.py re-exports distutils error classes (ByteCompileError = _distutils_errors.DistutilsByteCompileError) for migration convenience, then defines new domain errors (InvalidConfigError, RemovedConfigError, RemovedCommandError, PackageDiscoveryError) that inherit from the legacy base. RemovedConfigError inherits from both OptionError (legacy) to maintain backward compatibility and from the distutils base. The module documents that re-exports exist to 'facilitate migration to PEP632' (distutils removal).
patterns.rationale: When a library wraps a legacy system (distutils), error handling must bridge both worlds. Re-exporting legacy errors means user code importing from setuptools.errors works without changes. New errors inherit from legacy bases so existing except clauses still catch them. RemovedCommandError multi-inherits (BaseError, RuntimeError) because removed commands should be catchable as both distutils errors and runtime errors — the dual inheritance is a deliberate compatibility decision.

patterns.name: Immutable mixin via method override to TypeError
patterns.description: Immutability is enforced not by wrapping or freezing, but by mixin classes that override every mutating method (__setitem__, __delitem__, pop, clear, append, etc.) to call _immutable_error() which raises TypeError. The mixin is combined with the base type via multiple inheritance: ImmutableList(ImmutableListMixin, list). This allows the same data structure to have mutable and immutable variants without duplicating the read API. Hashability is added via _hash_cache for memoization. __reduce_ex__ is overridden to ensure pickling reconstructs the correct type.
patterns.rationale: HTTP request data (headers, form data, args) should be immutable after parsing to prevent accidental mutation by middleware or view functions. But the parsing code needs mutable containers during construction. Mixin-based immutability lets the same class hierarchy serve both needs: mutable during parse, immutable when exposed. The TypeError-on-mutation approach gives immediate, clear feedback compared to silently ignoring writes.

patterns.name: Type-converting dict.get with callable type parameter
patterns.description: A dict subclass (TypeConversionDict) extends get() to accept a 'type' callable parameter. If provided, the value is passed through the callable (e.g. int, float); if the conversion raises ValueError or TypeError, the default is returned instead. This provides inline type coercion at access time without wrapping the dict in a separate adapter. Overloads are used to provide precise return type signatures for each combination of default and type parameters.
patterns.rationale: HTTP form/query data arrives as strings, but application code needs ints, floats, bools. Rather than forcing every call site to do try/except int(value), the dict itself handles coercion. Returning the default on conversion failure (rather than raising) matches HTTP semantics where missing/malformed data should be treated as 'not provided'.

patterns.name: State machine for URL routing with weighted transitions
patterns.description: URL routing is implemented as a state machine (StateMachineMatcher) where each URL rule is decomposed into RuleParts (static or dynamic), and each part becomes a transition in the state graph. Static transitions match literal path segments; dynamic transitions use converter regex patterns. Transitions are sorted by weight (static before dynamic, longer static matches first, lower converter weight first). Matching is recursive: try static transitions first, then dynamic ones in weight order. Slash redirect and merge-slashes are handled as special cases within the matching recursion.
patterns.rationale: A flat list of regex patterns (used by many routing systems) is O(n) in the number of rules. The state machine shares common prefixes, making matching O(depth) for static segments and only branching on dynamic ones. Weight-based ordering ensures the most specific rule wins without backtracking. The state machine is built once at bind time and reused for every request.

patterns.name: Converter protocol with weight-based priority and __init_subclass__ auto-config
patterns.description: URL converters implement a base class (BaseConverter) with: regex (what to match), weight (priority for ambiguous matches), part_isolating (whether the converter can match across path segments), to_python (string → Python value), to_url (Python value → URL string). __init_subclass__ auto-configures part_isolating based on whether the regex contains a slash — converters that match slashes are automatically non-isolating. The Map holds a registry of converter name → class, overridable per-map.
patterns.rationale: URL routing needs extensible type conversion (int, string, UUID, path, any). The converter protocol makes this extensible: new converters register by subclassing BaseConverter. Weight-based priority resolves ambiguity (e.g. /<int:id> vs /<string:name> for the same position — int wins because lower weight). The __init_subclass__ auto-config removes a common configuration error (forgetting to set part_isolating when the regex matches slashes).

patterns.name: Sans-IO core with IO adapter subclass
patterns.description: Request is split into a sans-IO base class (sansio/request.py) that contains all HTTP parsing logic (method, URL, headers, cookies, content type) with no dependency on WSGI or ASGI, and a WSGI-specific subclass (wrappers/request.py) that adds environ binding, stream access, and form parsing. The sans-IO class takes plain values (method, path, headers) as constructor args. The WSGI subclass takes environ and extracts those values. This allows the same parsing logic to serve both WSGI and ASGI.
patterns.rationale: Werkzeug supports both WSGI (synchronous) and ASGI (asynchronous) request handling. Duplicating all HTTP parsing logic for both specs would be a maintenance burden. The sans-IO pattern separates HTTP semantics (universal) from transport specifics (WSGI environ vs ASGI scope). Flask and other frameworks built on Werkzeug can use the sans-IO layer directly for custom transports.

occurrences.snippet:
class Request:
    """Represents the non-IO parts of a HTTP request, including the
    method, URL info, and headers.

    This class is not meant for general use. It should only be used when
    implementing WSGI, ASGI, or another HTTP application spec.
    """
    parameter_storage_class: type[MultiDict[str, t.Any]] = ImmutableMultiDict
    dict_storage_class: type[MultiDict[str, t.Any]] = ImmutableMultiDict
    list_storage_class: type[list[t.Any]] = ImmutableList
    user_agent_class: type[UserAgent] = UserAgent

# wrappers/request.py:
class Request(_SansIORequest):
    """Represents an incoming WSGI HTTP request, with headers and body
    taken from the WSGI environment."""
    def __init__(self, environ, populate_request=True, shallow=False):
        self.environ = environ

patterns.name: Exception as callable WSGI application
patterns.description: HTTPException subclasses (NotFound, BadRequest, etc.) are themselves WSGI applications. They implement __call__(environ, start_response) that renders an HTML error page and sends the appropriate status code. This means raising NotFound() in a view function is equivalent to returning a WSGI response — the exception IS the response. Each subclass declares code and description as class attributes. get_response() can also return a Response object for programmatic use. The exception hierarchy carries HTTP status semantics (code, name) as class-level attributes.
patterns.rationale: In HTTP, errors are responses, not just crashes. Making exceptions callable as WSGI apps means view code can use natural Python exception-raising (raise NotFound()) and the framework's catch-all handler simply calls the exception. This unifies error handling and response generation. Subclassing HTTPException lets middleware catch specific HTTP errors while letting other exceptions propagate.

patterns.name: Event-driven sans-IO parser with state machine
patterns.description: Multipart form parsing is implemented as a sans-IO state machine (MultipartDecoder). The decoder maintains a buffer and a State enum (PREAMBLE, PART, DATA_START, DATA, EPILOGUE, COMPLETE). receive_data(data) feeds bytes into the buffer. next_event() returns typed Event objects (Preamble, Field, File, Data, Epilogue, NeedData) depending on the current state and buffer content. The caller drives the loop: feed data, consume events, repeat until NEED_DATA or COMPLETE. No blocking I/O, no callbacks — the caller controls when to read and how much.
patterns.rationale: Multipart parsing is inherently streaming — files can be gigabytes. A sans-IO parser lets the caller decide how to feed data (from socket, from file, from memory) and how to handle events (write to disk, count parts, enforce limits). The state machine handles partial data across receive_data calls — a boundary split across two chunks is handled correctly. This same parser serves both WSGI (synchronous file reads) and ASGI (async receive) without modification.

patterns.name: Descriptor-based property access for dict-backed attributes
patterns.description: _DictAccessorProperty is a descriptor base class that maps attribute access on an object to key lookup on a dict the object holds. Subclasses override lookup() to specify which dict (environ for environ_property, headers for header_property). The descriptor supports: default value, load_func (type coercion callable), dump_func (serialization callable), and read_only flag. __get__ applies load_func with ValueError/TypeError fallback to default; __set__ applies dump_func. This eliminates boilerplate for every header/environ accessor.
patterns.rationale: Request and Response objects expose dozens of properties backed by environ dict or headers list. Without a descriptor, each property would need a getter that does dict.get + type conversion + error handling + a setter that serializes. _DictAccessorProperty factors this into a reusable descriptor, making each property a one-liner declaration (header_property('Content-Type', load_func=mimetype.parse) instead of a 10-line @property).

patterns.name: AST-based code generation for URL builders
patterns.description: Rule._compile_builder() generates Python source code for URL building as a string, then uses ast.parse + ast.walk to prefix all variable names with '.' (to avoid collision with user variables), then compiles and execs the code into a namespace. The generated function calls converter.to_url() for dynamic parts and urlencodes kwargs. The result is a bound method on the Rule instance. Two builders are compiled: _build (known args only) and _build_unknown (append unknown kwargs as query string).
patterns.rationale: URL building from rules is hot-path code (called for every redirect, link generation). Pre-compiling the builder at rule bind time means the per-request cost is just calling a function — no regex, no iteration over rule parts, no conditional branching. The AST name prefixing prevents user-provided variable names from shadowing the generated code's internal variables.

occurrences.snippet:
def _prefix_names(src: str, expected_type: type[_ASTT]) -> _ASTT:
    tree: ast.AST = ast.parse(src).body[0]
    if isinstance(tree, ast.Expr):
        tree = tree.value
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if isinstance(node, ast.Name):
            node.id = f".{node.id}"
    return tree

_CALL_CONVERTER_CODE_FMT = "self._converters[{elem!r}].to_url()"

# In Rule._compile_builder():
#   1. Generate Python source as string
#   2. Parse to AST, prefix all names with '.'
#   3. Compile and exec into namespace
#   4. Return the generated function
self._build = self._compile_builder(False).__get__(self, None)
self._build_unknown = self._compile_builder(True).__get__(self, None)

patterns.name: Pluggable storage class attributes for type customization
patterns.description: Request and Response classes declare class-level attributes that specify the types used for storage: parameter_storage_class, dict_storage_class, list_storage_class, user_agent_class. These are overridable by subclassing — a framework can set parameter_storage_class = ImmutableMultiDict (default, safe) or parameter_storage_class = dict (faster, loses multi-values). The class is used at parse time to construct the storage objects.
patterns.rationale: Different applications have different trade-offs for parsed data: some need multi-value support (form data with repeated keys), some prefer speed (single-value dict). Making storage types pluggable class attributes lets frameworks customize without reimplementing the parsing logic. The same pattern is used for user_agent_class (plug in a parser like ua-parser) without changing the Request API.

occurrences.snippet:
class Request:
    parameter_storage_class: type[MultiDict[str, t.Any]] = ImmutableMultiDict
    dict_storage_class: type[MultiDict[str, t.Any]] = ImmutableMultiDict
    list_storage_class: type[list[t.Any]] = ImmutableList
    user_agent_class: type[UserAgent] = UserAgent
    """The class used and returned by the user_agent property to
    parse the header. An extension can provide a subclass that uses
    a parser to provide other data."""

patterns.name: RuleFactory composition for URL rule grouping
patterns.description: URL rules are composed via RuleFactory subclasses: Submount (prefix all rules with a path), Subdomain (set subdomain on all rules), EndpointPrefix (prefix all endpoints), RuleTemplate (string template substitution). Each factory implements get_rules(map) -> Iterator[Rule], yielding modified copies. Factories can nest (Submount containing Subdomain containing Rules). Rule itself is a RuleFactory that yields itself. This enables declarative URL organization without string concatenation.
patterns.rationale: Large applications organize URLs hierarchically (blog under /blog, admin under /admin). String concatenation is error-prone and loses type safety. Factory composition lets developers declare URL structure declaratively: Submount('/blog', [Rule('/<slug>', endpoint='show')]). Nesting factories composes transformations (prefix path + prefix endpoint + set subdomain) in a readable, type-safe way.

patterns.name: UpdateDictMixin: on_update callback for mutation tracking
patterns.description: A dict mixin (UpdateDictMixin) that wraps every mutating method (setdefault, pop, update, __setitem__, __delitem__, clear) to call self.on_update(self) after the mutation. The on_update callback is a class-level attribute set to None by default. The wrapper uses functools.update_wrapper to preserve the original method's metadata. This enables caches, session stores, and other systems to detect when a dict they hold has been modified.
patterns.rationale: Session management needs to know when session data changes (to trigger a Set-Cookie response). Rather than requiring explicit session.save() calls after every modification, UpdateDictMixin automatically notifies the session manager. The callback receives the dict itself, not just a key — the manager can re-serialize the entire dict. This is the observer pattern applied at the data structure level.

patterns.name: Cached property with __slots__ support
patterns.description: cached_property is a property subclass that evaluates fget once, then caches the result. It supports __slots__ by using a configurable slot_name (_cache_{name}) as fallback when __dict__ is not available. __get__ checks __dict__ first, then slot_name. __set__ writes to __dict__ if available, else to slot_name. __delete__ clears the cache, forcing re-evaluation on next access. This allows lazy evaluation of expensive properties (form parsing, JSON body) while supporting memory-efficient __slots__ classes.
patterns.rationale: Request objects have many properties that are expensive to compute (JSON body parsing, form data parsing, accept header negotiation). Computing them eagerly on every request wastes CPU when most requests don't access all properties. cached_property defers computation to first access and memoizes. The __slots__ support is critical for Request objects that may be created thousands of times per second.

occurrences.snippet: from propcache.api import under_cached_property as reify

patterns.name: MultiDict: dict subclass with multi-value key semantics
patterns.description: MultiDict extends dict to store multiple values per key while preserving dict-like single-value access. Internally, values are stored as lists. __getitem__ returns the first value; getlist() returns all values. add() appends; setlist() replaces all. Construction accepts multiple input formats (dict, list of tuples, another MultiDict). __getstate__/__setstate__ serialize as lists for pickling. The class raises BadRequestKeyError (a KeyError + HTTP 400) for missing keys, bridging data access and HTTP error semantics.
patterns.rationale: HTTP form data can have multiple values per key (checkboxes, multi-selects). Standard dict drops all but the last value. MultiDict preserves all values while maintaining a familiar dict interface for the common case (single value per key). The BadRequestKeyError bridge means a missing form field automatically becomes a 400 response when caught by the HTTP exception handler.

patterns.name: Mimetype-dispatched parser selection
patterns.description: FormDataParser.parse() dispatches to different parsing methods based on mimetype: multipart/form-data → _parse_multipart, application/x-www-form-urlencoded → _parse_urlencoded, unknown → return empty. The dispatch is a simple if/elif on the mimetype string, with the mimetype extracted from Content-Type header (including options like boundary). The silent flag controls whether ValueError from parsing is caught (returning empty results) or propagated. The stream_factory callback lets callers control where file uploads are stored.
patterns.rationale: Form data comes in different formats (multipart for file uploads, urlencoded for simple forms). Each needs different parsing logic. Dispatching on mimetype keeps the parser selection logic in one place, while the individual parsers handle format-specific concerns. The silent flag provides graceful degradation — malformed data becomes empty form data instead of a crash, which is usually the right behavior for web servers.

patterns.name: Signature introspection for parameter-to-dependency mapping
patterns.description: At route registration time, FastAPI calls inspect.signature() on the endpoint function and walks each parameter. For each parameter, it examines the type annotation and default value to classify it: is it a path param, query param, header, cookie, body, or a sub-dependency (Depends)? The result is a Dependant tree — a recursive data structure of all parameters and sub-dependencies. At request time, solve_dependencies() walks this tree, resolves values from the request, validates them, and passes them as kwargs to the endpoint. The key insight: the function signature IS the declaration — there is no separate config file or decorator argument listing parameters.
patterns.rationale: Eliminates boilerplate by making the function signature the single source of truth for what a route needs. Parameters, their types, validation rules, and dependencies are all declared in one place. Adding a query parameter is just adding a function parameter with a type annotation. This is the same principle as scikit-learn's __init__-as-parameter-contract, applied to HTTP endpoints.

patterns.name: Depends as parameter-level dependency injection via default value
patterns.description: Depends is a frozen dataclass that marks a function parameter as a dependency. When used as a default value (def handler(db: Session = Depends(get_db))), it tells the framework to call get_db(), inject its return value as db, and cache the result per-request (use_cache=True). Dependencies can be nested: get_db can itself depend on get_config. The dependency tree is resolved recursively at request time, with results cached by callable identity. Depends can also be used inside Annotated (Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)]), and the framework detects which pattern is used.
patterns.rationale: Parameter-level DI via default values is the most Pythonic way to declare dependencies — no decorator stacking, no config files, no string keys. The function signature clearly shows what the endpoint needs. The frozen dataclass ensures immutability and hashability. Cache by callable identity means the same dependency called once per request is reused, avoiding duplicate work (e.g. one DB session per request).

patterns.name: Dependency override for testing via callable-keyed dict
patterns.description: The FastAPI app holds a dependency_overrides dict mapping {original_callable: replacement_callable}. At request time, solve_dependencies() checks if a sub-dependant's call is in the override dict. If so, it calls the replacement instead of the original, and rebuilds the dependant tree for the replacement function. This allows tests to swap expensive dependencies (database, external APIs) with mocks without modifying application code.
patterns.rationale: Testing web apps requires swapping dependencies (database, auth, external services) without touching application code. The callable-keyed dict approach is type-safe (no string matching), explicit (you see exactly which dependency is overridden), and zero-config (no test framework integration needed). The replacement callable is introspected the same way as the original, so it can have its own dependencies resolved.

patterns.name: Nested AsyncExitStack for scoped resource lifecycle in dependency tree
patterns.description: FastAPI maintains three nested AsyncExitStacks per request: (1) fastapi_middleware_astack (middleware-scoped, closes files after response), (2) fastapi_inner_astack (request-scoped, closes request-scoped generator dependencies), (3) fastapi_function_astack (function-scoped, closes function-scoped generator dependencies). Generator dependencies (def get_db(): yield session) are entered into the appropriate stack based on their scope. When the request completes, stacks unwind in reverse order, ensuring cleanup runs in correct scope order.
patterns.rationale: Dependencies with yield need guaranteed cleanup. A single ExitStack can't distinguish between a request-scoped and function-scoped resource — both need cleanup, but at different times. Three nested stacks ensure that function-scoped resources are cleaned up before request-scoped ones, and request-scoped before middleware-scoped. This prevents resource leaks when a function-scoped dependency holds a reference to a request-scoped one.

occurrences.snippet:
async def app(scope: Scope, receive: Receive, send: Send) -> None:
    async with AsyncExitStack() as request_stack:
        scope["fastapi_inner_astack"] = request_stack
        async with AsyncExitStack() as function_stack:
            scope["fastapi_function_astack"] = function_stack
            response = await f(request)
        await response(scope, receive, send)
        response_awaited = True

patterns.name: Callable security scheme: __call__ as request-time auth check
patterns.description: SecurityBase is a minimal base class (just model and scheme_name attributes). Concrete security schemes (HTTPBasic, HTTPBearer, OAuth2) are callables: __call__(self, request: Request) -> credentials | None. They're used as Depends() arguments: Depends(security), and the framework calls them at request time to extract and validate credentials. The scheme object is both the OpenAPI metadata holder (self.model) and the runtime auth checker (__call__). auto_error flag controls whether missing credentials raise HTTPException or return None for optional auth.
patterns.rationale: Combining OpenAPI metadata and runtime auth in a single callable object means there's one declaration per security scheme, not two. The __call__ protocol is the natural interface for 'extract and validate from request'. The auto_error flag supports optional auth (try multiple schemes, use the first that succeeds) without conditional logic in the endpoint.

patterns.name: DefaultPlaceholder sentinel for distinguishing 'unset' from 'falsy default'
patterns.description: FastAPI needs to distinguish between 'user explicitly set this to False/None/empty-string' and 'user didn't set this at all'. DefaultPlaceholder wraps a value and is truthy/falsy based on the wrapped value, but isinstance checks can detect it. The Default() function returns a DefaultPlaceholder, and get_value_or_default() extracts the value. Used for response_class, generate_unique_id_function, strict_content_type — all parameters where None or False are valid user choices.
patterns.rationale: Python's default parameter system can't distinguish 'not provided' from 'provided as None/False'. For framework config where None is a valid choice (e.g. response_class=None means 'use parent's'), the DefaultPlaceholder sentinel preserves the 'unset' signal through multiple layers of function calls and class inheritance. Unlike None, it carries the intended default value, so child code can fall back to it.

patterns.name: Router include context as composable config overlay
patterns.description: When APIRouter is included into an app or parent router, a _RouterIncludeContext dataclass is created that merges parent config (prefix, tags, dependencies, responses, callbacks, etc.) with the include-time overrides. The context can be combined (combine method) for nested includes. Each field uses get_value_or_default() to fall back from child to parent. The context is stored per-route, enabling OpenAPI generation to know the full effective config without walking the include chain at render time.
patterns.rationale: Router inclusion is recursive (router A includes B includes C). Without composable contexts, each route would need to walk the include chain at every access. By computing the merged context at include time, route config access is O(1). The per-field merge strategy (tags append, dependencies append, response_class falls back, include_in_schema ANDs) is explicit in the combine method.

occurrences.snippet:
@dataclass
class _RouterIncludeContext:
    included_router: "APIRouter"
    prefix: str = ""
    tags: list[str | Enum] = field(default_factory=list)
    dependencies: list[params.Depends] = field(default_factory=list)
    default_response_class: type[Response] | DefaultPlaceholder = field(
        default_factory=lambda: Default(JSONResponse))
    responses: dict[int | str, dict[str, Any]] = field(default_factory=dict)
    # ...

    def combine(self, child_context: "_RouterIncludeContext") -> "_RouterIncludeContext":
        return _RouterIncludeContext(
            included_router=child_context.included_router,
            prefix=self.prefix + child_context.prefix,
            tags=[*self.tags, *child_context.tags],
            dependencies=[*self.dependencies, *child_context.dependencies],
            default_response_class=get_value_or_default(
                child_context.default_response_class, self.default_response_class),
            responses={**self.responses, **child_context.responses},
            include_in_schema=self.include_in_schema and child_context.include_in_schema,
        )

patterns.name: Cached OpenAPI schema with routes-version invalidation
patterns.description: The openapi() method caches its result in self.openapi_schema. To detect when routes have changed (added, removed, or modified), it tracks self._openapi_routes_version — a version number incremented by _mark_routes_changed() whenever routes are modified. If the cached schema's version doesn't match, the schema is regenerated. This avoids regenerating the full OpenAPI spec on every /openapi.json request while ensuring it stays correct after route changes.
patterns.rationale: OpenAPI generation is expensive — it introspects every route's dependant tree, Pydantic models, and security schemes. Caching with version-based invalidation gives O(1) response time for repeated /openapi.json requests, with correctness guaranteed by tracking route mutations. The version counter is simpler and more reliable than deep equality checks on the route list.

occurrences.snippet:
def openapi(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
    routes_version = self.router._get_routes_version()
    if not self.openapi_schema or self._openapi_routes_version != routes_version:
        self.openapi_schema = get_openapi(
            title=self.title, version=self.version,
            openapi_version=self.openapi_version,
            summary=self.summary, description=self.description,
            routes=self.routes, webhooks=self.webhooks.routes,
            tags=self.openapi_tags, servers=self.servers, ...
        )
        self._openapi_routes_version = routes_version
    return self.openapi_schema

patterns.name: Protocol for duck-typed route-like objects (_APIRouteLike)
patterns.description: FastAPI defines _APIRouteLike as a Protocol listing all attributes that an APIRoute has (path, endpoint, stream_item_type, response_model, summary, etc.). The _populate_api_route_state function accepts any _APIRouteLike, allowing _EffectiveRouteContext (a dataclass that proxies route attributes) and APIRoute (the real route class) to share the same state initialization logic. The Protocol is structural — _EffectiveRouteContext doesn't inherit from APIRoute, it just has the same attributes.
patterns.rationale: When routers are included with overrides (prefix, tags, dependencies), the effective route config differs from the original. Rather than mutating the original APIRoute, FastAPI creates an _EffectiveRouteContext that shadows specific attributes. The Protocol ensures both the real route and the shadow context can be processed by the same initialization code, without inheritance coupling.

class _APIRouteLike(Protocol):

patterns.name: lru_cache on callable identity wrapper for classification
patterns.description: FastAPI needs to repeatedly classify callables as sync, async, generator, or async-generator. Direct classification (inspect.iscoroutinefunction etc.) is expensive when called per-request. The solution: _CallIdentity wraps a callable and uses id() for __hash__ and identity for __eq__. _is_gen_callable_cached wraps the classification in @lru_cache(maxsize=4096) keyed by _CallIdentity. The cache is keyed by object identity, not by the callable itself (which may not be hashable or may have unstable hash).
patterns.rationale: Callable classification (is this a coroutine function? a generator? an async generator?) involves inspect.unwrap, partial unwrapping, and __call__ attribute checks — expensive per-request. Caching by identity avoids re-inspection. Using _CallIdentity instead of the raw callable handles cases where the callable is a partial or a class instance with __call__ that isn't hashable. The 4096 limit bounds memory for long-running apps.

patterns.name: Validation error with endpoint context for actionable diagnostics
patterns.description: RequestValidationError and ResponseValidationError carry an EndpointContext TypedDict (function, path, file, line) extracted from the endpoint callable via inspect.getsourcefile/getsourcelines. The error's __str__ formats this as a Python traceback-style message: 'File "path/to/handler.py", line 42, in get_items\n  GET /items/{item_id}'. This gives developers the exact location of the failing endpoint without needing to enable debug mode or search logs.
patterns.rationale: Validation errors in web frameworks typically show field-level errors (which parameter failed) but not which endpoint handler is involved. When an app has hundreds of endpoints, knowing 'body.item_id failed validation' is useless without knowing which route. EndpointContext bridges this gap by attaching the source file and line number of the handler, extracted once at route registration and cached.

patterns.name: Streaming response with decoupled producer via memory stream
patterns.description: For SSE streaming endpoints, FastAPI creates a memory object stream (anyio.create_memory_object_stream). A producer task pulls items from the async generator and pushes to the send stream. A keepalive inserter task reads from the receive stream, inserting ping comments on timeout. The streaming response reads from the final receive stream. This decouples generator iteration from response sending, so anyio.fail_after wraps only the receive (not the generator's __anext__), avoiding CancelledError that would finalize the generator prematurely.
patterns.rationale: Wrapping a generator's __anext__ in a timeout causes CancelledError which triggers generator finalization (GeneratorExit), preventing cleanup. By decoupling via a memory stream, the timeout wraps only the stream receive, which can be cancelled without affecting the generator. The keepalive inserter ensures SSE connections stay alive during slow generation. This is a PEP 789 compliance pattern.

occurrences.snippet:
@asynccontextmanager
async def _sse_producer_cm() -> AsyncIterator[ObjectReceiveStream[bytes]]:
    send_stream, receive_stream = anyio.create_memory_object_stream[bytes](
        max_buffer_size=1)

    async def _producer() -> None:
        async with send_stream:
            async for raw_item in sse_aiter:
                await send_stream.send(_serialize_sse_item(raw_item))

    async def _keepalive_inserter() -> None:
        async with send_keepalive, receive_stream:
            try:
                while True:
                    try:
                        with anyio.fail_after(_PING_INTERVAL):
                                            data = await receive_stream.receive()
                        await send_keepalive.send(data)
                    except TimeoutError:
                        await send_keepalive.send(KEEPALIVE_COMMENT)
            except anyio.EndOfStream:
                pass

    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
        tg.start_soon(_producer)
        tg.start_soon(_keepalive_inserter)
        yield receive_keepalive
        tg.cancel_scope.cancel()

patterns.name: Graceful-shutdown signal deferral with LIFO replay and escalating force-exit
patterns.description: A context manager installs SIGINT/SIGTERM (and SIGBREAK on Windows) handlers that, instead of terminating immediately, set a graceful-exit flag (should_exit) and record the signal number. A second SIGINT while already exiting escalates to a force-exit flag (force_exit) that makes shutdown() skip waiting for in-flight tasks and cancel them. On context exit the original handlers are restored and every captured signal is re-raised in LIFO (last-received-first) order, so after the server finishes its own graceful teardown the process's default OS behavior for that signal (e.g. SIGTERM propagation to a parent supervisor) is still honored.
patterns.rationale: Lets the server complete an orderly shutdown (stop accepting, drain connections/tasks, run lifespan.shutdown) in response to an interrupt rather than being killed mid-flight, while still preserving the signal's original intent once teardown is done. The repeat-signal escalation gives the operator an escape hatch (second Ctrl+C forces immediate exit) without a separate command, and LIFO replay approximates the OS's natural nested-signal semantics.

patterns.name: Backend class registry: alias-to-dotted-path table with arbitrary-path passthrough and auto-detection probe entries
patterns.description: Each swappable backend (HTTP protocol, WebSocket protocol, event loop, lifespan) is selected from a single config string via a module-level dict mapping short aliases ("auto","h11","httptools","uvloop",...) to "module:attribute" dotted paths. At load() time the chosen value is resolved with import_from_string; an unknown string is passed through as a dotted path via dict.get(key, key) (so any importable "pkg.mod:Class" works with no code change), and a value that is already a class object is used directly. The "auto" alias points to a probe module that, at import time, tries to import the preferred optional dependency and falls back to a pure-Python implementation, binding one name to whichever is available (httptools->h11, websockets->wsproto->none, uvloop->asyncio).
patterns.rationale: Gives users one uniform knob per subsystem that accepts a built-in alias, a third-party dotted path, or "auto" for best-available detection, without the server hardcoding if/elif chains or entry-point machinery. New backends are pluggable by passing a dotted path; auto-detection picks the fastest installed implementation transparently. Distinct from entry-point registries (no importlib.metadata) and from plain optional-dependency suppression (the probe selects between full alternatives rather than tolerating absence).

patterns.name: Lifespan protocol bridge: linear-await lifecycle over event-driven app protocol via background task, receive-queue, and completion events
patterns.description: The server orchestrates startup/shutdown as two straight-line awaitable calls (await lifespan.startup(); ...serve...; await lifespan.shutdown()). Internally a background task runs the application's ASGI lifespan coroutine app(scope, receive, send); the orchestrator feeds it protocol events by putting messages on an asyncio.Queue (the receive callable) and waits on asyncio.Events that the send callback sets when the app emits startup/shutdown complete-or-failed. send() also asserts lifespan state-transition invariants. In "auto" mode an app that doesn't support lifespan (raises) is degraded to an informational log ("appears unsupported") rather than treated as fatal; "on" mode treats the same exception as an error.
patterns.rationale: Decouples the server's linear startup->serve->shutdown flow from the bidirectional event-based ASGI lifespan protocol, so server code reads as straight-line while still correctly driving the app's receive/send event loop. The auto-degradation lets uvicorn run apps that predate the lifespan protocol without failing startup. Distinct from sync->async BlockingPortal bridges (same loop, no thread/Future) and from guarded-sender wrappers (the core here is the queue+event+background-task adapter, not the guard).

occurrences.snippet:
async def startup(self) -> None:
        self.logger.info("Waiting for application startup.")
        loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
        main_lifespan_task = loop.create_task(self.main())  # noqa: F841
        startup_event: LifespanStartupEvent = {"type": "lifespan.startup"}
        await self.receive_queue.put(startup_event)
        await self.startup_event.wait()
        ...
    async def main(self) -> None:
        try:
            app = self.config.loaded_app
            scope: LifespanScope = {"type": "lifespan", "asgi": {...}, "state": self.state}
            await app(scope, self.receive, self.send)
        except BaseException as exc:
            self.error_occurred = True
            if self.config.lifespan == "auto":
                self.logger.info("ASGI 'lifespan' protocol appears unsupported.")
            else:
                self.logger.error("Exception in 'lifespan' protocol\n", exc_info=exc)
        finally:
            self.startup_event.set()
            self.shutdown_event.set()
    async def receive(self) -> LifespanReceiveMessage:
        return await self.receive_queue.get()

patterns.name: Verify-before-retire rolling worker restart with startup-failure abort
patterns.description: When restarting multiprocess workers (e.g. on SIGHUP), for each worker a brand-new child is started and health-checked (ping/pong over a multiprocessing Pipe until it reports server.started) BEFORE the old worker is terminated; the replacement is swapped into the pool only once ready. If the new worker fails to become ready within the healthcheck timeout it is killed and the incumbent is retained, aborting that restart. Separately, when a worker dies on its own, if its exit code equals the startup-failure code (broken app/TLS/socket bind that would fail identically every restart) the parent stops itself rather than endlessly respawning; only transient deaths trigger a replacement.
patterns.rationale: Avoids dropping traffic during restarts by never retiring a worker until its replacement is actually serving, and avoids a restart storm / livelock by refusing to respawn a worker whose failure is deterministic rather than transient. The startup-failure-abort decision prevents the supervisor from spinning on a misconfigured deployment.

patterns.name: Result-returning event bus with first-result-wins query emission
patterns.description: An event manager where emit() invokes all handlers in priority order and collects every return value into a list, while emit_firstresult() returns the first non-None result. Events thus serve a dual role: broadcast (collect-all) and query (first handler to produce a result wins). Handlers are tracked by integer listener IDs (strong references) and registered against named events; non-SphinxError exceptions from one handler are wrapped and isolated so dispatch continues.
patterns.rationale: Lets the core delegate resolution to arbitrary extensions without knowing them: the 'missing-reference' and 'warn-missing-reference' events become extensible resolution queries where the first capable handler wins, enabling cross-reference resolution by third-party extensions (e.g. intersphinx). Distinct from fire-and-forget weak-reference signals (P058) because handlers return values and the bus aggregates them.

patterns.name: Registry-mediated component transplantation into namespace instances
patterns.description: A central registry stores extension-contributed directives, roles, indices, and object types keyed by domain name, separately from the domain classes themselves. When a domain instance is created, the registry merges ('transplants') these contributed components into the instance via dict.update / list.extend. Domain.__init__ deliberately copies its class-level component dicts/lists to instance attributes so they can be mutated by this transplant step.
patterns.rationale: Allows extensions to add directives, roles, and object types to built-in domains (py, std, cpp, ...) without subclassing or modifying the domain class — open extension of an existing namespace. The registry holds the contributions; the domain instance absorbs them at construction, decoupling extension registration from domain class definitions.

patterns.name: Two-phase transform pipeline split at the cross-reference resolution boundary
patterns.description: Doctree transforms are split into two phases with a hard boundary at cross-reference resolution. 'transforms' run during reading (priority-ordered, before references are resolved) to build document structure. 'post_transforms' run after cross-reference resolution during writing, and each declares optional builders/formats tuples; is_supported() skips the transform when the active builder name or output format does not match.
patterns.rationale: Some transforms (reference resolution, image candidate selection, signature-node fallback) require resolved cross-references or builder-specific output, so they must run in a later phase. Splitting the pipeline around the resolution boundary keeps pre-resolution structure-building decoupled from post-resolution output-shaping, and the builder/format gating lets a post-transform target only relevant output formats.

patterns.name: Config option registry with per-option rebuild-invalidation metadata
patterns.description: Every config option is registered as an immutable _Opt(default, rebuild, valid_types, description) in a class-level config_values dict. The rebuild field declares what must be regenerated when the option changes: 'env' forces a full environment rebuild, 'html' only HTML output, '' nothing. At build time the old and new configs are compared, iterating only options whose rebuild scope is 'env'; if any changed value is found the environment is invalidated (CONFIG_CHANGED). Defaults may be callables receiving the config, and values resolve lazily via a CLI-override > conf.py > default precedence chain.
patterns.rationale: Ties each configuration value to the granularity of build work it invalidates, enabling incremental rebuilds that skip unchanged scopes instead of always rebuilding everything. The metadata is consumed directly by the build's config-status comparison. This is a config-schema-as-invalidations-map design specific to incremental build systems.

patterns.name: Cross-reference resolution chain: domain inventory, extension event, warning
patterns.description: Each pending cross-reference node is resolved by a fixed chain: (1) the target domain's resolve_xref looks up its own object inventory; (2) if None, the 'missing-reference' event is emitted first-result-wins so any extension can resolve it; (3) if still None, the 'warn-missing-reference' event (first-result-wins) may suppress the warning; otherwise a warning is logged. The 'any' role additionally queries every domain's resolve_any_xref and warns on ambiguous multi-match.
patterns.rationale: Makes cross-reference resolution extensible at every step: domains own their inventory resolution, extensions can intercept unresolved references (e.g. intersphinx resolving to external projects), and warning behavior is overridable. The chain-of-responsibility with event fallbacks lets new resolvers plug in without modifying the core resolver.

patterns.name: Parallel build via pickled-environment round-trip with per-domain merge protocol
patterns.description: For parallel reading, docnames are chunked across forked workers. Each worker reads its chunk against a copy of the shared environment, then pickles the whole environment back to the main process, which unpickles it and calls env.merge_info_from. That delegates to each domain's merge_domaindata(docnames, otherdata) to combine per-document inventory data namespace-by-namespace. Parallel execution is gated by every extension's parallel_read_safe/parallel_write_safe metadata; an undeclared or unsafe extension forces a conservative serial fallback.
patterns.rationale: Parallelizes the expensive read phase while keeping domain-specific state consistent through an explicit per-namespace merge protocol rather than shared memory or locks. The extension-declared concurrency-safety metadata lets the framework automatically degrade to serial builds when any loaded extension cannot tolerate parallelism.

patterns.name: Doctree-level translation by re-parsing translated messages into node fragments
patterns.description: Translation operates on the doctree, not the source. The Locale transform extracts translatable messages, looks up msgstr in the message catalog (merged across a fallback chain of catalogs), re-parses each translated string as reStructuredText into a doctree fragment via the parser (_publish_msgstr), then patches the original node with the fragment through a _NodeUpdater. It runs in two passes (reference-id remapping for titles/terms, then content replacement) and validates that cross-references in the translation match the original (compare_references).
patterns.rationale: Translated strings may contain markup and cross-references, so they must be re-parsed into structured nodes rather than string-substituted. Operating on the doctree preserves document structure while allowing rich translations, and the reference-consistency check warns when a translator's markup introduces mismatched references.

class Locale(SphinxTransform):

            msgstr = merged.get(msg, '')        # merged catalog w/ fallback chain
            ...
            patch = _publish_msgstr(msgstr, source, node.line,

patterns.name: Final-locked template-method build pipeline with phase enum
patterns.description: The Builder defines the build lifecycle (build -> read -> consistency-check -> write -> finish) and marks every orchestration method (build, build_all, build_update, read, read_doc, write, write_doctree) with @final, preventing subclasses from altering the pipeline shape. Format-specific builders customize only via overridable stage hooks (init, get_outdated_docs, prepare_writing, write_doc, finish, get_target_uri). A BuildPhase IntEnum is assigned at each transition so the current phase is observable.
patterns.rationale: Locks the build contract so output-format builders (HTML, LaTeX, text, ...) can plug in only at defined hook points, guaranteeing lifecycle order and phase invariants while allowing format-specific output customization. The @final boundary separates unchangeable orchestration from extensible stages.
